When builders show the country seat, Old, picturesque, of easy access, Of lowest rent and trifling taxes, And point its prospect, fair and sweet, O'er fertile meads and smiling plains: Then, then's the time to look for "drains." ' PICKING OUT A HUSBAND,—CapeIIa and Ivens, in their recent two years' exploration in Central Africa, made a matrimonial match in a novel and expeditious way. They I had in their caravan the young widow of one of their car- riers who died on the march. Capella observed one day that the girl was looking very forlorn and dejected. He asked her if she'd like to marry again. She said she had no objections. That afternoon, when they halted for the day, the explorer announced to the 50 or 60 carriers, "The nice young widow whom we have with us says she is willing to marry again Now, all you men who have no wives, and who would like to have her for a wife, fall in line." The white men were highly amused to see every unmarried car- rier in the camp fall into line with alacrity. "Now, ray girl," said Capella, " make your choice carefully, and be sure and pick out the man you like best." The girl walked down the line, and the explorers say it was highly divert- ing to see the solemn and anxious aspects of most of the men as she looked them over and deliberated on her choice. NOT A MAN FOR A' THAT. "A man's a man," says Robert Burns, "For a' that and a' that," En: though the song be clear and strong It lacks a note for a' that: The lout who'd shirk his daily work, Yet claim his wage and a' that, Or beg when he can earn his bread, II not a man for a' that. If all who dine on homely fare Were true and brave, and a' that: An I none whose garb is " hodden grey, WAR fool and knave, and a' that: The vice and crime that shame our time Would fade and fall and a' that; And ploughmen be as good as kings, And churls as earls for a' that. , Yon see you brawny, blustering sot, Who swaggers, swears, and a' that, And thinks, because his strong right an' Might fell an ox, ani a' that, That he's as noble, man for man, As duke or lord, and a' that, He's but a brute, beyond dispute, And not a man for a' that.

A man may own a large estate, Have palace, park, and a' that; And not for birth, but honest worth Be thrice a man for a' that, An 1 Donald herding on the muir, Who beats his wife and a' that, Be nothing hut a rascal boor, Nor half a man for a' that. It comes to this, dear Robert Barns, The truth is old, and a' that, "Tail rank is but the guinea's stamp, The man's the gowd for a' that." And though you put the minted man On copper, brass, and a' that, The lie is gross, the cheat is plain, And will not pass for a' that. For a' that and a' that, 'Tis soul and heart, and a' that, That makes the king a gentleman, And not his crown and a' that. A mart with man, if rich or poor, The best is he, for a' that, Who stands erect in self-respect, Ant acts the man for a' that.

• CULTKRb At Malton, recently, a groom had to pay £2, the fine and coats, for '"gingering" a horse at a show, a cruel and un- necturary.practice. A very. unusual and interesting sight was witnessed at Coxhoe on the 21st and 22nd ult. Three old men, whose ages made the respectable total of 230 years, and whose re- spective ages were 70, 76, and 84, were hard at work cutting a field of wheat belonging to Mr. Toulson. An extraordinary death is reported from Carnebane, co. Donegal. A young man named Nicholas had been out feed- ing a young horse. Nicholas, who was learning to play on a fife, tied the horses reins around his body in order to dis- engage his hands, and began playing. The horse got fright- ened and ran away. The young man was dragged a quarter of a mile, and when found life was extinct. FEEDING WHEAT TO STOCK.—A correspondent writes:— "I have decided to feed all my wheat to the pigs. Lucky landlord! He will reap where he did not sow." That will be nothing out of the common; landlords are used to that kind of harvesting. But my friend may easily avoid losing his claim to compensation under the Agricultural Holdings Act. If he feeds stock with his own wheat he will have no claim; but if he agrees with a neighbour so that each can sell to the other a certain weight of wheat at the same price, they can exchange wheat, cheques, and receipts, and each claim for consuming purchased feeding stuff.

ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY'S B-HOWS AND THE BEE DEPARTMENT.—It having been recently stated that the management of the bee department of the Royal Agricul- tural Shows is a failure under the present arrangements' and that it should, therefore, be handed over to the County Bee- keepers' Association, the Rev. Herbert R. Peel placed him- self in communication with Mr. H. M. Jenkins, the secre- tary of the Royal Agricultural Society,ann has now received from that gentleman a reply stating that the Council "have always expressed themselves as perfectly satisfied with the manner in which their bee department has hitherto been managed by the British Bee-keepers' Association, and that they have never notified any desire to transfer the manage- ment of the bee department of the show to any other society." _ _ . . . . .

Times Law.—An American paper says that when Colorado cattle men qaarantine " against Texas fever, they do it in earnest. A herd of 2,000 head from the suspected dis- trict was stopped at Pueblo the other day by moral suasion ' and the exhibition of a quantity of fire-arms, and then those concerned met and adopted a practical resolution thus: "It is the sense of this meeting that all parties controlling such herds be notified that they will not be permitted to enter oar county until after a heavy host shall have pre- vailed. Further, Carl Stanley is hereby delegated to recruit and equip a force sufficient to carry out the foregoing reso- lution, and intercept any and all such herds." They have a rare good sort of local authority in Texas, according to the above and they take the right course to prevent inconsisten- cies of action.

A DEFECT OF THE GROUND OAHE ACT —A case showing the grievance of tenants who hold farms on which the shooting is let under an agreement current when the Ground Game Act was passed, was tried the other day at Tadcaster, Yorkshire. The landlord, Sir F. Milner, let the shooting on his estate to Mr. W. B. Denison for fourteen years from December l2Bth, 1877, so that until the end of 1891 the Ground Game Act will be of no avail to the tenants on the estate. One of them, Mr. Brewster, exasperated at the damage done to his crops, openly killed a hare under the eyes of the gamekeeper, and was summoned and fined. Of course, he was legally wrong, but not half so guilty as our legislators were when they insisted that current sporting leases shoald annul the provisions of the Ground Game Act. I Secier-Memt CHEESE.—A Mr. Lindbach, an Indiana farmer, who has had twelve years' experience in dairy work in Nor- way, has revolutionised the system of cheese-making in the district in whith he has settled. Ile uses quite sweet skimmed milk, which is heated to from 76 to 80 deg. Fahr , when he adds rennet sufficient to curd the milk in ten mintt,es, and in half an hoar it is firm enough to be cat. In cold weather he adds butter-milk to the skim-milk, and heats the latter to a little higher temperature, so that when the cold buttermailk is added it will be about right. The second time the mixture is heated it is raised to 89 deg. in winter and to 95 deg. in summer. The whole of the whey is drawn off before any acid is developed in the curd, and the latter its kept from packing together by continued stir- ring. It is got into the press entirely free from acid at 70 deg., and cured in a room which is rather moist than dry in temperature. The ventilation is perfect, and the tempera. ture is kept between 40 and 50 deg., the latter never being exceeded. Efe is very particular upon this point, and also upon the quality of the rennet, so that it shall act almost to the minute. An objection has been raised to the system that the cheese will sour when the temperature of the weather is higher than 50 deg., and consequently it is neces- sary that it should be kept in a cold room in the same way that batter is kept when it is requisite to retain its solidity. If, however, a good cheese can be made by this system from skim-milk, we should say put up with the temperature, for it would matter little if it could be maintained until sold for retail, as in the usual way shopkeepers do not keep chee.e very long in their stores. FEEDINCF GRAIN TO HORSES..—The capacity of the horse's stomach is about 16 quarto. this fact should be borne in mind by those who have charge of horses. In feeding grain to horses, it is important that it should be fed at such a time that it may remain in the stomach as long as need be to secure its complete digestion. The nitro- genous elements, in which grain is richer than other foods, , are better digested in the stomach than in the intettines. The grain should be fed after the hay has been eaten, and no other food or drink should be given for some time after, so that the grain may remain in the stomach until it is fully digested. If the grain is fed first, and then a ration as, for instance of seven pounds of hay, the grain will speedily be forced from the stomach by the hay. In eating the hay, it will be mixed with four times its weight of saliva, and an hour and a half will be required for masti- cating it. In ordet to have the stomach digest well, it should not contain more than ten quarts at a time, and in eating seven pounds of hay, the animal swallows at least two stomachic:de of hay and saliva, one of those having pained on into the intestines. If the grain had been fed first, before the hay, the grain would have speedily passed out of the stomach into the intestines, where it will digest less completely than if allowed to remain in the stomach. It is the office of the stomach to digest the nitrogenous parts of the food, and as oats or corn contain four or five times as much of these as the same amount of hay, it is obviously more important to have the grain subjected to the full action of the gastric juices than to have the hay re- tained there. Hence in feeding grain it should be fed after the hay ration has been eaten. This is a matter well worth remembering in feeding horses. THE Aanictmetree OUTLOOK.—A Manchester Guardian correspondent writes :—The change which has taken place within the last few hours comes with a hearty welcome, though wind is wanted to help the ingathering of the valu. able crops which are still lying in the fields. The weather for the last few days has been most unfortunate. If rain had kept off for ten days longer, there would have been com- paratively little grain left in the fields. The heat and damp have been favourable for the growth of grass, and espe- cially for eddish, and it has been very welcome to dry arid soils, which required further moisture to reach the roots. A further change has overtaken the potatoes, which are fast dying down in the tops. Champions, which are amongst the last to retain a fresh colour of haulm, have yielded to the advance of the season, and in another week, if the weather should continue dry, we shall witness a still more decided falling away of the haulms. Although we have had several nights of mild dampness calculated to encourage the disease, I hear very little in the nature of complaints. A few tubers are found which have gone off with the soft rot, but this is attributed to the heat which prevailed a few weeks back, and instances of this form of rot are very rare indeed. It is expected that the tubers will advance rapidly in size. From inquiries made of diggers at work in the field in various parts of the county, I have received very satisfac- tory reports both as to the weight of yield, soundness, and absence qf any great number of "chats." I have seen some splendid specimens. Digging is becoming more general, and will soon be in full swing among the stock crops. Bean cat- thig has been entered upon, and a few dry days will bring ready for reaping some of the finest beans that I have seen for years past. Farmers in the later districts, such as on the moss grounds where most of our Lancashire oat crops are grown, and near the coast, express their fears to me that oats will not " aware" so well as was thought when cutting commenced. It is feared that the great heat which pre- vailed several weeks back ripened the grain too rapidly, and instead of the grain developing as it otherwise might have done, it has been dried up and limited in size. I do not hear the same complaints with regard to wheat and barley. I have passed some splendid fields of tur- nips during the weeks, the roots being of extraordinary size, and still growing nicely. In spite of the unfor- tunate drought in May, there are many Lancashire and Cheshire farmers who will have very fine crops of this class of winter food. I venture to predict that with the present year's experience it will be long before the turnip ceases to be a field Crop with our local agriculturists. The quantity of grass upon the land is not so great as I anticipited it would be for "back-end" pasturage, but it is improving, and eddish, which is an excellent crop on the early meadows, is now growing on the later cut land. There is not that amount of eddish hay being made that I have often seen; this is due doubtless to the scarcity caused by the great heat. Cattle everywhere are looking well, and it is antici- pated that prices will go up a little. Pig breeding, which has not been ao very profitable during the summer, is more promising, and higher prices are anticipated very shortly. Those farmers who have combined willows in their list of crops are likely to be well satisfied with the year's growth, the yield where proper care of the ground has been shown being likely to be unusually good and remunerative. Con- sidering the favourable situations there are for willow beds it is rather astonishing that more of the better classes of willo we are not grown. There are many places in which the ozier would grow profitably which are either totally neg. lected or left to produce a very small quantity of poor her- bage. It is not necessary that the ground should be below the flood-line, as is too often erroneously supposed. More- over, the work required to be done in the ozier beds could be done at a time when some of the farmers are not forced to do other work. Some farmers who are more advanced with their harvest are busy dubbing hedges, and it is astonishing how long it takes some of them to acquire the simple art of hedge cutting; I do not mean slashing, but cutting in a neat and presentable way. Nothing adds more to the appear- ance of the farmsteads than neatly cut hedges, and it is with pleasure that I see that some of the local ploughing societies offer prizes for hedge cutting. A little more en- couragement in this particular is much needed.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 20. 1884 Si.

AN ABSURD GROUND GAME CASE—Lord Kinnaird ap- plied to the High Court of Justice, through Mr. Warring. ton, Q.C., last week, for an injunction to restrain a tenant from killing ground game on a farm belonging to him in Norfolk. The farm was let in 1871 for a year, and there- after from year to year, with six months' notice to quit. It was, therefore, as clearly a yearly tenancy within the meaning of the Ground Game Act as any tenancy could possibly be, yet there was a long argument on the point, and Mr. Justice Wills was full of hesitation about it. Ulti- mately he refused the application for an injunction; so Lord Kinnaird is floored in his monstrous attempt to annul the Act. _ .

Vicious BuLiz —lt is strange how few persons know how to deal with a vicous bull. Some allow such animals to go unrung until they are too big to be properly handled, while others are unable to manage them properly when they are rung, and it is only here and there that a stockman if found who is master of the business, and who has the requisite amount of pluck to carry his knowledge into execution. A bull retained for serving cows, if at all vicious, should have a pen 30f I. by dot t. in size, and this should be protected by boards naled on the inside so strongly that he cannot break them. In one cornet should be a stall sufficiently large for him to turn round in, and at the feeding end a hole should be made some 18in. square, through which he can feed, so that the attendant need not enterany more than is necessary. Cows can be turned into the yard, while the bull can be kept at his distance by the aid of a whip. Unless a bull is inva- riably loose in a pen of this kind, he should always be on the chain. For instance, when in his stall he should have a chain round his neck, and he will submit to this with readi- ness if he has been properly trained to it. Before loosing his chain to take him out, the staff should be attached to the ring of his nose, by which means he will be always under control. If very unruly, a man should be at either side of him, holding a staff on to the ring. There is, however, another way, which is adopted in America, which will render him perfectly harmless. A snrcingle is fastened round his waist, and thenv. three-quarter inch rope attached to his nose ring, passed between the horns, under the surcingle, and then round the tail, as in the crupper of a horse. This rope must be kept between the horns by means of a cord tied to the horns themselve. In handling the bull, the rope should be, pulled tight until his nose is lifted as high as the level of his back, and then he will be quite within the power of the herdsman. There is little fear of his being hurt, and indeed no man dealing with a bull should be afraid of him, because it Ic the only means of keeping him from doing damaeo. If he is too gently dealt with, the chances are that he will have no mercy upon his kind-hearted attendant. AN APPIX FARM IN NEW ZEALAND.—The Apple Farm Company, Limited, East Tamaki, was formed with a capital of £lO,OOO in 20,000 shares of 103. each. Fifteen thousand of these have been taken up by the present shareholders, and the balance are held in reserve. The farm taken over by the company, at a price of £25 per acre, con4sts of 226 acres on the east bank of the Tamaki River, being lot 43 and part of lots 42 and 46, Parish of Pakuranga. It is firet-class agricultural land, fenced, drained, and well cultivated. The soil is semi-volcanic principally, and in places purely so. There does not appear to be a dozen acres of secondary character in the block. The land is almost wholly level, but in some portions consists of gentle undulations. As showing the character of the soil, it may be mentioned that in September last a portion of the land was seeded down to grass, and about three.quarters of a bushel of oats to the acre sown with it, from which a wholly unexpected return of two tons to the acre of oaten hay has been reaped, and the take of grass, as now seen after reaping, unexceptionally good. In a paddock adjoining, the sixth consecutive crop of wheat has been reaped, which runs 40 bushels to the acre, and this almost without any artificial manure. About 90 acres of the farm have been planted out with apple trees. The trees selected were the pick of the local nurseries, being as fine an assortment as could be secured under the most favourable condition, the price averaging about 9d. each, ages ranging from one to five years, principally two years old. Forty-seven thousand trees were planted out last season, being one of the most extensive undertakings of the kind in the colonies. The planting was done at a cost of 4s. 6d. per one hundred trees, which is stated to be cheaper than it is done either in England or America. Planting operations were commenced in the third week in , August last, and finished in three weeks. Mr. Perry has planted three hundred acres in orchards in different parts of the colony. The trees are planted on the quincunx system, ten feet apart each way. It is pro- posed hereafter to remove all the ten-foot trees round the selected permanent trees (which will remain 17 feet apart every way), and replant them in other portions of the f arm. The ground has been kept well cultivated between the trees with disc-harrows and cultivators. None of the trees, which are seven and eight feet high, have been staked, and owing to the thorough cultivation of the land they have not been hurtfully shaken by the boisterous weather experienced during the past season. The outcome of this practice has conclusively. shown that this is the most judi- cious method by which to realise the most profitable re- sults. The orchard is not wholly artificially sheltered yet, but this has been partly done by planting the b st shelter trees, principally pions insignis, and will be com- pleted. We saw a specimen apple, of the Lord Suffield variety, weighing over Alba grown from a fruit bud put on last year—an incident of unusual occurrence. Some speci- mens of the fruit which we saw were all that could be desired as to size and quality. Fifty acres additional will be planted with apple trees during the coming season. The whole of the land among the trees will also be utilised in cropping, oaten hay and potatoes principally. A large portion of the land will this month be seeded down to grass, and in the course of four or five years will be in splendid order to receive the first thinning out of the trees planted 10 feet apart, which will then have borne a quantity of , fruit, and far more than paid all the expenses connected I with their "planting. The bulk of the varieties planted are • thoroughly blight proof, having been worked on Northern • Spy and Majetin stocks. A number of the varieties, noted as early bearers, have been selected, so as to secure an imme- diate return on the capital invested. The company's opera- tions will not necessarily be confined to the apple grow- ing, but oranges and lemons will also be grown on the sec- • tions which are specially suited for that purpose. The farm , has a deep water frontage to the Tamaki river, and there is • a pier and landing to which vessels can come, freight charges to and from Auckland averaging 3s. per ton.
TO WHAT EXTENT IS THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT ADOPTED?

The Mark Lane Express says there i$ a strange misap- prehension of the bearing of the Agricultural Holdings Act, 1883. Many appear to have confounded " adoption " with "operation." No doubt the Act may be, and is, adopted in many districts where it has not yet operated. But apart from this there is a much more general misapprehension as to the power of the Act, it being not clearly understood that where nothing has been done to set aside the compensa- tion provisions of the Act, those provisions will apply. "Every occupier under a tenancy current on the lot Janu- ary, 1884, who has not signed a special agreement providing fair and reasonable compensation' for improvements of the first class, will be entitled to claim compensation for any of them which he may have made since January, 1874, unless be is entitled to be paid for them under his contract, custom, or under the Agricultural Holdings Act of 1875. And here it is important to point out that if, under agree- ment, the custom of the country, or the Act of 1875, he is entitled to compensation for only a portion of the im- provements named in the 3rd part of the same schedule, he may claim for the rest under the Act of 1883. With respect to improvements of the first and second class (those named in the first and second parts of the first sche- dule) made between January Ist, 1874, and January let, 1834, tenants will not be able to claim any compensa- tion 'ander the new Act, unless during tbe present year they shall have obtained the written consent of their landlords, and then only for such improvements as cannot be claimed for under agreement, custom, or the Act of 1875. We do not suppose that it will be of any use for a tenant to ask his landlord for the written consent referred to, in relation to permanent improvements made before the commencement of the Act; but if any tenant thinks it worth while to' try it on,' he is reminded that he has not much time to lose. It is, however, improvements which, for shortness, we refer to as those of the third class, that occupiers under current tenancies are most concerned with; and it is very import- ant to assure such tenants that they are entitled to claim as above described. Those who are about to quit at Michael- mas should pay particular attention to this point. It may be too late, however, unless they gave notice of their intention to claim two months before the data when they will quit." Where a "current tenancy" is a lease which has yet some years to run, there is a time for the landlord to try to in- duce the tenant to adopt some agreement in substitution for compensation under the Act; but we advise leaseholders to refuse to sign unless they can make terms at least as good as those which are embodied in the Act. In several instances tenants have refused to sign such agreements when their landlords have endeavoured to force them to do so. Re- specting "current tenancy" and "future tenancy," it may be pointed out that in the case of a Michaelmas entry, if the term of notice agreed to was six months, a current yearly tenancy becomes a future tenancy next Michaelmas; but if a year's notice was required, as it was nnlesa the shorter term had been agreed to in writing by both parties, the tenancy will not be deemed a future tenancy till Michael- mas, 1855. In the case of a Lady Day entry, a current tenancy will become a future tenancy on Lady Day, 1885. Landlords, then, have in some cases till Lady Day, 1885, and in others till Michaelmas, 1885, before they need bestir themselves to endeavour to substitute agreements for such advantages as their tenants will be able to claim as occu- piers of future tenancies under the Act. From enquiries made in the counties of England and Wales, it is agreeably surprising to learn the extent to which the Act has been accepted up to the present. Probably many landlords are consoled by the belief that the scales of compensation agreed to by local Chambers of Agriculture and other bodiee will be adopted by valuers as the bases for estimating the I value of improvements to incoming tenants. It should, however, be borne in mind that the adoption of such scales is purely optional, and the tenants may choose valuers who I will not be bound by such limitations.

, ready. point of strength and durability he affirms that lhand-spun is better than machine-spun thread, and storage hancleyroven'than machine-woven linen. This advantage e-- he claims, even for the ruder work of those who have not long learned to spin and to weave; and whatever may be the case with weaving, spinning is an art which, in order to approach perfection in it, the worker should begin to prac- tise in early childhood. In England the art is nearly lost. One very old daleswoman Mr. Fleming found who recollected how to spin. From her he had procured teaching for other women, and as they have learned he has supplied them with spinning wheels and taken the produce of their labour at specified prices. It is impossible that within the few months during which Mr. Flezning's spinsters have been at their new work a very high standard of quality can have been attained. Ido not know how their thread would com- pare with what is produced by your great flax spinners; but if it is yet far inferior in firmness and evenness, that cannot, of course, be treated as inconsistent with Mr. Fleming's second proposition, which is that finer thread and muslin can be produced by hand than by machines. In sup• port of this assertion, he points to the products of the Indian spinsters and weavers—the muslins of Dacca—woven air, as some of it is called, which, he says, is far finer than any pro- duct of English machinery. Finer still is some of the Egyp- tian mummy cloth. In some of it there are 280 threads in the square inch. These are all the work of the spinning wheel, or of the distaff alone and of the hand-loom. In his bleaching operations, again, Mr. Fleming claims superiority to those of•famons dyeworks. In the dyeing conducted" on a large scale, chemical preparations are said to be used which save time and money at the cost of the strength of the whitened fabric. In every one of his three stages, therefore, Mr. Fleming claims to do his proposed work better in point of strength and durability than machinery and the cheaper than dyeing works can do it; and he believes that hereafter a superiority in fineness ,of manutacture can be attained. By the kindness of Mr. Fleming, and of Miss Twelves, a who superintends the work at Sc. Martin's Home, I have been permitted to see the experiment above described in operation. How far the ideas of the energetic and philan- thropic founder may be sound I am not competent to judge; but all, I think, mast admit that the experiment is an interesting one, and not even those concerned in spinning and weaving by machinery can wish that it should not suc- ceed. Its success would not affect appreciably the market of the millowner, while it would increase the income of many a poor country family, slightly arrest the depopula- tion of the rural districts in which the industry might flourish, and give to those who chose to pay the higher price necessary the stronger and more durable, and perhaps hereafter the finer, goods which the hand spinners and the hand weavers may, when more highly skilled, be able to produce.—Leeds Mercury Cor. COTTAGE GA RDENING. CABBAGE.—This is an important crop in the cottager' garden, but the present Beason has been a very trying one to the production of good early plants. The seeds might have been timely sown, but for want of rain they made so little progress that they might as well have been left in the seed bag. Many that were fortunate enough to get the seeds to vegetate, and the young plants nicely above ground, found them in a few days perforated by the turnip fly to such an extent as to reduce the leaves to mere skeletons. Those who may have been so fortunate as to escape such ill luck should have plants now sufficiently strong to plant out in the rows. Oars are just in that condition, and those from the second sowing will be ready three weeks hence. It is customary to plant them two feet between the rows, and the same distance from plant to plant. We practised this for a time, as we had never seen or heard of any different rule. It is quite correct where room is abundant. Once our position was the reverse of this, and we could not find space to plant out some lettuce until we fixed on the cab- bage rows and planted them alternately, with most satis- factory results. As we could not any longer see why a plant only requiring about four inches of space should re- ceive 24 inches for more than six months, we determined to reduce it to one•half by planting cabbage 12 inches distant each way, and in the spring, as soon as the plants touch each other in the row, the most forward are tied up rather loosely, and this admits air amongst the others. Those tied up, if anything, make greater progress, and in a fortnight will be ready for use, and fresh ones tied up, the same strung usually serving the purpose three or four times. It will be apparent that by this method we double the produce, and by tying the plants they are ready for use a fortnight ear- lier, which is an important consideration in the introduc- tion of early crops into the market, and if that is to be the destiny of the early cabbage, the ties should remain on them, as it protects the inner leaves from being bruised. The ground should be well trenched and manured for early cabbage, and, failing this, the next best place is the piece of ground that has been occupied by onions. Some growers invariably wait for this to be vacant before planting, and without any more preparation than clearing the surface, the plants are put in, and they succeed very well, because the Onion bed has been recently trenched and manured. HEDGES.—Where the garden is surrounded by a thorn hedge, the present will be a suitable time to cut it down, so as to improve the base, or trim the top to preserve it in nice form. Tam FRONT Crannmsr.—Where this is only furnished with what are termed bedding plants, it will soon wear a dismal appearance, and where cottagers are in the habit of purchasing such transitory subjects, we should consider it a better plan to spend the money on perennials. CLEMATIS.—What splendid objects these are to decorate the walls of dwellings, and if proof were needed, it was sup- plied a week or two back on the front of Mr. Goulding's residence at Leyland, which was covered with Clematis Jackmanii, which has flowers of intense violet purple, from 4in. to sin, across, which were almost as numerous as the bricks in the wall they covered. We have this year seen several cottages adorned with them; but in most instances such dwellings appeared to be connected with an adjoining estate, and the plants had no doubt been supplied by the owner, and their planting superintended by his head gar- dener. A tolerably accurate estimate may be formed of the character and disposition of employers from the appearance of the dwellings they supply their workmen with. We are alluding here to rural districts, where many a working man is as ill off for a little land for a garden as if he resided in the centre of a crowded town. Those of his class in towns are in some respects much better off, for they as a rule have a decent pavement in front; but the country workman's first step from his house is frequently into the gutter that passes the front of his dwelling, which is a source of offen- sive smells, the result of sundry accumulations of filth, which have been washed by the rain, and finally resting in the vicinity of the cottage, or in front of his door. TNE WlNDOW.—Fuchsias —As illustrating the advantage of placing these plants outside as we have frequently sag- guested in this column, we may mention that the finest Plant at the Hoghton Cottagers' Show had been placed in the open air for some weeks previous to the show. Its healthy appearance and unusual dimensions for a window plant in- dicated that it had not been for any length of time in con- finement. Ba/sanns —At the same show were most miser- able samples of these, but had they been placed outside or plunged in a sunny position in the garden and supplied with plenty of water, they would have borne quite a dif- ferent aspect. A balsam, grown according to the instruc- tions given in this column, would reach the dimensions of half-a-dozen of such plants moulded into one.

A story is told of a great French satirist which finely illustrates his knowledge of human nature. He was travel- ling in Germany, in entire ignorance of its language and currency. Raving obtained some small change for some of his French coins, he used to pay coachmen and others in the following manner Taking a handful ot the numisnaa- tical specimens from his pocket, he counted them, one by one, into the creditor's hands, keeping his eye fixed all the time on the receiver's face. As soon as he perceived the least twinkle of a smile, he took bask the last coin deposited in the hand, and returned it with the remainder to his pocket. Re afterwards found that, in pursing this method, he had not overpaid for anything.

CANADA'S LESSON ON lERLAND.—As I have put it else- where, here we have more than a million of people opposed in race, religion, character, and historical associations to the majority of Canadians, a people whose forefathers fought England for a century and a half on the soil on which the children are now living; a Celtic people, massed together in one province—a people proud, sensative, sub- missive to their priests, and not very well educated; this people half a century ago badgered every Governor-General that Britain sent out, stopped the supplies, embarrassed authority, and broke out into actual rebellion. Now, they are peaceable, contented, prosperous. They co-operate for all purposes of good government with the other provinces, do no intentional injustice to the Protestant minority of their own province, and are so heartily loyal to the central authority that it has become almost an unwritten law to select the Minister of War from their representatives in Parliament. Let him who runs read, and read, too, the answer of D'Arcy McGee to those who wondered that the young rebel in Ireland should be the mature admirer of British government in Canada: "If, in my day,. Ireland had been governed as Canada is now governed,. I would have been as sound a Constitutionalist as is to be found in Ireland." Ido not say that the problem in the mother- country is exactly the same, or that the remedy should be exactly the same. No illustration walks on all-fours. But Canadians can hardly help feeling that the solution of the Irish question lies in trusting the people of Ireland, and extending to them, with the least possible delay, as large a measure of Home Rule as is consistent with the preserva- tion of the central authority in unimpaired strength. It seems to me that Ireland should be governed in accordance with the constitutionally expressed wishes of its own people in every matter that does not involve the dissolution of the unity of the Emplre.—Contemporary Review. M. Brogniart has reported on some fossil insects found in the coal measures of Commentry, which were submitted to him for examination. They are 70 cmtr. in breadth of wing, and at least 50 cmtr. in length. M. Brogniart classes them with the large grasshoppers (phasma), though they differ from these in the organisation of the wing. JEle has named them protophasma.

The excavltion; of the Archaeological. Society of Athens at Epidaurus have resulted in the discovery of a Doric temple which some believe to be the temple of Artemis men- tioned by Pausanias. The theatre has been completely brought to the light of day, and four other buildings are being excavated. Some important sculptures have been found and taken to Athens.

An admirer of Mr. P. J.-Bailey's poem, "Festns" is pub- lishing a small volume containing striking extracts from it, and entitled" The Beauties of Festus " (Longmans, Green, and Co., London). " Festus " has passed through ten editions in England and thirty in America, and at the time of its publication received extraordinary commendations from the press of both countries, and from many of their celebrated literary and scientific men. It is noteworthy that the poem was first published in Manchester in 1839. I - -

. An important forward step has been taken by the pro- prietors of the Literary World. Eltablished fifteen years ago, it has attained a unique position as a popular literary paper. Its object is to notice the newest and best books as they appear, and to present such a statement regarding each that the readers will understand what is the purport, scope, and general character of every book reviewed. Since its first appearance, the Literary World has acted as a most useful friend to book buyers. Now that books are being produced in larger numbers then ever, the necessity of such a publi- cation is increasingly apparent. The site of the long-sought Roman station Clania is re- ported to have been found by Professor Zosmair, of Feld- kirch, and Dr. Jenny, of Hard. A 13th century road chart is extant, copied by a monk of the monastery of Tegernsee from an original of the year 230 AD. According to this chart a road led from Chur to Bregenz, on which lay Magia and Ginnie. The foundation walls of a building have been found on a high plain near Felkirch, at ten minutes' walk I from the Rhine. A courtyard surrounded by heating.
rooms was dug out and copper and bronze coins, floor mosaics, fragments of glass, lance heads, and other remains were found. _ _ _

THE BRITISH MUSEUM—One of the most interesting acquisitions lately in the printroom at the British Museum is that of a drawing by the r Ire Alsatian painter-engraver Martin Schonganer, the greatest artist of Germany before Darer, which has just been presented by a relative of the . .

• poet Rogers, to Whom it is supp,sed formerly to have be- longed. The drawing is in pen and sepia, with the flesh parts washed in colour, and represents a girl fanning a fire with a severed bird's wing, a practice common in Germany to this day. It is moreover remarkable as being the only known work of the master,who has signed it with his mono- gram and the year 1469. TEE SOUTH KENSINGTON MUSEUM is about to receive another valuable addition in the shape of the almost un- equalled collection of English pottery ware belonging to Lady Charlotte Schreibner. There is probably no other collection so rich in examples of the rarest native manu- facture. Not only the most elaborate coloured figures and groups of old Chelsea and the finest Battersea enamels, but the burst curious variety of the salt-glaze wares of Stafford- shire, as well as many other local fabrics, are to be found there. It is the intention of the owner to present the whole collection to South Kensington as soon as the cata- logue now being prepared under the direction of Mr. Franks, of the British Museum, is complete. GIG kNTIC EARTHWOEM.—The Cape Times says that gigantic earthworm has been rent from the colony for Mr. Frank Biddard, prosector of the Royal Zoological Society, who has been desirous of obtaining one of these monsters for _ . . . .

scientific purposes. The Rev. G. Fisk,F Z.S.,with whom Mr. Biddard has corresponded on the subject, received the worm from Mr. H. W. Bidwell, who found it in the Botanic Garden at Uitenhage. The longest measurement of the creature yet taken reaches six feet five inches, but it is thought it it were drowned the measurement would extend to ten feet, this mode of extinction having an extremely relaxing effect on the frame or substance of the worm. The surface of the upper portion of the body shows a bright green colour, of variable intensity, but otherwise it is a loathly animal. Lu2nbricus Dficroehola is the name by which it will be im- mortalised in the records of the Zoological Society. A NEW ELECTRIC MOTOR.—A novel electric motor was

lately tried on a Cleveland (Ohio) tramway. The experi- ment is stated to have been so successful that the company owning the line expect to change their entire system, com- prising over seventy mile% into electric roads. The system used is a combination of the Brush and Knight and Bentley systems, the current being carried on underground con- ductors laid in conduits, like those of cable roads. During the trial the cars were started and stopped and reversed with the greatest ease, It is affirmed that any number of cars up to 15 can be run at one time on a tingle circuit and from one machine, which is a result not attained by any of the Euro- pean systems now in operation. The success of the new road is said to have caueed a great sensation in both tram- way and electrical circles in America, and is expected to largely extend the field of electric development, as well as enhance the value of tramway properties in the United States.—lron; _ _

_ DR. RICHARDSON'S LETHAL CHAMBER.—In the current number of his Ascleniad, Dr. Richardson tells us that when he was quite young, "the blessed re-discovery of the pro- cess for rendering the bodies of men and animals insensible to pain during surgical operations was the grant event," an event that so possessed him as to render its improvement and extension a part of his whole life's work during the last forty years. The latest outcome" of these researches is described in the perfecting of a "process of making death itself entirely painless to the lower creation." The various steps of this research are described, the final result being the adoption of carbonic oxide as the most effective. cheap- est, and practically the most manageable ancesthetic ; and the construction of a "lethal chamber," wherein, without violence of any kind, a considerable number of animals may be caused to fall into a gentle sleep with the heart still beating, the blood still circulating, but all the centres of volition and sensation absolutely dead; the throbbing body still there, but the conscious creature gone. In this state the mechanical remnant may be left gradually to lose its movement, or, if required for food, the last pulsations of the heart may be used for ejecting the blood, and, I may add, for injecting boric acid. The lethal chamber is a wooden tunnel of square lOC lion, with double walls, holding a layer of sawdust between them to maintain an equable tempera- ture. This is closed by a valved screen or flap at the en- trance. A cage on wheels run freely inside it. When the apparatus is to be used, the animals are placed in the cage, and the chamber is charged with the lethal air. Then the cage is run in, lifVng the entrance valve as it proceeds, its own end closing the chamber in the meantime. A movable screen at the other end is pushed forward by the cage to allow for the displacement of air by the cage and its con- tents. Finally, the outer door of the chamber is closed firmly to make all air tight. The introduction of the cage and closing of the chamber occupies less than half a minute. This apparatus has been practically applied at the Dogs' Home, Battersea, and several hundreds of destitute dogs, that otherwise must have been clumsily and more or less cruelly killed, have been humanely relieved of life under the direct superintendence of Dr. Richardson himself. The next step should be the fitting up of a large slaughter-house with these appliances ; then the compulsory application of this method to all elatighter•honees; and, finally, its substitution for the gallows, by a modification allowing the criminal to effect his own despatch, in Japanese fashion, by simply opening a valve.—Gentleman's Magazine.

div.head: REVIVAL OF BYGONE HOME INDUSTRIES.
div.p: REVIVAL OF BYGONE HOME INDUSTRIES.

While the mills of the West Riding and of Lancashire are continuing to produce in ever-increasing quantities fabrics for the clothing of the world, an effort is being made just beyond the northern boundary of the last-named contyd to revive the manual industries which have been supersdene by the spinning jenny and the power-loom. Nearly every visitor to the district of the English Lakes is acquainted with the route of the favourite excursion from Ambleside through the Langdales. Those who make it see, soon after passing Skelwith Bridge, and on reaching the higher ground over which the road to Coniston passes, the little lake called Elterwater. Beyond it may be seen a grodp of houses, known by the same name, past which, on returning from the great Langdale, the excursionist will pass. One of those houses, now dignified with the appellation of St. Martin's Home, Mr. Albert Fleming, of Neaum Crag, has made the centre and, in part, the site of operations in spinning, weav- ing, and bleaching. The spinning is done by means of the old spinning-wheel and distaff, the weaving with a hand- loom, and the bleaching by the simple operations of boiling with soap and water and exposure on the grass. The work was begun little more than a year ago. Already upwards of twenty women have learned to spin, a loom is in work, and specimens of the fabrics have been and are still to be seen in a loan exhibition at Ambleside, while others have been presented to the Queen. The first impression which most minds will take upon hearing of such an undertaking will doubtless be that it is a futile attempt to restore the past and to fight again a cause which was for ever defeated long before the present generation was born. It is not, however, if I understand Mr. Fleming aright, any part of his theory that the work now done by machinery can be principally accomplished by hand. Mr. Fleming tb,inke that hand work has certain advantages over machine work; that there are many per- sons remote from factories who have leisure which they could and would be glad to occupy in hand work if they had skill and could obtain payment for their labour ; and that though machinery must be relied on for the produc- tion of the bulk of the textile fabrics of the world, yet there are and will be a sufficient number of persons who so value the qualities of hand.spun, hand-woven, and home. bleached linen, as to create a market which will support an industry of such a limited power as he has founded, and hopes to rear into thrifty life in the dales of Westmoreland. gut it will ba asked, and by many with surprise and in- credulity, whether in such operations as spinning and weaving any superiority of hand work over machine work can be looked for. Both seem to be of a kind in which the regular motions of machinery must excel in their effects the efforts of human fingers and arms, subject as those efforts must always be to the eber- ' varying powers and feelings of the person by whom they arepade. To these doubts Mr. Fleming has his answer

div.head: MR., _GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: MR., _GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.

Mr. Gladstone and the distinguished party at Mar Lodge had a long excursion on Saturday to the mountains. At night a grand torch-light ball was given by Lord Fife in honour of the Premier and other distinguished visitors. The affair was as far as possible kept a secret, in order that it might be of the nature of a surprise to Mr. Gladstone. The Duff Highlanders mustered in strong force, and a most weird and entertaining spectacle was witnessed. The clans- men, headed by three pipers, assembled in the rear of Mar Lodge shortly after nine o'clock in the evening and were marshalled by their captain, Mr. Leslie. Each man appeared in full Highland costume, but carried no arms. A ' bonfire of Mar Forest fir was kindled, and the men were supplied with torches, but it was not till 10-30 o'clock that the order to "light up" was given. Then each ILghlander plunged the end of his torch in the bonfire, and forming into two rows, and bearing the lighted torches aloft, they wheeled round into the quadrangle in front of the house, the pipers playing a lively tune. As soon as the High- lenders caught sight of the Prime Minister standing bare- headed under the porch at the main entrance, they raised a lusty cheer, which Mr.. Gladstone acknowledged by bowing. Besides the Premier and Mrs. Gladstone and Miss Helen Gladstone, there were assembled Lord Fife, the Earl and Countess of Dalhousie, Lady Lonsdale, Lord Ribblesdale, the Bishop of Durham, and other ladies and gentlemen. A dozen of the best men among the Highlanders were selected to dance the first reel, which was performed with blazing torches waved aloft and much shouting. Mr. Gladstone applauded vigorously, and was evidently much amused. That over, the lighted torches were cast into the centre, and another wild, fantastic dance was performed around the blazing pule thus made. In response to a request of Lord Fife and the continuous cheers of the Highlanders, the Premier spokea few graceful words of thanks,and thedancing was then resumed.—On Monday Mr Gladstone left Mar Lodge and drove to Ballater, where he took train for Haddo House, the seat of the Earl of Aberdeen, whose guest the right hen gentleman will be for some days. At every place where Mr Gladstone was likely to be seen numbers of people were gathered, and the Premier's reception at all the railway stations was very enthusiastic. On reaching Aberdeen an address was presented to him by the Lord Provost on be- half of the Town Council, and Mr Gladstone, who was heart- ily cheered by an immense crowd, expressed his thanks in a brief speech. He commented upon the extraordinary enthu- siasm which had greeted him asthe representative ot a great cause during all his recent movements, and said he believed that enthusiasm to be stronger now than even in 1879 and 1880. He referred to the political elisL, and told his fellow burgesses of Aberdeen that until the great cause of reform had been dealt with his strength and his services were en- tirely at the disposal of his countrymen. A special train conveyed the party from Aberdeen, and more addresses were handed to the Premier at several stations passed. At Kin- tore the Premier said :—I know well that the reason, and the just and sufficient reason, that gathers the people of Scotland in such numbers and such multitudes at every station is that they know that they are engaged at this moment in a great and just cause, and that it will be their duty on the one hand and on the other hand in their power to carry on that cause until it reaches a triumphant conclu- sion, favourable alike to the liberties of the people andio the securities of the Crown, which the people love even as they do their own liberties.—After leaving the railway Mr Gladstone Was driven to Haddo House, a distance of seven miles, with an escort of about 500 of the tenantry on horse- back, headed by the Earl of Aberdeen. Mr Gladstone remained indoors at Haddo House on Tues.

day forenoon owing to the dense fog which prevailed. A deputation from the East Aberdeenshire Liberal Association presented Mr Gladstone with an address, but the proceed- ings, which took place in the library, were informal, and Mr GI dstone merely conversed with the members of the deputation, who were introduced by Lord Aberdeen. In the afternoon Mr Gladstone visited Mettilick, and in a few words opened a training home for girls, which has been erected by Lord Aberdeen. The Premier excused himself from speaking on account of the fatigue he bad undergone. Mr Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs Gladstone and Miss Helen tiladstone, left Haddo House, the seat of the Earl of Aberdeen, on Wednesday morning, and drove into Aberdeen. whence they in the afternoon proceeded to pay a visit to Lord Dalhousie at Brechin Castle. The distance from Haddo House to Aberdeen is 19 miles, and on many parts of the road there were demonstrations of enthusiasm in honour of the Premier. At Bridge of Dun a number of mounted constabulary joined the carriage and escorted it into the city, the main streets of which were crowded with people, who cheered loudly as Mr Gladstone passed by. At the railway station thousands mustered, and admission to the inside was only obtained by tickets issued by the Liberal Association. The four horses which had drawn the carriage containing the Premier were unharnessed, and the carriage was then drawn by some railway porters out of the crowd into the reserved space. Cheer after cheer was given for Mr and Mrs Gladstone and Lord Aberdeen, who bad travel- led from Haddo with his guests. Many of the workhops were closed for the afternoon, and at all the public schools the scholars were given a balf-holdiay. Mr Prosser, chair- man of the Liberal Association, read an address from the Aberdeen Liberal Association. Mr Thompson, president of the trades Council, next read an address on behalf of the working classes of Aberdeen.

Mr CISLAnsroNE, on rising in the carriage to reply, was received with loud and long-continued cheers. He said : I am afraid that no physical power which I possess would enable me to convey to the ears of this vast assemblage the gratitude with which I receive this warm and cordial ex- pression ot yoer sentiments, and permit me to say that ef all the exhibitions of public and natural feeling which ever met my eyes in the course of a very long life, I have witnessed none more remarkable than that which has greeted me en our progress into Aberdeen to-day. (Cheers.) We are here of all classes, of all persuasions, united as one man in the present on one great and just cause. (Cheers.) I rejoice to see here the thousands of the working class. It is by a united action on your pelt, a constitutional and an orderly, but a perfectly determined action, that we shall, as I trust, achieve the purpose we have in view. (Cheers.) You de- plore and I deplore the unfortunate vote which threw out the Franchise Bill—(renewed cheers) ; but I rejoice to see that the working classes of Aberdeen speak of that vote as given by a majority of the House of Lords, for they know that there are many mem- bers of the House of Lords than whom there are no better friends to the cause of liberty. (Cheers, and a voice:. " Lord Aberdeen.") It is no desire of mine to carry the- public of this country into the discussion of wide constitu- tional and organic change if it can be avoided, and I yet hope it may be avoided. There is an opportunity yet re- maining, and I look with hope to the wisdom, which has on various occasions characterised the House of Lords to re- cover the consequences of the unfortunate step of last July.. (Cheers.) You may rely upon it that on my part and en the part of my colleagues no effort will be wanting. We- shall not in this matter leave you in the lurch. (Loud cheers and cries of " We'll help you. r We know pretty well the work we have to do, and we shall strive to do it. But it will not be our conviction and our judgment that will carry the Franchise Bill, it will be the firm, united, loyal action of the people of this country that will perform a great act of justice, and put an end to a painful controversy certain to grow if it continues into a much wider and more for- midable contest, and that will by the admission of two mil- lions of our fellow-citizens to the Parliamentary franchise strengthen the laws and the institutions of this country. (Loud and continued cheering.) The Premier, Mrs and Mias Gladstone were then con- ducted by Lord Aberdeen to the special saloon carriage which was attached to the ordinary train for the south leav- ing at 3-45. Peterhead was the first stopping place, and hem an address was presented on behalf of the Liberal inhabi- tants of the town, to which Mr Gladstone briefly replied. At Fordoun, Lawrencekirk, and Dubton there was no particular demonstration, the people contenting themselves with cheering and shaking hands with the Premier. At Bridge of Dun a deputation from Montrose was in waiting, the object being to present addresses to Mr Gladstone. This was done on behalf of the Town Council by Provost Leckie, and on behalf of the Liberal Association by es-Pro- vost Jopp. The Premier, in responding, paid a high tribute to the memory of Joseph Hume. The train then proceeded onwards to Brechin, where there was a demonstration exceeding in enthusiasm anything since the party left Aberdeen. Cann reaching the platform Mr Cdadstone'was presented with the freedom of the city, the ceremony being conducted by Provost Lamb. An ad- dress from the Liberal Association was afterwards read by Mr Duke, the vice-president. Mr Gladstone replied at some length,saying his resolution not to receive addresses had been conquered and broken down by the irresistible and general movements of the whole community. The right hou. gentleman then drove away to Brechin Castle, amid the cheers of the vast multitude, Mr Gladstone, who is stated to be no worse for his exer- tions of Wednesday, left Brechin early on Thursday morn- ing for a drive in the neighbourhood. The carriage was driven by Lord Dalhousie, and contained Mrs and Mr Henry Gladstone, in addition to the Premier, the second carriage being set apart for the use of Miss Gladstone aria other guests at Brechin Castle. The route was by way of Edzell andriretterciirn to Glendve. The Premier remains at Brechin Castle until to-day (Saturday).

The enarges in the Whalley will case were resumed an Tuesday. The witness Reece, in further examination, de- posed that when Thomas knew that witness was in commu- nication with Mr Priestman's solicitor he threatened to murder him. Witness admitted asking Thomas fo7.- money, out denied asking Gunnell. A terrible suicide was committed in Edinburgh at noon on Monday. A poor woman, jumping upon the parapet of Dean Bridge, frantically waved her arms for some moments, and then jumped from the giddy height into the river Leith, ' which flows below. This is the third suicide which has occurred at this spot within the past few months. Three children named Whitten ware at play at a farm homestead at Westbury, near Buckingham, on Monday afternoon, when one of them palled out the pin of an elevator, causing the chain to run out and the machine to fall upon them. They were e.xtrio•ated and medical attendance called, but no hope of their recovery is enter- tained. Sin E. Kum is to succeed the late Lord Ampthill as British Ambassador at Berlin. Sir Edward has been in the diplomatic service thirty years. and has had experience at Washington, Paris, Pekin, Athens, Rome, and Constanti- nople, and from 1879 to 1883 he was Agent and Consul- General in Egypt. Since then be has been Envoy-Extraor- dinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to Belgium. Ile has thus had experience both In china and Egypt—the two points of most diplomatic interest at the present time, and is also familiar with Continental diplomacy.

div.p: FOREIGN NEWS. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. ACCIDENT AT THE CATARACTS.—TRIBA.L CONFLICTS. CAIRO, MONII&Y.—Major Kitchener telegraphs to General Wood that Maimed Kiamil, late the chief clerk at Darfour, has arrived at Dongola, having walked along the Nile from Kordofan. He says that Maha.med Kheir is at Berber with '2.300 Turks, who are prisoners and disarmed, 200 Blacks, and 3,000 Gaalin Arabs with rifles. SUAXIX, SATURDAY.—The Amarars were repeatedly at- tacked at Arbat on the 11th inst by the friendly tribe of the Hadendowas. The attacks were repulsed, but the Anzarars were obliged to keep on the defensive. Mahmoud Ali's eldest son was killed in the fighting. Several deserters from Osman Dignee's camp are arriving here daily. They report that Osman has only 300 men at Tamai. The friendly and hostile tribes are facing each other near Handoub. Col. Chermside has supplied the former with some arms and provisions. The night attacks on Suakim are now rare and weak. Spaxier, Monnev.—ln the fighting which took place at Arbat on the 11th inst. the Amarar tribe are stated to have lost only one sheikh and thirteen men, but no arras. They ware able to remove their dead. Later news from the enemy's camp gives the loss of the friendly tribe of the Hadendowas in killed and wounded as seventy. The fight- ing lasted five hours, during which a handful of Suekim police behaved well. Nineteen camels were killed. WADY HALFA, FRIDAY—The steamer Nasoafkhier was -successfully hauled over one difficult cataract to-day. The 'reported victory of the Mudir of Dongola at Amikol is fully confirmed. The body of the Sheikh Ahmed Redia, who was killed in the engazeinent, has been found. WADY HALFA, SUNDAY.—YeSterday, while a boat manned by three Blue Jackets was being hauled up the Cataract it swueg round broadside to the current. The water poured in, and the men leaped oat immediately. 0/13 was awed, bat the other two were drowned, as also another who went to their rescue from the shore. It ic also reported that General Gordonhas been actively engaged tothe south of Khartoum, and has-cap- tured from the rebels-two islands near Senaar, on the Blue 'Nile. The hired transport Naranja left the Royal Areenal, Woolwich, on Saturday, with 39 Nile boats, under orders to call at Portsmouth foe 27 more. The Eritish India steam- ship, Bulimba left the Royal Albert Docks, Woolwich, on Saturday, with several hundred tons of stores. She proceeds to Portsmouth to take in six hundred and fifty troopsaand to fill up with Nile boats. The Bulimbe will be stationed as a hospital ship either at Alexandria or Suakim. The 'Neptune left on Monday afternoon wit h-900 tons of commis- sariat stores and ammunition. She will ship at Hole Meson, eix miles below Gravesend,l6,ooo lbs. of dynamite, blasting gelatine, and detonators, to be used for trying the effect of blowing up rocky obstructions at the Nilo cataracts. The naval and military authorities up the Nile are re- ported to be not only opposed to the river route, hut ales to the use of camels for crossing the desert, and telegrams were despatched on 'Saturday to Andalusia, Algeria, the e South of France, and Alexandria, to make enquiries as to the practibility of purchasing 30,000 mules for transport purposes in the event of the Nile route being abandoned, and that of the desert substituted. Five hundred 'Marines, from heedquarters at Chatham, Portsmouth, and 'Fie-month, will leave for Egypt in the early part of next week, under the command of Major J. Morris, R.M.L.T. Orders have been issued by the War Office for the helicon corps from Chatham to be held in readiness to proceed to Egypt. The hired transport Hid deo arrived at Woolwich Arsenal on Monday, and commenced loading beats and stores forthe ' Nile expedition. Tee hired transport Scheldt commenced loading provisions on'lelondav et Woelwich. THE REINFORCEMENTS FOR EGYPT. CAIRO, TUESDAY.—The statement published in Lenden this morning that at the request of Lord Wolseley the War Office had decided Co despatch 3,000 additional troopato Egypt for strengthening the British forces in that courntry is incorrect. Lord Wolseley has ordered a camel corps to be formed of detachmen,s of equal streneth from the three Household Cavalry regiments and sisteen other Cavalry regiments in England, as well as from the seven battalions of the Guards. The strength of each detachment is to be two officers, 44 rank and file, or 1,100 in all. They are to be formed in three die isions, the first to consist of heavy cavalry, the second of light cavalry, and the third of the Guards. A London cerreeporelent telegraphs that this despatch from Cairo is regarded an military circles as very important. Except in the recent campaign in Egypt, the Guards and Household Cavalry have not seen active toevice since the --Crimean war. WINIVICK CRICKET CLl7l3.—This club closed a success- fat season on Saturday, with a scratch match, in which the captain (Mr H .1 Longton) scored 45, D Ferguson 39, R Andrews, 26, Sac. The visitors found, on assum- ing the defensive, this by no means formidable score a great deal too much for them, for Wood, being in his best form, wks well on the spot, and his erpresses, backed up by good fielding,soon told a tale, none of the batsmen being able to get into double figures, while tsi:r failed to score at all. BIiIIiZT4T OF BRIGGS AT WIDNES.—On Saturday last, in beautiful weather, a match was played on the Widnes Cric- ket ground, between eleven gentlemen and professionals of the district and fifteen of Widnes (with John Briggs). The day's ,prcceedings were set apart specially for the benefit of Mr John Briggs, the Widnes professional, and father of Briggs, the Lancashire &sooty player. There was a numer- ous attendance of spectators, and the " take" at the gates must have been considerable. The Fifteen defended the wickets first, to the bowling of Shore and Joseph Briggs. They were all out for 116, to which John Briggs, junior, contributed4l, and Mr Colquitt22. Shore took the greater part cf the wickets. A rather poor start was made by the Eleven, but, after some bad luck, Chandlev and Shore made a stand, and put a brighter aspect on the game. Joseph Brigga also made a stand, and put together 25 runs by good cricket; but the last wicket fell for 03, the Fifteen thus winning by2o runs. In the evening the teams assembled at Deakin's Hotel, Simms' Cross, where they dined together. —After dinner Mr FT Parry occupied the chair, and pro- posed the health of the younger Briggs, who has been selec- ted to accompany the English team to Australia, to play in a series of matches, during the coining winter. He wished him every success during the tour, and a safe return journey home. Briggs responded in an appropriate speech, remark- ing that he should do his utmost to maintain the honour of the old country. The singing of "Auld Lang Syne " ter- minated a very enjoyable evening. SEFTON v. WARINNOTON.—This match was played on the krpley ground, Warrington, on Saturday, and resulted in a decisive victory for the home team by 68 runs. The home team consisted of the regular players, while Sefton had got a very strong team, being reinforced by several well-known players. The Sefton men won the toss, and began batting with Messrs Jones and Wood, the bowling being entrusted to CG Lawton and Denison. Jones was missed in the long field off the fourth bell of the innings, and compiled 16 be- fore he was taken by T Lawton. VVocds was splendidly caught at slip, and Ravenscroft and Bird became partners. The former was smartly run out from cover point, and Wall came in. This player hit hard and clean. He was missed at long on by Clarke from a very lofty hit, but was clean bowled.the next ball. From this time, the score being 76, the Sefton team collapsed entirely. England fielded very smartly at point, and J C Lawton made an excellent catch off Evans at slip. The innings closed for 90. Great credit is due to Messrs Lawton for their excellent bowling, while the fielding was extremely smart, and ably seconded the efforts of the bowlers. Warrington began with the usual pair, Wallington and Fairclough, to the bowling of Evans and F Jonec. Fairclough hit away merrily, but was caught at 31 from a very fast hall by Roper at short leg. The ball split tbeCelder's hand, and a short adjournment took place. Ropor was greeted with great applause on his re- appearance to Cold. Denison, J C Lawton. England, and Hind played well for their respective scores. England has tot been sees, both in the field and batting, to greater ad- 'vantage than on Saturday. Hind hit up 14 from an over from Wall, and the innings closed for 158. Wood bowled finely for Sefton, mhile Jones bawled consistently through- out the whole innings.

ITS WEIGHT IN Goxr, —The aggregate produetion of gold, in the United states of America, up t, June, 188:3, we have tist been told on the authority of the Times, was 18,985,572 troy ounces. When we saw this particular weight of gold given as the accumulation of all preceding years, we were at once struck with the remarkable approximation of the weight given to what had just come to our knowledge was the output of Cocoa in this country by one firm (James Epps and 0)0 for one year only, the last twelve month, it being 88,433,333 troy ounces, or 2.645 avoirdupois tons, and. on the moment we could not withstand recalling to mind the old adage—" Worth its weight in gold."—Adot.

DEFEAT OF THE CHINESE TROOPS. SHANGHAI, WEDNESDAY.—Two thousand French troops have landed at Kinpai Pass, and have attacked and de- feated the Chinese with heavy loss. The Chinese are in full retreat. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—The statement that detachments of the troops at present in garrison in France would be sent to Tonmain is incorrect. The Ripublique Franyaise of to-day demands that an end shall be put to the reprisals in the East. The journal believes that in order to bring China to a sense of repentance it will be necessary to operate on Yang Tee Kiang, and to strike at Nankin. Fines, WEDNESDAY. A despatch received yesterday from Admiral Courbet states that the French boat engaged in carrying despatches to Pic Argo, having each time been exposed to the fire of the Chinese batteries, had received orders to return it. Admiral Courbet desires to leave the Chinese the initiative of opening 6re in order that they may be held responsible for any losses sustained by neutrals who have resumed the navigation Of the Min. THE CHOLERA.—MESSAGE FROM QUEEN VICTORIA. ROME, MONDAY.—The official buEetins for the last three days state the number of cases of cholera at Naples as— Saturday 872, with '2BB deaths and 107 fatal cases among cases already under treatment; Sunday 181, with Ed deaths, 39 being ameng patients already under treatment; Monday 643 cases and 281 deaths, 140 of which were among former patients. In the other provinces, the numbers were as follow for three days: Avelino, 4 cases, 3 deaths; Benevento, 3 cesee; Bergamo, 46, and 18 fatal : Bologna, 2 cases; Campobasso. 2; Caserto, 20, and 8 deaths; Cremona, 4; Cuero, 47, and 18 deaths; Foggia, 1; Genoa, 67, 32 deaths; Spezzia, 52, 12 deaths; Leghorn, 1; Lucca, 1; Massa Carrara, 7, 4 fatal; Salerno,`7 ; Turin, 5, 2 fatal; •' Parma, 4, 1 fatal ; Reggio d'Emilia, 3, 1 fatal. King Humbert and the Duke of Aosta left Naples on Sunday afternoon. The Ring, on bidding farewell to the Mayor, said he went away more relieved, as the cholera was manifestly decreasing. Signor Dezerby, President of the White Cross Com- mittee, bi a telegram to the Italian Press Association, states that offers of personal assistance for the cholera patients at Naples are reaching him from all parts of Europe. He explains, however, that such aid is not what is required, the real want is funds. A telegram from Foggia reports that a serious disturbance has occurred there. The inhabitants having heard a rumour that a person who had come to the town from Naples had been -seized with cholera, went in large numbers to the railway station with the avowed purpose of preventing any other corner frost Naples from leaving the train. They had eventually to be dispersed by armeeforce. ROME, FRIDAY —The Queen of England has sent a telegram to Queen Margaret, at Monza, expressing her sorrow and sympathy at the outbreak of cholera in Naples, and her hopes for its speedy abatement.
