-------- , At Glasgow, on 'Monday, Mr. Alex. Hay, steamship ow- ner, was flood £lO or a month's imprisonment, for allowing the Straithnairn to go to sea overloaded. On Monday ;roaming the Rev Philip Browne, vicar of St James's, Edgbaston, was found dead in bed at his residence at Edgbaston. Deceased went to bed on Sunday night in his usual health, after officiating at 'service. It is stated that the receipts of Messrs Cook and Sons, the tourist agents, for foreign tours this season are only one-fifth of the average, so that it may be fairly calculated that four- fifths of the number of people who usually go abroad have stopped at home. PENNY DINNERS FOR SCHOOL CHILDREN.—The Gates. head School Board have unanimously agreed to commence the experiment at some of their schools of supplying the children with penny dinners. The experiment has resulted satisfactorily at the Church voluntary schools in Gates- head. . Robert Hoe, the famous printing press maker, is dead. He made a large sum out of his printing machines, which were hailed as g great improvement on their pre- decessors, though their rate of printing has since been superseded. They were first sent over to the United Kingdom in 1858. APPREHENSION OF A DYNAIIITARD.—On Monday, at the Whitehaven Police Court, Patrick France, miner, was charged with attempting to murder Mr. Thomas Isioffat. Cleator Moor, by means of dynamite or other explosive sub- stance, on the 30th August. The prisoner was only appre- hended on Friday. He was remanded for a week. MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A SURGEON.—The body of Mr Charles Palmer, surgeon, of Yarmouth, who has been visit- ing Eastbourne, was found on Saturday night on a lonely part of the south coast, between Eastbourne and Birling Gap. An examination showed that he had been stabbed to death with some sharp instrument. Ihe police are investi- gating the matter. A HEAVY SENTENCE. —At Dorchester, on Saturday, Thomas James Fowler, a warder with 18 years' service at Portland Convict Prison, was sentenced to three montbs' hard labour, in default of paying a fine of £25, for traffick- ing with convicts. The prisoner, who has hitherto borne an exemplary character and was on the point of being promoted, has a wife and ten children. A CURIOUS ACCIDENT happened to the steamer Countess of Bantry on Saturday. Among thecargo was a deck-load, consisting of 200 pigs, shipped at Castletown, Berehaven, Mr Bantry. The pigs pushing to one side caused a heavy list, and it became necessary to throw about 70 of the pigs overboard. The steamer then righted. With one or two exceptions the pigs Swam ashore and were saved. THE SALVATION ARMY.—Claims were made at the Worth- ing Police Court, on Saturday, in respect of the damage done on Sunday, the 7th met, to Mr Head's premises during the Salvation riots. At Brighton, on Saturday evening, the Salvation Army was protected by a body of police while in the procession, but a large crowd followed and drowned the singing by yells and groans. WIFE MURDER —An inquest was held in Liverpool on Saturday, on the body of Sarah Jane Jordan, wife of a cooper, who at the time of the inquiry was in the Isle of Man. The deceased and her husband quarrelled on Thurs- day, when the latter, it is alleged, kicked her savagely in the back. The woman was taken to the workhouse hospital, where she died from injuries to the spinal cord. A verdict of "Wilful murder " was returned against the husband. BLOWING A HOUSE UP. The Cumberland police have apprehended Patrick France, miner, of Cleator Moor, on the charge of blowing up the dwelling-house of Mr Moffatt, manager for Mr Stirling's mines at Cleator Moor. Mr Mof- fatt had discharged certain miners who had been concerned in the Cleator Moor riots, and'France was suspected. He is abatit SC years of age. After his apprehension he was re- moved to the Whitehaven police station, taken before Mr John Musgrave, J P, and remanded. MOONLIGHT OUTRAGE —A serious moonlight outrage has occurred at Mitchelstown. It appears to have been the act of labourers. The house attacked belonged to a farmer I named Walsh, who recently purchased the interest in the house and a plot of ground occupied by a labourer. A few nights ago a numerous party surrounded his house, and hav- ing first demolished the windows, fired into it. The bullets were found embedded in the wall, and appeared to be revol- ver and rifle balls. The house of Walsh's father-in-law was also attacked and damaged. No arrests have been made. THE TICHRORNE Caanaaarr.—Contrary to general expec- tation, the Claimant will not take up his abode at the Gran- ville, St Lawrence-on-Sea, on hie release next month. Mr Quartermaine East has taken a furnished home in Hamp- shire, and there the Claimant will take up hi abode when set at liberty. The exact address will not at present be made public. During the imprisonment of their father, Mr East has maintained and educated the Claimant's two daughters,' and the elder will, upon her father's release, go to reside I with him and undertake the supervision of the household. COCOA WORKS DESTROYED BY FlRE.—Early OD Mon- day morning a fire was discovered on the premises of Messrs. Thornes and Co., chicory and cocoa manufac- turers, Lady-lane, Leeds. The building is four storeys high and about 20 yards in ,length. The fire, which commenced in the lower storey of the building, and owing to the infl Learnable nature of the contents, favoured with a slight breeze, the flames quickly spread, and the bnilding became one mass of flame. The prin- cipal portion of the building was entirely gutted. This is the third serious tire that has occarred in Leeds in less than a week. TIM WHALLEY WILL CASE. Est Bow.street Bolice Court, on Monday, Charles Thomas, (Thomas W. Nash, and Edward Gunnell were charged on remand with forging the will of James Whalley. Edward Reece, surveyor, of Leominster, deposed that about April 1881, he was taken by Thomaa to the latter's houss, and there saw Mr. Whalley, who asked witness to attest his signature. Mr. Whalley signed two pieces of blue paper, which witness attested. Nash afterwards cajoled some writing Mem a piece of paper, and above the signature of Mr. Whalley Thomas asked Nash and witness to sign their names, pro- mising to give them £lOO. They signed the paper, and at Thomas's suggestion they saw Mr. \Yardley, so that if any inquiries were made they could say they had seen him. Mr. Whalley was very bad, and could scarcely speak.—The prisoners were again remanded. FATALITIES FR M THE USn OF FIREARICS.—A fatal OCT:- dent occurred on Saturday to a volunteer marksman named Peers, of the Knutsferd corps of the 15th Cheshire Ride Volunteerc, who was marking at a shooting competition on the moor between the railway station and Tattoo Park, at the 600 yards range. Peers, without hoisting the danger flag, looked out from his covering, when at that moment a bullet fired by a competitor struck him on the forehead be- tween the eyes. He died in an hour afterwards.—At Ilfracombe, on Saturday, an inauest was held on the body of Mr Seeley, stockbroker, of London, who was supposed to have committed suicide by blowing out his brake on board a yacht whilst gall shooting. It was proved, however, that the gun was a dangerous one which had previously ex- ploded accidentally, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."--A gentleman travelling by rail alighted at Menai Bridge Station on Saturday night, and as he did so a revolver, which he had in his coat pocket. some- how discharged a shot. Luckily for him the ball did not reach his body. He had, however, a narrow escape, as his watch chain was blown to atoms. The chain, doubtless, saved his life. BODY SNATCHING IN IRELAND —EXTRAORDINARY DIS- APPEARANCE OF Two BODlES—Particulars of a most mysterious affair in the South of Ireland have just been made public. Th^re is little doubt that an outrage similar to that not long since perpetrated in Scotland, when the body of the Earl of Crawford and Balcarres was stolen front the vault, has been perpetrated. A gentleman well known in County Clare died twelve months ago, and was buried in the churchyard of Kilmorley, where the remains of a female relative had previously been interred. Recently, in accord- ance with the wish of the deceased gentleman's widow, it was resolved to transport both bodies to a spot in the family demesne which had been selected as a burying place. But 'to the astoniahment and horror of the friends, when the graves were dug up. the corpses could not be seen, and it was manifest that an act of desecration had been perpe- trated. Two theories have been mooted by way of account- ing for the extraoroinary affair. One is that it is due to agrarian revenge, and the other that it is attributable to superstition. The first of these is repudiated by the family as improbable, but there is a certain amount of colour for the second. Kilmorley churchyard happens to be in another parish from that in which the deceased lived, and many of the Irish peasantry have a great objection to bodies brought from a distance being buried in their places of sepralture. CO-OC'ERATIVE WHOLESALE SOCIETY.—A. commemoration of the tweuty-first anniversary of this society, the head- quarters of which are in balloon-street, Manchester, was held on Saturday by the London Branch District at the Crystal Palace. There were present 370 delegates, representing 60,000 co-operators. After dinner, which was served in the terrace-room, a social gathering was held, Mr George Hines presiding. Mr 11 Pumphrey (branch secretary) read an abstract from the history of the society, from which it ap- peared that the Wholesale Society commenced business in Manchester in March, 1861. It was started by a combina- tion of fifty societies, numbering 17,545 members, who sub- scribed capital for its establishment. In 1872 the bank department was opened, and the turnover was, then and now, as follows:—First year's turnover, 1873, £1,051,764; last year's turnover, 1883, £14,753,432. At the present time there are connected with the society 678 retail societies which are shareholders, comprising 446,184 members. It has a subscribed share capital of £215,950, of which £195,618 is paid up. It has invested with it, as loans and deposits, £482,739. It has property comprising land, build- ings, steamships, and fixtures which have cost £305,988, but which have been depreciated £74,408, and therefore are only taken in the assets of the society at £231,578. Its sales for the 21 years, up to Jane quarter in present year, amount to £38,609,674, and out of the profits realised in both trade and bank departments, it has paid interest on share and loan capital amounting to £217,247; dividend on purchases, £356,108; dividend to customers in the bank department, £7.673, or a total benefit to its members and customers of £611,026. It has also written off as bad debts £74,333; has contributed £7,476 to charitable and other in- stitutions, and has an insurance fund, which is practically a reserve fund, of £22,812, and a reserve fund proper of £23,247, or a total reserve fund of £46,059. Mr Spurgeon has been unable to preach for several weeks on account of illness, but occupied his pulpit on Sunday morning, when he looked very ill and careworn. A married woman, named Eliza Maddock, died on Mon- day at her residence in Openshavr, it is 'suspected, from in- juries inflicted by her husband on the previous Saturday. The husband, a labouring man, is said to have ab- sconded. The Mayor of Bradford on Saturday opened a recreation ground formed out of 48 acres of moorland. The Corpora- tion have spent £B,OOO in the ornamentation of the land, the formation of lawns for tennis, football, cricket and other outdoor games. Proceedings against Henry Hughlings, James Wilson Golden, and Frederick Pope, accountants, in connection with the Grosvenor Bank frauds, were continued at South- wark Police Court on Tuesday. The charge against Golden was withdrawn, and he turned Queen's evidence.—Case adjourned. DESECRATING A OHITRCIIYARD.—The mysterious removal of a gravestone from the churchyard of Donnington-on-Bain, near Louth, caused great excitement in the village on Mon- day. It was a memorial cross erected by the vicar over the grave of his son. After a search it was discovered in the bed of the river, tied to another memorial etone previously removed from the same churchyard. There have been burial fees disputes with the vicar. A PARLIAMENTARY paper issued on Monday contains the report of Dr Crichton Browne on the alleged pressure of work in elementary schools. With reference to home lessons, he says he has met with many lamentable instances of derangement of health, disease of the brain, and even death resulting from enforced evening study in young children, and he is fully persuaded that even when it does no per- ceptible injury to health it is ihimical to true progress. ATTEMPRD MLEPER OF CONSTABLES.—Oa Tuesday, at the Old Bailey, James Wright, 38, and William Wheatley, 25, were found guilty, the first-named of wounding with intent to murder Police-constables Wm. Chambsrlain at Islington, and David Gamer and Wm. Snell at Hoxton, with intent to murder; and the second-named of wounding with intent to resist apprehension. Wright was eentenced to penal servitude for life, and Wheatley to twenty years' penal servitude. Tan GREAT PLATE ROBBERY IN IRELAND.—Ths Irish police have made some important discoveries in connection with the extensive robbery of plate belonging to Lady Tighe, for which a butler named Kelly and his wife are now in custody. Some diamonds from a costly necklace, pre- sented to the Queen by Lady Louisa Tighe on her marriage, have been discovered sewn up in a pillow. The stolen plate was, it seems, made up in sealed boxes intended to be given as presents in the manner set out in her husband's (the late Colonel Tighe's) will after her decease, and this was the reason it was not missed for a long time. A few days ago Lady Tighe went to get a valuable gold watch, presented to the family by the Great Duke of Wellington, to show as a memento to a friend while conversing about his son's (the late Duke's) death, when she first discovered it was stolen. This led to the search for other articles of value, which I were also missed. After a fruitless inquiry the matter was I put into the hands of the police. THE BISHOP OF BLINCEIESTEY ON 111 E EGYPTIAN QUE - TIOIL—The Bishop of Manchester in the course of a sermon preached on Monday night on the occasion of the harvest festival at St. Anne's Church, Manchester, said his hearers would be thinking 'what we should do in Egypt, and par- tieularla whether we should be able to rescue that gallant 11 man' General Gordon, from Khartoum. Us had always hoped that we should go from Egypt, if not having accom- plished that which we hoped to do, at least without gross disaster; and he cherished that hope still, and would tell them why. Because our motives in going to Egypt, what- ever Frenchmen and other foreigners might think of them, were pare and disinterested. He entirely believed oar Prime Minister when he said that the only object of her Majesty's Government had been to leave Egypt independent, strong, and free. And it was just because he believed that our motives were pure and worthy he had that confidence in the moral power which governed the world—though it was not for him to prophecy—still he hoped we should come from Egypt without gross disaster. He thanked God he could still trace a moral power governing the world Whatever some men who pretended to speak in the name of science might say, things were not as they are by chance, nor was evil stronger than good, nor were lies in the long run more persuasive than truth; and, recognising the hand of God in what befalls nations, as well as what befalls individuals, he could call upon them, if they felt our motives as English- men to be worthy and unselfish and pure, as David upon his People, to be thankful; for, said David, "it becometh well the just to be thankful." Tins TRADES UNION CONGRESS.—RESOLUTION ON OVER. Sul/ca.—The 'Trades Union Congress, at Aberdeen, was re- sumed on Saturday, Mr J C Thompson presiding. There was a large attendance of delegates. Mr Foster. Hull, moved, and Mr Madden seconded, the following resolution, viz.: "That this Congress, being of opinion that a general adoption of the Public Libraries Act would tend to greatly improve the social condition of the people, strongly recom- mend that the adoption of these Acts should be made com- pulsory in all towns, parishes, or districts where the Com- pulsory Education Acts are in force."—Mr Johnstone, Glasgow, moved, and Mr Blackie, Edinburgh, seconded, an amendment that the Congress b 3 content with simply re- commending the adoption of the Acts, and should not go so far as to recommend that they should be made compulsory. —Upon a division the motion was carried by a majority of 27 to 22,—Mr J Burrows, Padiham, moved: "That an in- struction be given to the Parliamentary Committee to urge upon the Government to abate, as far as possible, the evils set forth in the official report of Dr J H Bridge and Mr Osborne, arising out of the oversizing of cotton yarns and the infusion of steam into weaving sheds, where so many women and children are employed." He stated that as much as 200ib. of size was used on 1001 b. of warp, whereas it was only necessary to have 10 or 15 per cent. The manu- facturers stated that foreigners could not afford to bay good calico, and therefore they must make material that they would purchase. With regard to the infusion of steam into the weaving sheds, he explained that that was done for the purpose of retaining the moisture on the cloth. The un- healthy conditions under which the women and children worked would be understood when he explained that all the ventilators and doors were kept closed, and not a breath of fresh air admitted.—Mr Barker, Blackburn, seconded the motion.—Mrs Ellis and Mr Luke Park, Preston, supported the resolution, which was unanimously adopted.—Mr Freak, of London, next moved, amid some symptoms of dissent, that it be an instruction to the Parliamentary, Committee to use their best endeavours to secure the opening of the national museums and art galleries on Sunday, in order that the subjects might have a better opportunity of being adequately discussed. Mr Freak, after making his speech, expressed his desire to postpone the motion until an earlier day of next year's Congress, but upon a division the pro- posal to withdraw the resolution was rejected by 34 against 27. The previous question was then moved, and upon a further division was carded by 40 against 21 votes.— Resolutions were afterwards passed in favour of the Congress being represented at the forthcoming Industrial Remunera- tion Conference lobe held in Jianuary,lBBs, against the Con- tagious Diseases Act, and in support of the proposed working men's memorial at Stafford, in honour of the late Mr Alex- ander Macdonald, M.P.—The usual votes of thanks con- cluded the Congress.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Boardroom at the workhouse, on Wednesday. There were present Messrs Cooper (in the' chair), Blackhurst. Appleton, Greenhall, William Houghton, Mackie, Jolley, Humphreys, Worthington, Grange, Caldwell, John Houghton, Harrison, Darbyshire, Owen, Eibson, Kilshall, Rev G F Roberts, J C Sutton (clerk), and S Sutton (assistant clerk).

div.head: SALARIES REPAID.
div.p: SALARIES REPAID.

The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board stating that they had directed the sum of £456 E3s 3d to be paid to the treasurer of the Guardians, this being the amount repayable to the Guardians in respect of the salaries of medical officers, schoolmasters, &c.

AN INCORRIGIBLE RUNAWAY. On the minutes of the School Committee coming up for confirmation, Mr HARBYSHIRE mentioned that the boy John Warrington had again run away, and had put them to some expense to bring him back.—Mr HARRISON: I wish you could persuade him to coange his uadie.—Mr DARBY. SHIRE: I wish we could persuade him to change his be- haviour.

ANTI-VACCINATION AND OTHER MATTERS. The CLERK mentioned that be had received a copy of a letter sent to the Home Secretary by Alexander Forster, anti-vaccinator, of Newton, regarding him (the clerk). The copy of the letter had been sent to him by the Local Government Board. It read as follows :—August 11th, 1884.—T0 the Right Hon. Sir William V. Harcourt. Right Hon. Sir. lam so convinced of your innate (here the clerk mentioned that there had evidently been a word missed out) of that which is just and right, and that you will endeavour to put things so whenever you have the power, that I take the opportunity of pointing out to you the fact that, con- trary to the instructions of the Local Government Board, in article 16 of the Board's General Order of the 31st October, 1874, Mr. J. C. Sutton, Clerk to the Board of Guardians of the Warrington Union, is taking it on himself to Vrosecute defaulters under the Vaccination Acts at the Newton-le- Willows Petty Sessions. The error has been pointed out several times to magistrates trying the cases; but either the latter as well as the magistrates' clerk do not under- stand the law on the subject, or elsi they knowingly ignore the same; as I understand the question, no one but the vaccination officer has any right to prosecute in such cases except a solicitor, which Mr. J. C. Sutton is not. Hoping you will put the matter right, I am, right hon. Sir, your obedient servant, Alexander Forster, 19, Regent-street, Earlestown, Lancashire.—To this letter he (the clerk) had replied to the Local Government Board—" lam in receipt of copy letter by Mr. Alexander Forster to the Secretary of State for the Home Department. It is not for me as Clerk to the Guardians to justify the decisions of the magistrates ; as, however, my observations on Mr. Forster's letter are invited, I have to say that the justices were not only right but that under the circumstances they could not have acted otherwise. The prosecutions referred to were instituted by their vaccination officer by direction of the Guardians, and in obedience to their resolu- tion I appeared with the officer in support of the informa- tions. Objection was made to such appearance by the persons summoned, and the magistrates decided to hear me. The concluding portion of Mr Forster's letter evidences a popular error. Magistrates are not nor were they ever pre- I eluded from hearing the non-professional representative of a complainant. The right to be represented by a solicitor is not the right of the solicitor, but of the complainant or the other party. Creation of this right did not in the least dis- turb the discretion of the justices. Had it been otherwise the authosity to non-professional clerks to Guardians to ap- pear before justices notwithstanding anything contained in the Solicitors Act is expressly provided by statute, and as the statutory provisions had been complied with the justices had no ol4aoll. I regret that absence from home prevents me from referring to the orders sod statutes applicable to the subject."—Dr MACKIE said it was evident Mr Forster had bees misled by the ruling of the Coroner, Mr Brig- house, who had ruled that nobody could speak in his court unless they were solicitors. If that gentleman were not specially informed on the subject he would naturally take the ruling from the general reports in the newspapers as be- ing applicable to the vaccination cases. He was glad that Mr Sutton had unearthed what would perhaps be a valuable means of bringing coroner's court matters into a better State than they were at present. (Hear, hear.) —Mr Ilemarsost said the coroner was no doubt technically rigbt. He was judge in his own court, and could please himself whether he heard a solicitor or not. But in the case of the magistrates, if they had decided not to hear Mr Sutton, Mr Sutton would perhaps have bowed to their decision.—The CLERK: Oh, no.—Mr HARRISON', continuing, said magic- trates certainly had a full right to permit anybody to be heard if they thought fit. In the case of Mr Brighouse, un- fortunately, he had the power to say whom he would hear in his own court. Mr Forster, the writer of the letter, had eYidently been under an impression which non-legal minds were liable to. He had not read with that legal acumen he would have done lead he hag a legal education.—Dr MACKIE: I understand from Mr Sutton that a client can select a party to appear for him.—The CLERK said the magistrates had the discretion to listen to a representative of a complainant, although he was a non-orofessional man. He (the clerk) then referred to the case of the well-known editor of a Lancashire newspaper, who many years ago in- sisted upon attending the coronet's inquiries. The Coroner refused to allow him, and the case was taken to the Superior Courts, and the decision was that inasmuch as the coroner's court was only a court of preliminary inquiry, the Coroner could exercise his own discretion, and that if he chose not to permit Mr Garnett to be present that gentleman could have no lawful right to be there. There was no doubt that while that was the decision of that day, the entire practice since has been otherwiee—(hear, hear,)—and his own view was that if the question again came before the Superior Courts, the judges would do what they were in the habit of doing, namely, say that the circumstances of the present day were so widely different that the usages of society and the good order of the courts was preserved by the presence of gen- tlemen of the position of Mr Garnett. There was another peculiar case which occurred before the passing of the Sum- mary Jurisdiction Acts, and which also went to the Superior Courts. A man wa.s summoned to the Petty Sessions for an offence. He took a solicitor with him, and the magis- trates said to the solicitor, " We won't have you fellows ,coming here to bother us about points of law. (Laughter.) We will not hear you." If the meitistrates had been con- tent to have simply made the statement and proceeded no farther, it was clear that no further difficulty could have followed, because they were probably right, but the solicitor insisted on remaining, and was somewhat unceremoniously bundled out of court, bag and baggage, for no doubt his papers went with him. (Laughter.) He brought an action, and the judges held that the magistrates had exceeded their power* that the solicitor had appeared in court as the friend and not as the solicitor of the person summoned, and, that being an open court, he was in that capacity en- titled to be present. The judges held that the magistrates in turning hiin out exceeded any authority they possessed. Those two decisions enabled them to see the distinction between summary jurisdiction courts and the courts of pre- liminary inquiry, and the propriety and perfect legality of non-professional persons appearing before the Courts of Petty Sessions if the magistrates had no dbjection.—ln answer to Mr Appleton, the CLERK also stated that his right to appear before the Newton magistrates in the vacci- nation cases arose from an express authority given by the statute under which the cases were tried.—The subject then dropped.

div.head: VACINCIES ON THE BOARD.
div.p: THE VACINCIES ON THE BOARD.

.—.-.-- Mr BIACIMURST roie to move a resolution of which he gave notice at the last meeting, to fill up the vacancies caused on the Board by the deaths of Major Cartwright (Warrington) and Mr Walmsley (Newton). As some gentle- men, he said, might think the Newton ratepayers were strongly enough represented already—although he did not think that was so himself—he would only move that they fill up the vacancy caused en the Board by the death of Major Cartwright. They might say that an election might cause them some expense, but he did net think that was a matter which rested with the Guardians. For his own part he believed that if the political parties kept quiet they would have a very proper representative sent there without a contest. But of course they could not interfere with these outside parties who had their reasons for what they did, but if they did cause an election the onus of the expenditure would not be on that Board, but on those parties. He thought that inasmuch as the Local Government Board said they were to have ten members for Warrington, and as there would be 18 months to intervene before a regular election, they ought to fill up the vacancies. Or if they did not do that and thought nine members sufficient, they should ask the Local Government Board to fix nine as the number. —Mr Ifertnesme suggested that Mr Blackhurst should move that the vacancy for Newton be also filled up.-Mr BLACKHURST then said he would do that, and in doing so said he was sorry to see that Newton was not so well represented as it used to be. The work seemed to be left in one or two bands, and there seemed to be a very strong feeling in Newton in favour of filling up the vacancies.—Dr INIAcruE said he had very much pleasure in seconding the motion, expressly as regarded Warrington. They were aware that there was a difficulty in finding Warrington Guardians on account of the Board meetings being on Wednesdays, and the attend- ance ol ef a tsht einWtahrer icnagsteosno fG snoawr d aonf s them. Ara s n o tTohf e rt eh ewva es r tyh be rees.t mark.—Mr Hamstge felt it bis duty to °ppm that reso- lution. At the meeting of the Board a month previously they decided to take no notice of the matter, and he thought ' it was unfortunate that it had been revived. He did not think that it added to the credit of any public body that et the character for vacillating conduct. It they should decide not to move in that matter and then a tdilidey appear shouidtoghim to be rather vacillating that a month ago month afterwards to come forward and endeavour to undo what they did then. Re wanted to know what advantage it would be to them if they were in the first place to involve Warrington in a contest and do the same for Newton ? toi incur to eb eexrpefeenrsree.d to the Local Government They would stir up a great deal of strife and cause the ex- penditure of a very considerable amount. The law had very properly provided that a Board of Guardians should not needlessly incur expense, and therefore the question of filling necessarypuevohs aea td vacancy wll was s malt called call cenittrasloi:twiocnu:lbdu tcosnosildoenrgwahsetithedriditexwiasst Board, and they in their superior wisdom—he sup- they had to deal with it. They had ni(ntehemeMmabyeorsr) War- rington who very fairly attended to their duty; at Newton they had four members, three of whom attended. ("No, fordetested no.") Well, as to their attendance they bad nothing to do. Whether one attended or three attended that was a question in the hands of the ratepayers of Newton. If the ratepayers elected gentlemen who did not attend to their duties the

fault rested with themselves. Besides, they had a host in Mr Appleton, who had been a Guardian 21 years, and con- stantly attended to his duties. He did not think the Lccal Government Beard would sanction an election, and he was afraid they would court defeat if they went to them. ("No, no.")—Mr JOLLEY would support Mr Harrison even if it was just because that if they passed the resolution they would be undoing what they did a month ago.—Mr CALD-. WELL said that if they made it a rule to fill up the vacancies they might have another election within the next six months.—Mr APPLETON thought it would very vacillating conduct on the Board's part to undo what they aid a month ago. He had heard no desire on the part of the ratepayers of Newton to fill up the vacancies.—Mr BLACSIILMST What about that petitioa ? (Hear, bear.)—Mr APPLETON said it was not a petition in the sense. It was simply to the effect that if there was to be an election and a con- teet he could put a nomination in. For his own part he should certainly vote against the resolution, for he was act an anti-vaccinator. tie had no faith in their views at all. He had simply said that if another candidate was nominated and they were bound to have a contest in Newton, he woald place the nomination of the anti-vaccinationism in. and they could then stand their chance. He thought himself, that they had a very poor chance in Newton. He hoped they ' would have a little consideration for the ratepayer-, of New- ton, and not cause the expense of an elecrion —.M.r OWEN opposed the resolution. There had been an expression dropped to the effect that if the political parties would let the matter alone here would be no contest, but, it struck him very forcibly that there would he a contest, and that it would boa party contest —Mr. DARSYSIIIRE supported the resolution. At the previous meeting, he said, when the matter was discussed, there were two or three members came into the room just as the motion was being put, and from what he had heard he believed that had they thoroughly understood the motion they would have voted tne contrary way. He had been thirking in his own mind why it was the Mayor led the opposition to filling up these vacancies, and he did not think he would be correct in saying that it was per- haps that it might save the Mayor trouble in its capacity as Mayor of Mrarrin,gton. He hoped the Mayor had not given way to that feeling. With regard to the number of mem- bers for Newton, they must not forget that the eopnlation of that township had increased to such an extent as to lead the Local Government Board to increase the memleere to four. He did not think they had ton many members when they had four, and they must remember that there was not a quorum at the Newton committee meetings unless there were three members present. They could not expect the , present three always to attend the committee meetings. It had always been the custom even when they had annnal elections always to rill up the vacancies, and it seemed to him to a certain extent to redact on the late members to say by not tilling up their places that their services could have been done without. ("No, no.") He hoped every sensible member of the Board would support the resolution. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—Dr Memets asked the clerk what had been the practice hitherto with regard to tilling up vacancies? For his part, he added, he thought such a man as Major Cartwright was worth half a-dozen of some of them —Mr EIARRISON : If we were to have another Major Cartwright it would be all right —The CLERK, in answer to Dr Mackie, said there had been only ene vacancy that he could remember that had not been tilled up, and that was not filled up because it occurred about a month before the election, and he himself advised that they could not fill it up before the annual election.—Mr HARRISON said that Mr Blackhurst had said there would probably not be an electioa if it were not for the political clubs. That "if " was a very important conjunction, and his belief was that the political feeling run so high at the present time in b sections of politicians that there would surely bs brou.;et out some gentleman to contest any vacancy that might oc- cur on that Board. They knew that there was a pa-ty crisis, almost just before a general election, and each pa-ty would endeavour to make their own body as strong as they possibly could in every department of local government. Therefore be had no doubt theme would be a contest.—Mr BLAME:MST, in replying, said that if any ratepayer in War- rington liked to write to the Local Government Board oa the subject it would not be a question whether they would allow the vacancies to be filled up; the Local Government Board would compel them to do it. It would say that the Board consisted of so many members, and we will compel von to keep that number of members.—The Cnairman being about to put the motien, Dr MACKIE said he hoped the names of those who voted would be taken. He did not wish it to go to the public that he had been disfranchising his fellow-ratepayers. (Hear, hear.)—Mr Ideanisose said he did not often differ from his friend, but he did not think that remark was quite fair. —The motion was then pot, when there voted for it : Messrs John Houghton, Gib- son, Kilshall, Derbyshire, Worthington, Mackie, and Black- burst. Thirteen voted against it, and it was accordingly declared lost. _ _

CONTRACTS The contracts of the following persons for the supply of the undermentioned articles for the ensuing half-year were accepted:—Beer and porter, Mr W Bolton; bread, Mrs Eckers- ley ; flour and meal, deferred; shoes, Mr Sudlow ; groceries, Mr Percival ; firewood, Messrs Nunnerley Co.; stones, Mr Robert Heaton ; coal and slack. Messrs Richardson and Co.; wines and spirits, Mr Scotson ; 'drapery, Ma Fletcher ; leather, tender referred to the House Committee; printing and sta- tionery (12 months), Messrs Gill and Wardrnan; glazing, Messrs Gaskell • coffins, Mr Barnes; clogs, Mr William Jones; milk andbutter, for new schools, Mr Joseph Hough- ton; workhouse, milk and butter to be obtained by Mr Mackey from Mr Warburton; potatoes, Mr Joseph Hough- ton • brushes, Mr Chester; drugs (12 months), Mr Hales, Bridge-street. THE REWARDS FOR RUNAWAY HUSBANDS. I Mr BLACKHURST said that no doubt the members of the Board had seen large placards on the walls offering I irge rewards for the apprehension of runaway husbands. It had ' been thought by many of the inhabitants that the rewards had been too large; people could scarcely understand why there should be such a large number of offenders. The mat- ter had, if he remembered rightly, been spoken of in the Town Council. He had met Mr Shearer, their assistant re- .. _

Hewing office', who had supplied him with some information on the subject, and the statistics he had prepared would show the Board there had been no extravagance. One man who had deserted his wife and seven children had cost the Guar- ' diens and ratepayers £250. another £l7l, another .i.:102„ 'another £53, and another £6o—altogether over £6so.—Dr MACKIE said he hid nothing additional to say on the sub- ject, except that it was alluded to incidentally at the late meetiteg of the Town Council. Some remarks were also made with reference to the drinking habits of the young I women of the town. The two subjects got mixed together, and a reply was made by one of the ablest members of the ' Council, but in somewhat ever stroog language, and calcu- lated to suggest that these cases were not so bad as they ap- peared to be, and that they were the product of a newspaper not named, belonging to some other town than Warrington—in fact, that the reportere ' manufactured the news on purpose to make a sensation. Warrington was not referred to, but if he had had the chance he would hive denied the charge made on the part of all the newspapers connected with Liverpool or Manchester. (Hear, hear.) All that the editors had said, and all the whips that had been manufactured, were not too much to lash these rascally husbands when they considered that Eve persons had cost the Guardians upwards of .£B5O in the maintenance of their wives and families.—Mr CALDWELL said Warrington was not the only town in which runaway husbands were as plentiful as blackberries. They were just as numerous in Macclesfield, Rochdale, Manchtstir, and other towns -Mr HARRISON said he thought these statistics would help to dispel the idea that the Guardians had offers I extrava- gant rewards for the apprehension of delinqeents of the character which had been describnl. It appeared that five men had cost the Guardians and the ratepayers upwards of MOO. That it was necessary to offer rewards in cases of Ithis kind was beyond all doubt.—Mr JOELEY thought it would be false economy not to offer rewards—Mr DARBY- SHIRE said he had been spoken to in an opposite sense to iwbat Mr Blackhurst had. He had been told that they were 'behind other towns in offering rewards.—Mr ApELETON said a substantial reward would not only bring mote apprehen- sions. but act as a deterrent in preventing men who were contemplating running away from doing so.—The CHAIR- MAN said his experience had gone to show that a good deal of wife desertion Was owing to too early marriages, the Venn.' husband not being able to keep his wife, and in con- sequence taking his "hook."—After a little further discue- , eion on this subject the Board adjourned.

ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A Poracriwts.—A miner named Bell is in custody at Gateshead on a charge of attempting to murder Police-constable Briens. The offieer give infor- mation a few days ago against Bell for poaching, and he was fined. Next day he came out of a plantation at Haworth as Briens was passing and fired several shots from two re- volvers at the constable, who escaped uninjured. CHESTED, CASTLE PRISON.—The final Seen in cmnection with the closing of Chester Castle Prison to civil prisoners took place on Saturday, when, by order of the Home Office, all the prisoners were removed to Knutsford Gaol. The ("Ale now remains in exclusive possession of the military authorities as an establishment for military prisoners. The whole of the staff of officers and warders have received ap- pointments at other gaols, Mr Lloyd, the late warder in charge, having been promoted 0 the governorship of Hun- tingdon Prison.

17.0DGEn CLATMS.—The Plymouth Revising Barrister's Court was held on Tuesday. When the lodger claims were considered. the Revising Barrister suggested a compromise, and the Liberal agent offered to let all the Conservative claims piss if the Conservatives would do the same with regard to Liberal claims. This offer was loudly cheered for the assembled claimants, and after a little disculsion the ; Conservative agent consented. Bv the result of thisdecision the Liberals claim a large majority on this lodger franchise, as there were no less than 1,600 objections made by the Conservative agent. RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending 25th March. 1888.—The GUARDIANS of the FOR of the RUNCORN UNION are desirous of receiving TE NDE RS from parties willing to CON- TRACT for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter; Cod Liver and Paraffin Oil; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein arui brisket pieces, the price to include about 301bs. per week of the best bktcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; Best Brand lets American or English Bacon: Potatoes; Wheat Straw; Drapery and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, .as per samples, to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile. and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the above-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars may be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be lomat ded to the Clerk's office, Frodsbam, on or before Monday, the 29th day of September. 1884, endorsed Tender for ," The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 30th September, 1884, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if re- quired by the Guardians. By order of the Board, H. LINAKER, Frodsham. 2nd Septembar. 1885. Clerk to the Guardians,

THE Tories, whatever their shortcomings, possess one English quality in an eminent degree—they don't know when they are beaten. They had hoped against hope, until they had finally almost persuaded themselves, that the tide had turned against the PRIME MINISTER even in Scotland. They had gone the length of asserting that he did not dare to meet his constituents; and now when he is received again with open arms, when the people are more enthusiastic than ever— when he has, to use a homely figure, carried all before him —they will not hear of sur_ render, but show rather, like MACBETH, that they will at least die with harness on their backs. Sir RICHARD CROSS Was sent forward last week as a sort of scout, but nobody ex- pected much of him, and nobody has been disappointed It is otherwise with Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE ; he is the recognised leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons, and as such he has gone to Edinburgh to attempt to reply to Mr. GLADSToNE. He made sundry little speeches on Monday which were in the nature of apologies in view of the big thing which was promised for Tuesday. The "big thing" has come off, but in contrast with one of the Midlothian speeches of the PRIME MINISTER it seems rather small. There is a good deal of talk about the misrepresentation of the Liberals; but nothing is furnished in the way of proof, while as to the main issue—the question of the Franchise Bill—Sir STAF- FORD NORTHCOTE flounders hopelessly in the vain attempt to make the worse appear the better cause. It is to his credit that he does not resort to the " howling " which Lord HOPETOWN seems to have expected of him, and that he is always good-tempered if not always coherent. He turned to pretty good account a reference to the "fatted calf" by suggest- ing that Mr. GLADSTONE had "set up the Franchise Bill not with the hope that it would do good to anybody in particular, but in the hope that it would induce the electors

of Scotland and other parts of the United Kingdom to give down their milk pretty freely to his support." This statement was received with laughter and cheers, but, taking it at its best, is it not an admission on the face of it that Mr. GLADSTONE, as the leader of the Liberals, lays himself out to serve the people, while the Tories have neglected to do anything of the kind? To say, however, that the Franchise Bill has not been set up with the hope that it will do good to anybody in particular is, we are persuaded, a rhetorical lapsus. Nobody knows better than Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE that Mr- GLADSTONE'S life gives the lie to such an assertion, and, to do him justice, nobody amongst the Conservatives is, as a rule, more ready to acknowledge the benevolent mo- tives of the PREMIER than the leader of the Conservatives in the House of Commons. Still, people who complain so loudly of misrepresentation should avoid occupying a " Crystal " Palace which is anything but a "Palace of Truth," for when stones are thrown under such circumstances there is some risk of windows being broken. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE was scarcely more felicitous in his remark as to the Franchise Bill and Redistribution that "the Liberals were endeavouring to place them in the same position that a man would be in if his friends insisted upon his marrying, but refused him permission to see the lady." The compari- son, like the policeman's lot, is "not a hapPY one ;" it is too suggestive of bigamy or poly- gamy. So far as the Franchise Bill is con- cerned, it has been on view for months, and its virtues or failings, such as they are, have been proclaimed from the house tops. There can be no pretence that permission has been refused to see that lady; and as to No. 2-- the lady Redistribution—the Master of the Household has given pod account of her, and promised that she, too, shall be "On view" at the proper time. All he insists on is that No. I is charming in herself, and that marrying one lady at a time is quite enough to undertake. What more would the Tories have? If they want to "Americanise our institutions" in the very worse way, they had better go at once to Salt Lake City? Touching the fact that the Franchise and Redistribu- tion have not been dealt with in one session because there was not time for passing both bills, Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE remarks that "a large proportion of the 25 nights spent on the Franchise Bill would have been saved altogether if the two bills had been brought forward at the same time." No doubt fewer nights would have been occupied iwith the Franchise Bill, for the Tories have been a,t their wits-end in prolonging their opposition to it ; but is anv sane person pre- pared to say, judging from what has happened last session, that the two bills would have been likely to pass? Sir STAFFORD NORTH- ! COTE does not say so, and until he can honestly make that statement, it is just SO much dust thrown in the eyes to make anY other. But if we go the length of assuming that the House of Lords, in whose behalf so much is said, were convinced that two measures of this magnitude could have been passed during the past session, the question still arises whether they are justified in throw- ing out a bill admittedly good because the Government have committed. as they think, an error of judgment. The issue is narrowed in this case to one not of principle, but of procedure; and the doctrine that an obsolete body like the House of Lords, non-representative and irresponsible alike to crown and country, shall become a Caucus to supersede the Cabinet as to the conduct of the business of the State is so monstrous in its nature, so utterly opposed to the traditions of a people determined to be free—as to warrant and to ensure, if persisted in, the utter extinction of the House of Lords as a part of the constitu- tion. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, in the course of his speech, incidentally points out that those who contend for the Franchise as a right are "going a long way towards the statement of universal suffrage ;" and, he adds, "that which they have to consider is the proper distribution of power." This is good. old-fashioned Toryism, and if those who are doing all they can to prevent the Franchise Bill becoming law would take their stand upon it, as of old, we could respect their honesty however much we might question their judgment. But the fact is the leaders of the Tory party are at "sixes and sevens" as to their "principles." Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL flies from pole .to pole, and shouts anything anywhere between, ' while as to Lord SALISBURY it is not many weeks since, at Manchester, he enunciated the doctrine of numbers pure and simple as a basis of redistribution. This conflict amongst the guides is discouraging. Why not "toss for it" as to which of their new or old notions they will stand by? Coming to the question of finance, the EX-CHANCELLOR of the Ex- CHEQUER was much concerned to repair the reputation which has been so much damaged by the PRIME MINISTER. He tossed figures about pretty freely, but did not shake the main contention of Mr. GLADSTONE that, comparing the four years of Liberal rule with the last four years of Conservative adminis- tration, there was a balance to the credit of the present Government of at least nine mil- lions. It is remembered against Sir STAF- FORD NORTHCOTE that he was a treasurer who didn't pay his way; that he, went into office with a surplus of six millions, and went out of office leaving a debt of over six millions. He might well propose on Tuesday to "leave out altogether what is spent on debt." It is convenient no doubt to him, but confusing to the nation. Slightly altering Byron one may say— Explaining his finances to the nation I wish he would explain his explanation. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE must try again; he has not yet replied in Midlothian to "the Midlothian speeches."

ST. HELENS has been more favoured than Warrington in having had the honour of a visit from Cardinal MANNING. It was a matter of deep regret that his Eminence was not able last week, by reason of temporary in- disposition, to fulfil his engagement to de- liver a temperance address at Warrington ; and it was feared that the people of St. Helens would, from the same cause, be sub- ject to a similar disappointment. Happily, by taking care in time, he was sufficiently re- covered to give an address to St. Helens scholars on Sunday afternoon, to preach at the Church of the Holy Cross in the evening, and to open the Providence Hospital on Monday forenoon. It is characteristic of his Eminence that he should have lent his in- fluence and eloquence to a work of this kind. Wherever the name of Cardinal MANNING is known—and that may be said to be through- out the British Empire—it is associated with measures for the bettering of the condition of the poorer classes. He has had a long and wide experience of the evils ensuing from ,the drinking habits of the community, and,

as he is a practical philanthropist, he has worked hard, and still works hard, in the cause of temperance. By precept and ex- ample, he has stimulated the clergy of the Roman Catholic Church to grapple with the evil in their midst, and the result is that thousands have been saved from the curse of strong drink who would other- wise in all probability have filled drunkards' graves. In advocating the cause ot the Pro- vidence Hospital at Hardshaw Hall, Cardinal MANNING was engaged on Monday in a not less sacred duty. St. Helens has been some- -what behind other towns of its size and im- portance in not possessing an Infirmary or Free Hospital. The Cottaire Hospital at Peasley Cross could scarcely be said to belong to St. Helens, and beyond this consideration it was not a Free Hospital. The institution begun by the Sisters of the Holy Cross in a house in George-street, eighteen months ago, has from the first been open, as the report states, "to all corners who have the claim which poverty and sickness give." The patients are received without distinction of creed, and the institution can therefore legitimately appeal to every section of the community for that aid in its new and enlarged sphere which we do not doubt will be readily forthcoming. St. Helens may now be congratulated, not only on its Free Hos- pital, but on its being opened by so distin- guished a prince of the Catholic Church as •his Eminence Cardinal MANNING.

AT a meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, a motion was sub- mitted in tavour of filling up two vacancies on the Board—one in the Warrington and another in the Newton district. Assuming that there was no special objection to the course proposed, it would be supposed that, so far as the Board are concerned, they would not stand in the way of the vacancies be. ing filled up in the usual fashion. But they do; they have so much faith in their own wisdom that they do not want any addition to the stock. It is nothing, it seems, to them that the ratepayers may have ideas of their own as to completeness of representation; they are the men in possession, and they are not dis- posed to open the door to anyone else. Mr. HARRISON (the Mayor of Warrington), in leading the opposition to the proposal, urged that an election would "stir up a great deal of strife, and cause the expenditure of a very considerable amount." But on this principle it would be convenient to avoid any election of Guardians, or for that matter a general Parliamentary election. How would he like to see a Liberal Government in power till doomsday as a means of avoiding strife and expenditure? Or, to take narrower ground, would he be satisfied to see the borough un- represented, say for eighteen months, in case • the present member should resign? It seems to us that the Board have been thinking too much of themselves, and too little of those whom they are elected to represent, One member appeared to wonder if Mr. HARRISON objected to an election in order to save himself "trouble in his capacity as Mayor of Warrington ;" and, seeing that he was dumb as to this consideration, we are in- clined to wonder too. It is a motive which certainly ought not to have weight; for those who are anxious to take office should at least be willing to perform such duties as may devolve upon them in their high estate. Whatever the reason, the Board by a large majority rejected the motion, thus in a mea- sure, as one member remarked, disfranchis- ing their fellow-ratepayers. Whether the ratepayers will be content to be thrust aside in this way remains to be seen. They may appeal to the Local Government Board, in which case it may be found that the Guar- dians are not, after all, masters of the situa- tion.

RuNconet PARISH Cnusen.—At this church, on Sunday, the Rev T Abraham, formerly a missionary at Toowcomba, Queensland, preached two sermons in behalf of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. The collections amounted to £l2 CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.— The first meeting of this society was held on Friday even- ing last week, whm the Rev T Hackett delivered a lecture on "The use and abuse of the sense of humour." Mr H Randle, the president, was in the chair. Bare RIBBON ARMY, RUNCORN —The usual weekly entertainment was held on Saturday evening, in the Co- operative Hall, and there was a good audience. The band of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen gave vocal and instrumental selections of music. FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL SCHOLARSHIPS.—The free scholarships given by the Widnes Council of Educa- tion, tenable for three years at Parnworth Grammar School, were competed for during last week. They have been carried off by Charles Bate, of the Simms Cross Board Schools and George Henry Sherratt, of the West Bank Board Schools. CONCERT AT WIDNES.—On Saturday evening an enter- tainment was given in the new Temperance Hall, under the presidency of Mr J R Taylor, of St Helens. There was only a poor attendance. A programme consisting of vocal and instrumental music and recitations was gone through in good style by Messrs F Hayes, T Wilson, and W Mil- lington (Runcorn), Jessop, Smith, and Taylor, and Miss Polly Bradburn (Widnes). WESLEYAN DAY SCFIOOL, WESTON.—The scholars of the above school held their avanual exclusion on Friday, at Mersey View, Overton. Messrs James Ford. William- and Thomas Griffiths, James Dunbabin and John Roberts, farmers, of Weston, kindly conveyed' the children to and from Overton in their spring carts and waggons. Numbers of the parents and relatives gathered during the day, and all seemed to make the most of their day's outing. on the return journey fruit was distributed. The party arrived safely at Weston shortly before eight o'clock, well pleased with the day's enjoyment. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT WESION POINT. The annual harvest thanksgiving services in connection with Christ Church, Weston Point. were held on Friday and Sunday. The sacred edifice had been tastefully decorated by Mrs Bryant, Miss L Clarke Miss B Clarke, Miss K Rosenberg, the Misses McLean, the Rev J J Bryant, and Messrs L Res- enberg, John and Thomas Jeffs. Flowers, fruit, &a, were given by Dr Steele, Messrs J Brundrit, J P, J B Hughes. L B Wells, J T Brunner (Northwich), L Rosenberg. John Jeffs, and Captain Clarke. On Friday evening the preacher was the Rev A Anderson, vicar of Dunham Mae- may. There was a large congregation. The choir rendered the anthem "Ye shall dwell in the land." Mr Appleton singing the bass solo in excellent style. Miss M Clarke presided at the harmonium. On Sunday the Rev J J Bry- ant occupied the pulpit. ATTEMPT TO WRECE A. TRAIN NEAR WIDNES.--What can only be cheracterised as a diabolical attempt to wreck a train was discovered on the Cheshire Lines Railway be- tween Widnes and Hough Green on Sunday afternoon. As NO train passes Moor-lane signal box between the hour of 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. on Sundays, the signalman is permitted to be off duty during that period. About two o'clock on Sunday, Signalman Martin was walking aleng the line to- wards the box, when he saw some object on the metals about fifty yards ahead. He proceeded to the spot, and dis- covered that the platelayers' trolley bad been placed across the metals, with a large heavy sleeper placed against it in order apparently to enable it to give more resistance to a train. Martin obtained assistance and removed the formid- able obstruction. The exprEss from Manchester to Liver- pool was due in a quarter of an hour. The Company's detectives are investigating the matter.

div.p: JUBILEE SINGERS AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.—The North Carolina coloured vocalists and jubilee singers on Monday evening gave a concert of sacred masic in the National In- fanta' School, Runcorn, in aid of the funds to erect a chapel in connection with the Shaw University, Raleigh, North Carolina. The Rev J M Armson presided, and there was a moderate attendance. On Tuesday and Wednesday evenings the vocalist performed in Lacey-street Wesleyan School- room, Widnes, and received a fair amount of support. FIRE AT FARNWORTE.—REROIC ACTlON.—Shortly after seven o'clock on Thursday evening a fire was discovered in one of the bedrooms at Charles Ville, Farnworth. the resi- dence of Mr W A Watts, M.A., head master of Farnworth Grammar School, by Ann Dodd, the domestic servant. Dodd had only a few minutes previously placed one ot Mr Watt's children is a swing cot, which is placed near the window. Between the cot and the door of the room is a four-prst bedstead, and it was in this that the fire origina- ted. The bedstead was rendered totally useless, but not altogether destroyed. The child would have been suffocated but for the heroic action ef a young man named Walter Patten, who rushed through the smoke and flames to the cot and brought the child in safety, but in an unconscious state. The smoke was so dense that he had to grope his way to the cot. Dr Booth's assistant attended the child, who recovered two hours afterwards. Mr Watts was in Widnes at the time visiting a friend. The flames were extinguished by neighbours; and the damage is of trifling extent. How the fire originated is a mystery, as the servant states she did not take a light in the room. ALARMING ACCIDENT TO SUPERINTENDENT LEAH, OF RUNCORN.—About nine o'clock on Friday evening Superin- tendent Leah and Constable Smith were returning to Run- corn in a trap loaded with weights and measures, and when near the farm of Mrs Parry, Halton, the horse took fright at a large dog, and ran violently against a wall. The occupants of the vehicle were thrown into the road, and the horse pro- ceedea down Halton-road at a wild gallop. Mr Thomas Wright, of Halton, accompanied by his wife and daughter, , was driving up the lane at the time, and hearing the runa- way coming he drew his conveyance close to the hedge side. Notwithstanding this precaution the trap came in contact with the conveyance, smashed several spokes in the wheel, twisted the axle, and knocked one of the shafts out of its socket The runaway. however, continued its mad career for a farther distance of 30 Yards, when the trap turned over, and threw the horse to the ground. The vehicle' was Smashed and the weights were scattered in all directions. I while the horse received a serious injury to the head. Mr Leah was seriously wounded on the forehead, and both his hands were also injured, but after he had been attended to by Dr Carruthers he was able to proceed home. Constable Smith was fortunate enough to escape uninjured. MARRIAGE OF A RUNCORN CLERGYMAN'S SISTER. A fashionable marriage, and one in which particular interest wee taken, took place at Gleneglary Church, Kingstown, on' Thursday, when Mr John Macenchy, M D of Downpatrick, son of the late Rev W Vaconchy, rector of Coolick. was united to Miss Henrietta Gertrude Preston, daughter of the late Rev D Preston, rural dean and rector of Tonwegan, a grand-daughter of the late Right Hon Lord Carberry, and of William Preston, Judge of Appeal. The bride wag given away by her brother, the Rev J Evans Preston, rector of Julianstown. She was attired in an elegant bridal dress of rich cream coloured satin, trimmed with broche and fine lace, with a flowing veil as a head dress. The bridesmaids were Miss Mabel Preston, Miss Preston. and Miss Irvine. The ceremony was performed by the Rev Win Preston. MA, vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, assisted by the Rev George Preston, rector of Mount Temple (brothers of the bride), and the Rey W Green. The wedding party was large, and in- cluded many persons of distinction. At the wedding break- fast there was a numerous and distinguished company. The presents to the bride were both costly and nu- merous, and: amongst them were an elegant diamond and and sapphire ring from Lady Castlemaine ; an exquisite bracelet from Lady Preston; and a chaste Indian pectoral cross from the Hon Miss Hancock. The happy couple left Ireland to spend the honeymoon in Wales. CHARGE AGAINST A WESTON PUBLICAN.—Bcfore Mr F Rigby and Mr James Handley at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. Phcebe Barrow, landlady of the Royal Oak Inn, Weston, was summoned to answer a charge of having on the 30th ult kept open ber premises for the sale of in- toxicating liquor daring prohibited hours, to persons not bona-fide travellers or persons lodging therein. She was also summoned for selling liquor at the same time.—Mr E A Fletcher appeared for the defendant. The witne.ses were ordered out of court.—P.C. Cooper stated that about twenty minutes past one on the morning of the day in question he was on duty near the defendant's house. In consequence of sounds he heard he went roiled to the backyard door, and finding it fast he climbed over. He waited for a few minutes and then a man named Samuel Jones who lives in the house, opened the house door, and he (witness) walked into the kitchen. Here be found Peter Brookes, John Costello, Bartley Costello. Thomas Mclntosh. James Austin, Kate Murphy, and Annie Costello, all persons who did not live on the premises. On the table were four glasses three-parts full of beer, and several wine glasses containing either wine or spirits. He asked the landlady to explain how it was she had all these persons in the house, and she replied in a jocular tone that they were all lodgers. He said, " Mrs Barrow, I know better than that; they are not." "Well," she replied, "They are only having a bit of a party."—By Mr Fletcher: The persona in the house were all Mrs Barrow's friends and customers.—By Mr Rigby : There had been a previous conviction against the house during Mrs Barrow's husband's lifetime.—Mrs Barrow said her last husband had only been dead ten months. She had lost three husbands out of that house.—Mr Fletcher having briefly addressed the Bench, called Mrs Barrow, who deposed that Friday, the 29th August was the anniversary of her birthday, and she invited the persons named by the constable to a supper. With the exception of Kate Murphy, who was her servant, they were all intimate friends. They arrived at the house about a quarter to ten, but as most of the guests were Catholics, and debarred from eating meat on Fridays, the supper was not commenced until midnight.—Elizaheth Ann Carson, daughter of the defendant, corroborated this state- ment. —Annie Costello, Bartley' Costello, James Austin, and Peter Brooks also gave evidence agreeing that they were in- vited to a supper, and did not pay for any liquor in the house after closing hours.—Superintendent L3ah elicited that John Costello had only been in the house about five minutes when the constable arrived, but they denied that he had anything to drink.—Mr Rigby said the Bench were of opinion that the charge was not proved, and the case would therefore be dismissed. The evidence for the defence NM not, however, altogether satisfactory. A WARNING TO RUNCORN PUBLICANS. Thomas Wil- liamson, landlord of the Queen's Hotel, Waterloe-road, ap- peared before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday morning to answer acharge of having on the sth 'twit exposed for sale a certain article of food, to wit, whiskey, and that he did unlawfully refuse to sell a pint of the same to Superin- tendent Leah, for the purpose of analysis.—Superintendent Leah said in consFquence of something that came to his knowledge, he went on the fifth September to the defend- ant's house to take samples of spirits for analysis. Before entering the house he sent in Constable Smith in plain clothes to purchase a small glass of whiskey iR order to as- certain where the defendant supplied customers from. He followed the constable in, and asked for a pint of whiskey. The barmaid named O'Neil recognised him, he presumed, for she immediately called her master, and he (the superinten- dent) gave him the bottle to place the whiskey in. He at once walked into the back place as if to fetch the whiskey from a cask in the cellar, and although the superintendent called to him would not return. In a short time be came back, to the bar with a pint of whiskey, and the superintendent told him that be did not want the whiskey from the cask in the cellar, but from where he sup- plied customers from. The defendant replied that be did not supply whiskey from the bar, and added, "You asked me for a pint of whiskey and I shall fill it you from where I you like." The superintendent asked him repeatedly to supply him from where he supplied customers, but the de- fendant ref used.—By Defendant: He did not say there was not a pint of whiskey in the keg or that it was impossible to serve him from it as there was none in it.—P C Smith, assis- tant inspector of weights and measures, deposed that he was I served with a small glass of whiskey from a keg marked brandy in the bar. He afterwards pointed out the keg to the superintendent. When the superintendent asked for a pint of whiskey there was nothing said about there being no whiskey in the keg. The spirit flowed plentifully when she served him.—Annie O'Neil, servant to the defendant, said when the superintendent came in she told the defendant a 1 man in the bar wanted a pint of whiskey and there was no more in the keg. The defendant told her to bring him the bottle and he would serve him out of the kitchen. There was not a drop in the keg. She had a hard job to get a half of a glass for Smith. The Superintendent questioned the witness why she did not tell him there was no more whiskey in the keg, but she did not give a satisfac- tory replv.—Julia Riley said she heard last witness tell de- fendant there was not sufficient whiskey in the keg; and the defendant filled the keg up after the superintendant had left. She did not hear the defendant say he would serve the su- perintendent from where liked.—Mrs Williamson gave cor- roborative testimony.—Defendant was told that he could be sworn an I give evidence if he desired, but he declined, stat- ing the witnesses he had called were sufficient to show the true facts of the case. He alleged that the superintendent did not tell him who he was. but PC Smite was recalled and denied this statement, and added that the defendant knew the superintendent very well.—The Bench fined the defen- dant £2, and costs 14s 6d,

SUCCESS OF LIEUT. A TIMMINS, OF RUNCORN.—In the list' of officers who have successfully passed the July examina- tion in tactics, held at Salford 'Barracks, Salford, there ap- pears the name of Lieut. A Timmins, of the F Company, 2nd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers. Out of the large number of officers who presented themselves, Lieutenant Timmins is one of the six who passed with Bpecll mention. THE ROBBERY AT SOUTHPORT —On Friday week, at the Southport Police Court, a young man named Joseph Crompton, who said he was a weigher in a chemical works at Widnes, was charged on remand with stealing three silver albert guards, a silver pencil case, some studs and solitares, from the shop of Mr James Watts, watchmaker and jeweller, Lord-street, Southport, under circumstances pre- viously reported.—The Chairman (Mr J Atkinson, J.P.) said the magistrates had much commiseration for the parents; and would deal leniently with him. They then sentenced him to two months' imprisonment with hard labour. The value of the articles stolen was aBs lid. THE BLOCKING OF WEST BANK-STREET. WIDNES.—Last evicting the Highway Committee of the Local Board held special meeting to consider the action to be taken with regard to the blocking up of West Bank-street by Messrs. Bolton and Son, ironfounders. The fourteen days' notice given to the firm to remove the obstruction had expired, and no attempt had been made to comply with the Board's re- quest. A representative of Messrs. Bolton attended the meeting in order to obtain some concession from the Board, hut the committee firmly declined to compromise the matter in any way whatever. The consequence is that Messrs: Bolton have undertaken to remove the obstruction immediately.

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—Tbe Rev S B Handley, of Stafford, preached the anniversary ser- mons on Sunday to good congregations. The collections amounted to about £6. SINGING•CLASSES AT HUNCORN.—Mr John Holford, who last year successfully conducted classes in singing by the tonic solfe method, has arranged a concert for next Wed- nesday evening, as a preliminary to the commencement of the classes for the winter months. The concert will take place in Ellesmere-street schoolroom, and a certificated choir will illustrate in a practical manner the system taught by Mr Holford, who will deliver an address. .
