RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The Bev. Canon Barclay presided at the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. There . were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and John Lock- wood, Messrs. Handley, Norman, Mclntyre, Stokes, Smith, Aaron, P. Speakman, Midwood, Hamilton, Wallington, C. Rigby, Weir, Campkin, W. Whittaker, Mounfleld, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (d eputy clerk). MR, NORM&N DEFENDS HINSELF.-Ar. Aaron asked, as Mr. Norman was present, for some explanation of the ex- penses of the " pic-nic" to Chester Asylum.—Mr. Norman replied that if Mr. Aaaron would look into these things pro- perly and keep his mouth shut he would do a great deal better.—Mr. Rigby said he wanted a bill of particulars.— Mr. Norman : You will get no bill of particulars from me. —The Chairman, we have passed a cheque for the expenses. —The Rev. J. Lockwood did not think it reflected credi- tably upon the Board that the deputation !lurid' give their time and labour, and be bested in this fashion when asking for their mere expenses to be paid. Ile suggested that in future the clerk should pay them througta the petty cash book.—Mr. Midwood : It appears you would rather go through the beck door.—Rev. J. Lockwood: Not at all.— Mr. Midwood : It has every appearance of it.—Rev. J. Lockwood I hope we are not ace.mstomed to. bank door

business at this Board.—Mr. Norman remarked that Mr. Midwooct was quite aware that when a deputation went from &public board the clerk always paid the expenses.— Mr. Midwood said he had not a word to say about that; but be contended that every Guardian ought to know the cost. Mr. Lockwood was proposing that the Bbard have nothing to do with it.—Mr. Norman: Nothing or the kind. The clerk would pay the expenses, but you would have just the bill brought you in the same manner as usual.—Mr. Mid. wood eaid he did not understand that.—Mr. Norman observed that at the present time, when the deputation went to Chester one member wonld say he had'nt got any money, another that he hadn't sufficient, and a third that he wouldn't pay if he had any—(laughter)—and the lot fell upon Jonah— (renewed laughter)—who always got insulted when he brought the bill in. (Laughter.)—Rev .3, Lockwood, to show that he did not want any back door business, suggested that the sum to be expended by the deputation should be limited to so much—(Mr Rigby: "That's it")—but don't let the deputation be reflected upon year after year.—The discussion then ceased. A NOVEL APPLICATION —The Deputy Clerk read a letter from Messrs A and J B Fletcher, solicitors, of Northwich, who stated they were instructed by Mr Owen Gough, jun. of Lower Whitley, to respectfully request the Guardians of the Runcorn Union to Call upon Mr George Mounfield, assistant overseer. of Lower Whitley, to find another surety for the due discharge of his duties in lieu of Mt Gough. Mr Mounfield had behaved to Mr Gough in such a manner as amply to justify the writer's client in the application he now made, and as there was an end of all confidence between surety and principal they trusted the Guardians would accede to his request.—The Deputy Clerk said. the Board were satisfied that they had got two good bondsmen, and , why, therefore, should they interfere in this matter P—Toe letter was placed on the table. Da McDoooari,—The following letter was read : " Argylt Villa, Heaton, Bolton. My dear sir,--rt is at a time of deep sorrow that one feels much the need of the sympathy of friends and the resolution of condolence passed by the Board of Guardians at their last meeting is an assur- ranee to ins of bow much they feel for me in my over- whelming grief and irreparable loss. Will you kindly con- vey to the rromibers of the Board at their next meeting my sincere thanks for, this expression of their sympathy, and let me add also how much I appreciate your own senti- ments expressed in your kind letter.—l am, yours very sincerely, F. McDouoratt.. Henry Linaker, Esq , Frod- sham." FINANCE.—Mr Handley reported that the Finance Com- mittee recommended the payment of £1,515 Ils 83 county rate, and £3 to Mr Foulkes as compensation for damage sustained. He found from the tre,tsurer's statement that there was only a balance of £540 5s 10d at the bank, and those townships who had not paid their rates ought certainly to send their contributions. The Clerk had just reported a gift of £232 from the Government, and there would therefore only be a balance of £772 5s 103 to work the union.—The accounts were passed. The Board then went into committee to consider the ad- ministration of relief in the Runcorn district.

ALLEGED OUTRAGE ON WIDNES YOUNG MEN. It is alleged that on Saturday night a murderous outrage was committed between Hunt's•cross and Woolton, the par- ticulars of which have only just leaked out. Two young men, named Alfred Moore and George Stanley, clerks in the employ of Messrs W Pilkington and Soo, chemical manu- facturers, Moss Bank. Widn-s, went by the 9.20 Cheshire Lines train to accompany a friend. named Robert Moore. a painter, home to Wootton. Alter leaving the train they walked together along the road, and when near Mrs Todd's house, between Host's-cross and Woolton, they met a score of Irishmen, to whom they, in a quiet friendly way, bide "Good night." The Irishmen made a rush at them, saying, "We will give you ' good night,' you —," and pushed them down on the ground. They then, while prostrate, stabbed, kicked, and beat them in a shocking manner, and with great brutality. Moorst has seven different wounds on his head, which the assistant to Dr Woods, of Wootton, says must have been inflicted by a cutting instrument. Stanley is very much injured about the head and upper parts of the body as the results of kicks, and his flesh is much swollen. Their cries for help brought to their assistance Mr Holbrook Gaskell's groom and helper, and as soon as the Irishmen heard the footsteps approtching they made off. Stanley was then on the ground, insensible, in a pool of blood. Moore and !goof-a, together with the groom and helper, followed the Irishmen, in order to see if they could capture or identify any of them. On overtaking them the Irishmen again brutally assaulted them, and on a sergeant ! of police and six constables, who in the mean Nine had been ' apprised of the occurrence, coming up they made off again. The five injured men were takea into the houses in the ! locality and medically treated, and the miscreants were followed, and three of their number—named respectively Patrick, Anthony, and Michael Ginley, two brothers and a cousin—were arrested. They will be brought up at Wootton on Friday. All the young men have been much injured and prostrated by the treatment which they received. _

FUNERAL OF COLONEL TALBOT, OF ASTON. The funeral of the late Lieut-Colonel Hervey Talbot, who died on toe 11th inst. at Aston Grauer., Aston, near Prod- sham, took place at Aston Parish Church, on Monday, amid a scene of the utmost sorrow. The funeral was not strictly a military one, although many miiitary men were present. The cortege left Aston Grange about three o'clock in the afternoon, and proceeded to the chuich at Aston. The in- terment took place in the private ground of the family, and the officiating clergy were the Bev Arthur Talbot, half- brother to the deceased and rector of Cho rcheaton, in Staf- fordshire ; the Rev Edward' 2%larsilen, vicar of Aston; and the Rev E Blot, curate of Aston. The coal was An aken one, polished and mounted with silver, h ivimmic a sift,r plate bearing the inscription—" Hervv Talbot, bo.n titai October, 1838; died 11th Septenab,2r, 1884:" The coffin was covered with the Union Jack, and on rime top were plac-'d th- sword and helmet of the deceased officer. A detachment of staff- sergeants carried the coffin, there being eight bearers. The commissioned officers and non-conpnisiioned officers present numbered about 35. They were from the 3rd Battalion Ist Staffordshire Militia (King's own), .quartered at Lichfield, of which the deceased was Lieut-Colonel. The funeral pro- cession was headed by the labourers on the Aston estate, latter which the coffin, and immediately following this the relatives of the deceased, among whom were Mr Algernon i Charles Talbot, of Aston Hall, nephew of the deceased, Mr j Arthur Chetwynd, also a nephew, the Hon Wellington P j M C Talbot, honorary Colonel of the list Staffordshire regi- ment of Militia, and uncle to the deceased, the Hon Geoffry Hill, la, other-in-law to the deceased, Mr Gramshaw, Mr W Crawshaw, Mr F B Herbert, solicitor, London, Mr Henry Linaker, ana Mr C E Linaker, agents to the ; Aston estates, Messrs yr H Linaker (solicitor), and ' H G Linaker, all of Frodsham. These were fol- lowed by a numerous train of tenants on the estate. and a large number of other tenants and dwellers in the dis- trict who attemied out of respect to the deceased gentleman. The rear of the procession was brought up by several private carriages, in which were the widow of the deceased, Mrs Grarnshaw (niece), Lady Barclay Paget (niece), Miss Craw- -1 shay (sister-in-law), and Mrs Heron, of Manley Hall, ecc. The interior of the grave was lined with yew and flowers, and decorated with floral crosses. The coffin was completely covered with beautiful wreaths- and crosses. The spectators were very numerous but they conducted themselves in a decorous and respectful manner. Mr Thomas Davies, of Frodsham, had the superintendence of the funeral arrange- ments. Lieutenant-Colonel Hervey Talbot was the second son of the late Hon and Rev Arthur Chetwynnd Talbot, rector of Ingestre and Churcheaton, Staffordshire. ; He was cousin to the late Lord Shrewsbury. His mother was Har- riet, only daughter of the late Henry Charles Hervey, Aston, and niece to the late Sir Arthur Aston, G C B. of Aston Hall. Lieutenant• Colonel Talbot was born October 6th, 1838, and married Eva Julietta, youngest daughter of the late Henry Crawshay, of Oakland-3 Park, Gloucestershire. Deceased leaves a son and a daughter. He was Lieut-Col of the let Staffordshire Militia, with which regiment he was connected in his youth. After the Crimean war, and before the Indian mutiny, the subalterns in the Militias in- tending to join the army were offered a commission if they could raise a certain number of men, who were then in de- mand. Colonel Talbot, who was very popular at the time, raised the required radmber very quickly, and so gained his cemrnission. He entered a regiment of the line and served in indir returning home on the death of Sir Arthur, his grand uncle. Be again joined the Staffordshire regiment on return- ing, and was made Lieutenant-Colonel. The deceased; gentleman was a.J Ps for Cheshire and Staffordshire. Hie bad lived at Aston Grange for about three years, and seas. very much respected by all.

FRODSIIAIII. BRITISH AND, FOREIGN BIBLE BOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the Frodsham branch of the British and,Eforeign Bible Society was held in the Town Hall, Frodshana, on Tuesday evening, when there was a moderate attendauce. The Rev F F Edmonds presided, and there were also on the platform Rev A Grier (curate), Rev E Marsden (vicar of Aston), Rev J Mosscrop (Wesleyan), Rev J.. Lewis (Free Church), and. the Rev J Symons, deputation. The meet- ing opened with singing, after Which prayer was-offered by the Rev J Lewis. The Rev B Marsden' hon. secretary, an- nounced that the net amount contributed ,to the funds of the society from the Frodsham branch during the past year was £55 12s 61. The deputation gave an excellent ad- dress, and stated that the society were now publishing the New Testament complete for the sum of one penny, and handed a sample book for inspection, which was printed in goad type, and contained 240 pages. A collection was made at the close of the meeting. THE BLUR RIBBON ARMY: MAMILIAGE Olf A CAPTAIN.— The popularity of Captain Kerr was strikingly shown on Monday, on the occasion of his marriage with "Captain Grace Vie," another willing working on the staff of the Blue Ribbon Army. A large number of people assembled at the Trinity Chapel, Frodshata, to watch the arrival of the, bridal party, headed by the banner and band. After the ceremony a shower of rice was liberally scattered over the- newly-married couple. In the afternoon a large company partook of the cup that cheers" at the headquarters of the army, the mission room having been, decorated for the occa- sion; and in the evening &public meeting was held,, when there was a crowded audience. The bride and bridegroom each gave a vigorous address, the latter reviewing the pro- gress of the army at Frodeham since its felte.7.tiOll nine months ago, daring which time, the captain sall, there had ' been 400 converts at Frodsharn to the Gospel Temperance ' Army. A liberal *read of refreshments was provided at the • close of the. meatina, an,d, the proceedingi VASeted off very pleasantly.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. If Emperors have any sense of humour their Majesles of Germany, Austria, and Russia cannot failed to be tickled when they think of the solemn farce at which they have just been assisting in a little village in Poland. A time has come which, in the opinion of Prir.ce Bismarck, demands the taking of a certain step, which can be accomplished only in concert with Russia and Austria. It is said to be in the direction of reducing the military armaments, which one would like to believe, and might with great reason do as. The matter, whatever it is, has, beyond doubt, been slowly approached through the ordinary processes of diplomacy. Prince Bismarck has doubtless had much correspondence on the subject with M. de Giers and Count Kalnoky, and the basis of an understanding has been reached. But it is only in England that ministers can devise and carry out a policy without apportioning some distinct and prominent share to the Sovereign. In Germany, Austria, and Russia an Em- peror is still a very real thing, a phenomenon that must be honoured.

-- Accordingly there was arranged this dramatic scene at Skiernievice. There was much kissing on the right cheek and on the left when the Emperors met. They sat in a room together for half an hour, and made believe to talk statesmanship. In the meantime the three Ministers were holding a simultaneous sitting where business was seriously dealt witb. On the next day the Emperors parted with more kissing on the left cheek and on the right; snux boxes were exchanged ; orders distributed by the bushel, and every- thing passed off happily. It is not a good thing for the people of Russia, Germany, and Austria that the Emperor for the time being should hold such a position that it is necessary to get up these elaborate proceedings in order to humbug him. But at least it is well to know that the per- formance is a farce, and that, certainly in Germany, power whether ill or well used is in the hands of a man sprung from the people, who received his first mandate from the people, and who in his place in Parliament can be, and is, called to account by the representatives of the people. Mr Gladstone is continuing his triumphal tour through Scotland, and though wbat with torch-light dances at night and popular receptions by day the excitement is great, he is in excellent health and spirits. He has made several little speeches within the toast week, but it is notable that he has not varied by half a tone from the notes struck in Edinburgh. He still experesses the hope that the Lords will be wise in time, and that in the approaching autumn session they will find some means of delivering themselves from dilemma. But be utters no threats and studiously avoids any reference to what may folMw upon the Lotus rejecting the Bill a second time. His influence upon petvaie persons and public opinion is &Town tin the remarkable moderation of the speeches made at the Liberal demonstra- tions which continue to be held throughout the country. The audience is nearly always in the earns mood, impatient of beating about the bush alai insistent upon coming straight to the point, and saying what shall be done with the How-, of Lords. But no counter action is taken. There are no amendments going beyond those submittel from the plat- form, and, on the whole, with some gestures of impatience and some ominous mutterings, the multitude are content fOr the present to limit themselves within the lines laid down by the Premier. But it is plain to see that this is a temporary and conditional understanding, the rebound from which would be all the greater because of the difficulty with which the attitude is preserved. Supposing the Lords again throw out the Bill meetings that would be held through Decembor and January will be of a very different character from thos I held from August to the present date. Meanwhile Sir Stafford INorthcote has been feebly bleating through the pastures where of late Mr Gladstone's strong , speech resounded. Bikt his visit attracts very little atter.. tion, and is mildly jeered at even by thz.Standard, which, like Lord Randolph Churchill, has now returned to the Conservative fold.

-- - The re-conversion of the Standard forms an episode in a very curious chapter of journalistic history. It will not be forgotten that about two years ago the Standard created profound astonishment in the Conservative camp by be- coming suddenly and uncompromisingly frank in its speech. It scathingly criticised Lord Salisbury, cudgelled Lord Randolph Churchill, sneered at Sir Stafford Nerthcote, and even spoke disreqpectfully of Mr James Lowther. At the same time it did justice to the honesty of intention on the part of the Liberal Government and habitually said things of Mr Gladstone sufficient to make the hair stand on end in many a quiet country rectory. At the same time it dis- played enterprise in other directions, distinguishing itself by the earliness, accuracy, and fullness of its special corres- pondence. The effect of this combined revivification in a paper well-known in former days as the personification of Sairey Gamp was immediate and extraordinary. The sale went up in a bound. People began to read the Standard, and it was everywhere seen and talked about. The Conservatives talked largely but vaguely about starting an opposition paper, a matter in respect of which both in Lon- don and the provinces some of them had painful experience. Fortunately the Morning Post was available. It was re- duced in price from threepence to a penny, was ostenta- tiously adopted as the organ of the Conservative party, and every good Tory gave up his Stan43rd (which, however, he was very careful to read at his club and elsewhere) and took the Morning Post. The fortunes of the Post were made. Those of the Standard were too collossal and too deeply rooted to be shaken by this storm. It went its way increasingly prosperous, and now has gone back into the old ruts and people wonder why.

div.head: explanation is very simple. Three years ago there
div.p: The explanation is very simple. Three years ago there

joined, the editorial staff one of the ablest, certainly the most vigorous, writer on the English press. He had one apparent disqualification for this close connection with a Conservative journal. He was, and is, one of the most ad- vanced Radicals of the day. In writing for the Standard I he was-what he called moderate. But it was his moderation that shocked the Conservative party. His incisive touch, his knowledge of affairs and his attractive literary style gave new life to the faded. energies of the old Standard, and made it a really powerful political organ. Then this eagle in the dove's cote was made editor of a monthly magazine whith, as the Standard had done, immediately felt the impulse of his personality. His duties there became so engrossing that he resigned his position oaths Standard, which has, per- haps, with a sigh of relief, wobbled back to its old ways. It will be noted that from the list of speakers on the Con- servative side who have readily and loyally responded to the call to take part in the campaign, the name of,Mo Wet- test is conspicuously absent. He fills so large a place in the House, being ready at any moment to obstruct business by articulate or inarticulate speech, that this retiaence is the more striking. Soule time ago it was stated in one of the newspapers that Mr Warton was about to visit his consti- tuents and render an account of his stewardship. This was ;only a malicious joke. Mr Warton never has visited his 'constituents since he was elected, and probably never will. 'lt is questionable whether he would be personally safe in the town. Certainly any attempt to address-an audience would lead to hopeless uproar. The romantic circumstan- ces connected WM his candidature are not likely to fade from the memory of the electors. He went down to Brid- port an unknown man, save that he had tho. reputation of being fabuloualy rich. Shortly after. his arrival, whilst the question of his acceptance by the party was pending, he fell seriously ill, appeared to be even on the paint 0 death. At this crisis he senl: for the Ccemervative agent and, for some of the lead- ing members of the party, including the clergy. He elate sent for a lawyer to make his will,. Having ascertained the pressing necessities of everybody, a thousand pounds bare towards repairing a church, a couple of thousand for the local haErmary, personal bequests to the Conservative agent and other iniuential electors, were bestowed, and there was much mourning in Bridport at, the approachirg dem:se of so kiad-hearted and interesting a personage. Fortunately, however, almost immediately-after his will bad been drawn up, Mr Warton got better and the electors could do nothing less-than place him at the bead of the poll. It was-shortly alter this that misunderstaadings arose. It was ;lamented that-safer from being a wealthy man Mr Warton'a income was limited by a few huadreds a year. There was evert difference of opinion as to pecuniary liability for bills, print- ing, and other expenses connected with a contested election. This is the story that is told at Bridport, and is probably exaggerated. Howe eer it bs, Mr Warton's personal coanec-, tion with Bridport is absolutely closed, mad unlesa it be worth the while of the Party to get him a. safe seat some-. where—and probably it ie—bit Parliamentary career is over. There was sometbieg of pathos la a remark he made to a friend on the day of prorogation. lam sorry it is over," he said, Pm somebody here whilst the House is sitting. When Parliament is up I'm nabody." The Presidential election in the United States, always a melancholy spectacle, is at the present epoch weighted with exceptionally painful circumstances. There are two can- didatee bgtwees whom the contest, ig held to lie, Mr Blaine,

the Republican candidate,•has beetr disgraced in the eyes (li— the nation by the publication of correspondence which shows that whilst holding an important office in the House of Representatives be suborned himself and sysfeicatieally took bribes. This discovery seemed' to place him out of the running. The Republican party, to their credit be it said, declining to farther the candidature of such a man. Then Mr Cleveland, the Democratic candidate, came to the front and seemed certain to win. When suddenly out of the blue sky there drops a thunderbolt that is lihely to ruin hire. It is made known that some years ago he was living with a woman he had not married. Hereupon there has been a swift falling off from Mr Cleveland's aide, Mr Ward Beecher, amongst other inflttential persons, having publicly renounced him.

Just at this time last year, I believe on this very day, I dined in New York at a party given by Mr Whitelaw Reid, of the Tribune, to Lord Roseberry. Thera were twelve present, all told. Three were English guests, the fourth the host, and every other man in the room, Mr Reid told me, waft a candidate for the Presidency, and had a more or less good chance. Two of the men, I remember very well, were Mr Blaine and Mr Cleveland.

div.head: HARVEST FESTIVALS IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS IN WAR- RINGTON.

During the past week several harvest festivals have been held in connection with several churches in Warrington. On Wednesday evening the annual festival in connection with Christ Church, Latchford, was held in the church, and was attended by a very large congregation. The fol- lowing clergymen took part in the service: the Revs B B Prescott (vicar of Christ Church), J Prescott (curate), F Slater (St. James', Latchford), Canon Greeraall (Grappen hall). and A Jones (Walton.) The chancel, pulpit, reading!, desk. font, and windows, were all prettily decorated with a I rich variety of flowers and fruit, the decorations havii g chiefly been done by the ladies of the congregation. T 1 *- sermon was preached by the Rev H G Youard, vicar of VVhitegate, Northwich, from the text" Consider the lilies of the field." After alluding to various lessons which might be derived from the lily, the preacher said the ladies of the ' present day would do well to consider how the lilies are clothed by God, and get their ideas of dress from them, taking our Lord's prin- ciple of taste as their standard. Must they not deem that mach of the present fashion of dress was simply a caricature of the principles of true taste. Taking the lilies as their guide how much the dress of this age was wanting in the glory of beauty and colour, because it was wanting in the pure delicate simplicity of the lily. A harvest thanksgiving service was held in St. Barnabas' Church, Lovely-lane, on Wednesday evening, when an ap- propriate sermon was preached by the Rev. J. Anton% vicar. The Rev. G. Ward assisted at the service. The church was tastefully decorated with flowers, fruit, and, products of the field, and mottoes suitable to the occasion were placed in prominent positions. The communion table and rails, the pulpit, lectern, and font, were artistically adorned, and the effect was chaste and pretty. Miss Houghton presided at the organ in the place of Mr Evans, and the anthem "Ye shall dwell in the land" was sung by the choir. There was a large congregation. The offertory was in aid of the Sunday school.. On Thursday the annual harvest festival was held in con- nection with St James's Church, Litchferd. Holy Commu- nion was celebrated at half-past seven o'clock in the morn- ing, matins at eight o'clock, and in the evening there was a service in the church, which was largely attended. The officiating clergymen were the Revs W H Marcie]] (vicar St Luke's, Southport), J K Marsden, Canon Crreenall Grappenhall), B B Prescott (Christ Church), and a G Smith. The interior of the church was profusely and taste- fully decorated with plants, flowers, fruits, and vegetables. A notable feature in the decorations was the large bides of splendid vegetables of various kinds placed at the sides of the chancel rails; and the embellishment of the pulpit also attracted a good deal of attention, the redhetic sunflower being used so largely for that purpose as to suggest ,that it bad been a labour of love to some devotee of the beautiful. The sermon was preached by the Rev W H Marsden, who took as his text the 18th verse of the 35th Psalm. In the course of the evening suitable hymns were sung, the urgan- let being Mr Bowes. On Thursday evening a harvest thanksgiving service was held at Holy Trinity Church, Sankey-street, when the pul- pit was occupied by the Rev Canon Maclure, M.A., vicar of Rochdale. The church was adorned in a very tasteful manner with flowers and fruit, and bore an attractive ap- pearance. Hymns suitable to the occasion were sung. The congregation was large.

and T P Norris.

ILLEGAL WEIGHTS —Robart Leigh, farmer, was charged with having had two unstainped weighs in his possession for use in trade on the 27th July. Superintendent Leigh- ton stated that on the day in question he went to High Leigh to inspect weights and scales, and on passing defen- dant's field he saw they were bolding potatoes. He went into the field, and found that a 561bs and a nibs weight were being used, the same not being stamped. He (the superintendent) coaccl not say whether the weights were un- just or not, as he did not test them. The Bench said they were inclined to take a lenient view of the case, and fined the defendant the costs, 7s.—George Platt, farmer, of High Leigh, was charged with having a 60lbs weight in his pos- session, this weight not being recognised by the Board of Trade. The weight was also 10 ounces light. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs, Is.—John Straughan, farmer, Broom Edge, WAS alse fined the costs, 83, for having had two unstamped weights in his possession on the 15th August.— Thomas Brazindale, farmer, Lymm, was charged with having had two 601bs weights, wnich are not legal weights, in his possession on the 15th August, and was ordered to pay the costs, 7s.—For similar offences John Walton, farmer, Warburton, was ordered to pay the costs on two charges. .

DIII7I4KENNESS.—WiIIiam Atkinson, a young man, was fined Sc and costs for having been drunk and diso:derly at Lynam, on the 12th July. ALLEGED AssauLT.—James Owen, a young man, was charged with having assaulted a lad named George Bragg on the 15th inst at Lyinua.—Defendant stated that the com- plainant persisted in going into his father's field, although he hsd warned him several times. On the day in question he saw the c implainant and followed after him and hit him once on the face with his open hand.—Complainant admitted having been in the field.—The case was. dismissed, and a counter summons charging Bragg with having damaged Owen'a fences was withdrawn. A FISHING CASE ADJOURNED.—A case was to be heard in which William Dodson, .1 C Downward, and Florence Wilson were charged with fishing in the Bollin at Warbur- ton on the 16th met, the prosecutor being E S Hargreaves, of Mill Bank, Partington, who claims the exclusive right of fishing. Solicitors were ratainrd on each side, the prosecutor being represented by kfr Hocking, of the firm of Messrs Simpson, Hocking,and Baby, Manchester; and the defendants by Mr Ainsworth, of the firm of Messrs Brown and Ainsworth, Stockport. On the case b.‘ing called upon, Mr Hocking stated that negotiations were ping on for an arrangement out of court and asked for an adjournment till the next court day. This application was granted.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. P. Stubs and Mr. Ziba DRUNKENNESS —The following were fined for drunken- ness :—John Stokes, at Orford, 103. and costs, or 14 days; Joseph Woods, ss. and costs, or seven days ; Joseph Taylor, at Croft, ss. and costs, or seven days; William Bentley, at Penketh, Sc. aril costs, or seven days. OnsTrtucTioNtsYs.—Walter Naylor and William Norman, young men, were charged with obstructing a footpath at Orford, but as it appeared that the officer who summoned them had not ordered them to move on, they were dis- charged. MAINTENANCE. A man named Robert Kirk was summoned in respect to an order made upon him to pay 3s. a week towards the maintenance of his child in a Reforma- tory, the stun of £3 3s. being in arrear. The case was adjourned for a month to enable defendant to carry out an arrangement with the police for the payment of the money. A BAD FELLOW.—George W.lsby, who did not appear, was summoned by his father, Thomas Welsby, for doing damage to the house of the latter to the ameunt of 12s.— Superintendent Johnson said that the defendant had turned out a bad fellow and was a trouble to his father.—An order was made for him to pay the damage, and the costs of the case.
SLEEPY Carasas.—James Smith and John Ford were each tined ss. ana costs, or seven days, for being asleep whilst in charge of hors.s and waggons, on the Liverpool. road at Sankey, on the 3rd inst.

RUNCORN PET nr SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Rigby (chairman) and Mr. James Handley. LICENsING MATTEES.—CharIes Whitfield was granted temporary authority to sell at the Lord Rodney Inn, in Church-street. Authority was also granted to John Ormesher to sell at the Grapes Inn, Halton-road. A NUISANCE.—John °Achill was summoned by the Run- corn Rural Sanitary Authority with regard co a nuisance upon his cottage property at Weston.—Inspector Farrington said be had intended to ask the Bench for an order to be made upon Mr. Oakhill to abate a nuisance on his cottage property, arrising from defective drainage, but he had been informed by Mr. Collier, Mr. Oakbill's agent, had obtained a tender for the work of remedying the nuisance. He therefore asked the case to be adjourned for a fortnight.— The adjournment was granted. A PROFANE Worraw.—Sarah Clark, of Robert-street, was summoned for using obscene laneuage in Penketh-lane on the Bth inst., and on the evidence of P.C. Wallace she was fined IN. and costs, 9s. ed., or fourteen days' imprison- rnent.

THE POLICEMAN'S Bove—Peter O'Neil, a labourer, living I at 30, Water-street, was charged with assaulting William Clavey.—Mr. Burton appeared for the complainant, who stated that on Saturday evening, the 6th inst., he was in Finegan's beerhouse, Mersey-street, where the defendant and two other men were. The defendant said, " Here's Carey, the policeman's boy," and followed up his remarks by throwing two glasses of beer in his face. The defendant then pushed the complainant to the ground as he was leav- ing the house. His forehead came in contact, and was severely bruised, blood flowing very freely. The defendant "swore" that if be got a summons from him it would be his (the complainant's) end—The defendant alleged that the complainant was drunk and unable to stand, and that his falling to the ground was accidental. He called James Rowley, and a man named Mulvaney, in support of his statement —P.S. Walley stated that on the same evening Clayey went to the police station to lay a complaint. He was bleeding very much from a wound on the forehead. He could walk quite straight and talk rationally.—The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for three months in his own recognizances of £5, and pay the costs, 15s. 6d. MISCELLANEOLS.—Ann Joyce was convicted of using threats to Joseph Handley, an old man living in Chol- mondley-place, and she was ordered to pay costs, lie. and be bound over to keep the peace for three months.— Richard Tilley, an old offender, was charged with acting as a pedlar without a certificate in Br'dee-street on Saturday night, and on the evidence of P.C. Morris he was fined 20s and costs, or a months' imprisonment—Edward Johceon, a blind man, and Michael Mulligan, were each fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr F H Gossage. DIMNICENNESS.—The following persons were each fined for drunkenness and disorderly conduct : Thomas livers., Patrick Dydon. Ann Plant, -John Robinson, Patrick Ken- nedy, Michael Gilleson, Mary Daley, Michael Arney, Brid- get Campbell, and Bridget Manning. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr H S Hall and Mr F H Goseag,e.

MISCELLANEOUS —Thomas Welsh was fined ss, and costs, 6s 6d, for being drunk on the previous day. A penalty of 7s 6&l and costs was imposed on Thomas Slater for a like of- fence; John Slater, John Thompson, and John Woodward were each fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly; Mary Riley and Catharine Kenny were brought up on separ- ate charges of committing breaches of the peace and they were bound over in the usual sureties.—Susannah Giblin was, on the evidence of P C McMasters, convicted of wan- dering abroad without any visible means of subsistence on the previous night, and as she had been several times con- victed of various offences, she was sent to gaol for seven days.—Elizibeth Hyslop summoned Lydia Smith for using defamatory language, but the Bench die missed the CASO. John Giblin and Matthew Hughes were summoned for neg- lecting to send their children regularly to school. Mr Danby prosecuted, and the defendants were fined in the usual penalty of ss.
ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Mr A Sinclair.

HIGHWAY OFFENCE.—George Pye was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse in Tontine-street.— P.C. Massey proved the case, and defendant was fined 10s and Costs. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Mr A Sinclair.

HAWKING WITHOUT A LICENSE —Patrick Dolan, Parr, was charged with hawking without a liceuse.—P.C. Tem- perll deposed to seeing prisoner hawking in Peter-street, on Friday last.—Supt. Johnston remarked that the prisoner had been fined for a similar offence before, and he snew he was doing wrong.—Prisoner said he was only "swopping" paper colour for rags.—He was fined 5s and costs, or in de- fault to be sent to prison for seven days.

MONDAY.—Before Mr T Pilkington and Alderman Mcßryde. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—John Henry Dixon, Parr, was charged with committing a breach of the peace on Thursday last, at Parr-street, by striking his wife in his own house.—P.C. Carruthers proved the case,—Defendant did not appear, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. —George Woodward was charged with a similar offence.— P.C. Moss said he saw him fighting in Parr-street.—He was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in one surety of £lO and two of £5. ASSAULTS —Rachel Finney was charged with assaulting Margaret Glover, on the 7th instant, in Stanley-street.— Prosecutor said that about half-past four on Sunday after- noon defendant came to her house and knocked her dowu and pulled some of her hair out. Witness's son interfered and prevented her doing any further injury.—Fined 5s and costs.—James Waring was fined 103 and costs for assault- ing his wife on Tues.day night last, at Parr.—Prosecutor stated that she had had to charge him on several previous occasions.

STEALING A COAT—Thomas Johnson, Windle, was charged with stealing a coat, value 3s 6d, the property of Patrick Machin, who stated thaton Sunday evening, the 17th instant, between eight and nine o'clock he was going home up Liverpool-road. He was attacked by three men and the prisoner. One of them struck him, and he pulled„,off his coat to tight with the man. When the fight was over ho missed his coat. He next saw the prisoner wearing the coat in the Derby Arms. He asked him to give it him, and asked him where he got it from. He said " What has it to do with you," and made an attempt to strike him.—Evi- dence was brought forward to prove that the coat was the prisoner's property, and that he bought it in Scotland.— Ultimately the Bench decided 0 discharge the prisoner, allowing him to keep the coat.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

Sr. MMUS'S CHURCEL—The annual sermons on behalf of the Sunday schools were preached on Sunday in St. Thomas's Church, Ashton, by the Rev. Cumming Macdona and the Rev. R. G. Matthew, vicar of St. Michael and All Angels, Wigan. The former preached in the morning and afternoon, and the latter in the evening. The offertories amounted to .LIS. Ram's HEAD BOTANICAL SOCIETY—The fifth annual dinner in connection with the above was held on Saturday at the Rim's Head Inn, Stubsoaw Cross, Ashton, when about 40 sat down to an excellent dinner, provided in Mr Bridge's usually good style. Mr Piinblett was voted to the chair, Mr Thomas Dix assisting as vice. The health of the patrons was responded to by Mr Joseph Pimblett in a neat speech. Songs followed by Messrs H Litherland, J Houlton, T Dix, J Pimblett, J Adamson, &c. Mr T Jameson presided at the piano. The National Anthem brought the gathering to a close.

_ RISING STAR FOOTBALL AND CRICKET CLUB, NICOL- LANE.—The above club opened their football ground on Sat- urday with a match between a team picked by the captain (Mr T Edwards) and one picked by the secretary (Mr T Kenyon). The game was a spirited one and resulted in a draw, each side scoring two goals. Afterwards the players and friends to the number of forty sat down to tea at the Star Hotel. Mr McGeever (president), was elected to the chair, and Mr J Hill to the vice-chair. Dancing at inter- vals threugh the evening followed, and the meetiug was brought to a close shortly before eleven o'clock after a very enjoyable evening.

_ :ASHTON LIBERAL CLUB —The members.of the newlV for- med Liberal Club held their first meeting on Monday even- ing week in the British Schoolroom, off Bolton-road, when Mr Thomas Roberts delivered an address on "The House of Lords, past and present." Mr Joseph Mitchell occupied the chair, and there was a very fair attendance. At the conclusion of the address a discussion followed, after which the customary votes of thanks to the speaker and the chairman were carried with acclamation. We understand that it is intended to invite others to follow the example of Mr Roberts, and to deliver addresses on various subjects dur- ing the winter months.

Speaking on Wednesday, at the annual meeting of the Northern Union of Mechanics' Institutes at Blaydon-on- Tyne, Mr Cowen, M.P.. presidentforthe year, appealed to the working classes to do their thinking for themselves, and not be led in swathes and strings by the adroitest of advi- sers. Having won personal, they should strive for intellec- tual enfranchisement, regarding nothing as sacred but truth, and shrinking from no inquiry. CANNIBALISM AT SEA. —The following is the cap- tain's version of the incident in connection with the wreck of the Mignonette, which has already been described in our columns :—We went on from the fifteenth to the twentieth day without any food at all or drink, and by that time we had begun to look each other in the face very black. The boy, who had drank some sea water at night, had said, "We shall all die," and I remarked, "We shall have to draw lots, boys." This was ignored by all, and they said. We had better die together," to which I re- plied, "So let it be, but it's hard for four to die, when per- haps one might save the rest." A day or two before I sug- gested we should try and make eome kind of sail, which we did with our shirts rigged on an oar for a mast, and a strand of the painter for shrouds and stays. Things now looked as bad as they could. On either the 19th or 20th day the boy was lying in the bottom of the boat, where he had been for two days, gasping for breath and nearly dead. At about three o'clock in the morning I said to the mate, " What is to be done? I believe the boy is dying. You have a wife and five children, and I have a wife and three children." I said that human flesh had been eaten before. Stephens re- plied, "See what daylight brings forth." Brooks took out his watch at six o'clock, and we made motions to each other. Brooks said he could not do it, and Stephens said he could not do it. I told Brooks to go forward, which he did. I 'then took hold of the shrouds, and had a last look round to see if anything was in sight, but there was nothing. I offered up a prayer most fervently that God above might forgive us for such an act, and then I knelt down by the boy and said, "Now, Dick, my boy, your time has come." He murmured, " What, me, sir ?" I put the penknife in his throat, and he was dead instantly.—The charge against Dudley, Stephens, and Brooks of having murdered Rickard Parker in a boat on the high seas was resumed on Thurs- day at Falmouth police court. As Brooks was neither actor nor participator in the crime be was discharged, and then examined. He related in detail the experiences of the sur- vivors from the foundering of the yacht to the time of their rescue, stating how Captain Dudley first suggested the drawing lots when their situation seemed hopeless, and how the boy Parker was subsequently killed. Captain Dudley committed the deed, but they shared the blood, and for days lived on the body. This concluded the evidence for the prosecution, and, after a few remarks from the solicitor for the defence, the magistrates decided that the charge was too grave and important to be settled by them. The pri- soners were accordingly committed for trial, but admitted to bail.

div.p: IRE FX A:MINER SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 20. IRB4.
THE REFORM AGITATION.

"The complete failure," says the Daily News, "of the great picnic in Lord Egmont's part at Midhurst on Satur- day week was scarcely more complete Vian that of last Saturday in Lord Boston's park, near Maidenhead. Every attraction had been offered. Seventeen Conservative asso- ciations had distributed 11,000 admission tickets, and arrangements had been made by which people could travel to Bourne-end and back for a fare and a quarter; but fewer than 2,000 availed themselves of the opportunity, and nearly half were ladies. At the open-air meeting about 500 persons gathered round the platforms. Compared with this miserable result, the picnic at Ipawich on the same afternoon may be regarded as successful. It certainly came much nearer to exhibiting the eminently social character which Sir W Charley perceives in Conservatism. It was truly a picnic. Men took not only their wives but their families, and a favourable estimate gives 12,000 to 15,000 at the total of the numbers present, iecluding a very large number of women and children.' These two picnics seemed to have summed up the Conservative effort at 'meeting numbers with numbers' on Saturday afternoon. The Liberal meetings on the same afternoon need hardly be put in contrast to these. Their character is so entirely different that no common measure can be applied to them. On the lowest ground, that of number of meetings, there was the usual proportions of more than thrpe to one. On the next ground, that of numbers, the comparison was yet more in favour of the Liberals. There were not fewer than 30,000 persons in Victoria Park on the lowest estimate; at Oldham, Mr Hibbert spoke at a demonstration at which 10,000 people were present; at Kidderminster, the whole town was out to protest indignantly against the novel and unconstitutional pretensions of the House of Lords;' at the village of Alfreton, in Derbyshire, there was a large gather- ing of the unenfranchised miners of the neighbouring dis- tricts ; an equally important meeting was held at Mount Seirrel, in Leicestershire ; another at Watford, another at Rumford, and two others across the border at Alloa and Kilmarnock."

Mr John Morley, M.P., addressed his constituents at Newcastle-on-Tyne on Monday night, and referring to the Nile Expedition, he said it promised to be one of the most hazudons we had ever undertaken. Referring to the action of the House of Lords on the franchise question, the hon. member said the important question now was to execute a reform of the House of Commons then, when the people of the country were no longer muffled and manacled by a fraudulent system of representation, it would net be long before the urgent task of still further shortening the arm of the House of Lords was undertaken.

Five meetings in favour of the franchise have been held within the last few days in Dorset. They were all held in the open air, in the evening, " by candlelight," and were at- tended principally bv agricultural labourers, many of whom were known to have walked four, five, and even six miles after their day's work. SIR STAFFORD NORTHCOTE AT EDINBURGH.

Sir Stafford Northcote arrived at Edinburgh, on Monday, from Pitlour House, Fifeshire, where he has since Friday been the guest of Mr Skene. At Granton, in reply to an address, he sal I it was an entire mistake to suppose that the question now at issue was between those who were for the extension of the franchise and those who were against. The only question was whether they were to go into the exten- sion with their eyes open or shut. If on the re-assembling of Parliament the Government were prepirel to submit the whole scheme, it would receive fair consideration from the Conservatives. At the Scottish Conservative Club, Edin- burgh, be received addresses from the Edinburgh and die-

trici Conservatives.—Sir Stafford, in reply, said the work which Conservative associations were doing was a work of a most valuable character, even if it did not lead to imme- diate results. (Hear, hear.) Speaking at a luncheon which took place afterwards, Sir S Northcote said he di t not think it necessary in order to defend the Conservative position to make slashing attacks on their op4onents. He thought seriously that the Constitution was in future in danger, and he felt it was their duty to take every opportunity to re- sist and combat the fallacies that wee put forward. Sir Stifford Northcote opened the second day of his political campaign in Midlothian on Tuesday morning by congratulatory addressee at Hopetown 1101193, where he re- ceived from between 200 and 300 delegates representing the Demonstration Committee of the Scottish Conservative Club, the Scottish National Constitutional Association, the National Union of Conservative Associations for Scotland, and the local associatiotis from 16 counties.—ln the even- ing a great Conservative meeting was held in the Corn Ex- change, the building in which Mr Gladstone recently ad- dressed the electors of Midlothian. The decorations were on the same lines as at the Liberal meeting, except that the prevailing colours and the mottoes on the walls had been changed. The Duke of Bnccleuch presided. and amongst those on the platform in addition to Sir Stafford Northcote were Lord John Manners. M.P.„ the Marquis of Waterford, the Firl of Galloway, Lord Hopetown, Mr Chaplin, M P., the Marquis of Lothian, and numerous other noblemen and gentlemen. On entering the building, Sir Stafford was re- ceived with enthusiastic cheering, which was renewed when, after a brief speech from the Chairman, the right hon. baronet rose to address the meeting. Sir Staff r 4 Northcote said he was sorry to see the great amount of misrepresentation which from time to time tound place in the utterances of their opponents. The Government would not meet the Opposition on the question whether the extension of the franchise and redistribution ought to come together or not, but they would insist on declaring that the Conservatives were not honest in the view they took. He contended that if the two bills had been brought forward together they might have been passed last session if the Government had not brought forward a large number of other measures, most of which ended in an unsatisfactory manner. (Cheers.) The right hon baronet proceeded to criticise in detail Mr Gladstone's recent remarks on the financial condition' of the Government. He declared that it was not true to say that the expenditure on the debt was increased under the late Government, and stated that the whole expenditure of the Conservative Government, leaving out the debt exnendPure, was £213,000,000, \ /bile that of the Liberals was 2231 mil- lions. (Cheers). A vote of thanks to Sir Stafford and confilence in the other Opposition leaders was adopted with enthusiasm on the motion of Me Chaplin, and the proceedings ter- minated.

On Wednesday afternoon Sir Stafford Northcote, accom- panied by the Earl of Hopetoun, the Earl of Selkirk, the Marquis of Waterford, and a number of lidies and gentle- men, who are guests at Hopetoun House, paid a visit of in- spection to the Firth Bridge Works at Queensferry. At dinner in the evening there was a large gathering of the nobility and gentry to meet the right hon. baronet. Sir Stafford Northcote gave an interview in Edinburgh on Thursday to a number of lady supporters of the movement for obtaining the franchise for women. He expressed his agreement with the principle advocated, but reminded the deputation of the practical difficulties in the matter and declined to pledge himself to any action in the approaching discussion of the question of Parliamentary reform. In the evening Sir Stafford addressed a meeting at Dalkeith. Speaking of the agitation now going on. he expressed the opinion that when it was started the people were not at all prepared to join in a crusade against one of the leading branches of the Constitution till it was suggested to them by certain Radical "wire-pullers." He was very much afraid that the Government if they were left to themselvesand were spurred on by their Radical allies would in their redistribu- tion scheme take far too much to the principle of mere numbers, and thus introduce a most dangerous element into the Constitution. The right hon, baronet then proceeded to criticise the Government's management of affairs in Ireland, and also their foreign policy.
ST. HELENS AND THE FRANCHISE BILL.
DEMONSTRATION AT RAIN FORD.

An enthusiastic demonstration of the householders of St Helens in favour of the Franchise Bill was held on S ttur- day afternoon. Fortunately the gathering was favoured with beautiful weather, and in consequence the proceedings throughout were of a very hearty and successful character. The demonstration had been arranged under the auspices of the St Helens Liberal Association, whose headquarters are in Harishaw-street ; and an excellent meeting place was found in the grounds of Rainford Hall, which had been very kindly thrown open by Mr Richard Pilkington, J.P., presi- dent of the Council of the Liberal Association. Early in the afternoon large numbers of persons began to assemble at the Liberal Club premises, where there was a display of bunting; and a streamer across the street bore the words "Success to the Liberal Club" and "Welcome." In due course an im- posing procession of members of the club and friends of the Liberal cause was formed. It was headed by the Ravenhead Brass Band and the banner belonging to the Liberal Associa- tion ; after which came the carriage of Mr H S Hall, J.P., and other well filled coaches. The Roughdale Brass Band occupied a position about the centre of the procession, and it and the Ravenhead Band alternately played selections of national and popular airs. Numerous bannerettes and mottoes were carried in the ranks, the principal inscriptions being—" Stand on your rights and sit on the Peers," "Lords, act op the square you've chiselled us long enough ; " "Will the Lords defy the Labourers ? " " Think what the Lords have cost the People ; " "We demand the vote as our right ; " "Let us have right, not might ;" "Those who now ought to reap.', The franchise loaf and the Salisbury loaf—made in proportion of about 201bs. for the former to 2lbs. of the latter—were also displayed, and attracted considerable attention. Though the number of persons forming the procession was not very large at the commencement, as it marched through the town it received numerous additions, and attracted con- siderable notice. For the conveyance of the " demonstra- tors " to Rainford Hall arrangements were completed with the London and North-Western Railway Comp,any, and a special train was run. After the arrival of the procession at St Helens station the platform was thronged by a hearty crowd, who eagerly entered the carriages of the " special." The company alighted at Crank station, the nearest station to Mr Pilkington's residence, and made their way to the hall. In the grounds a considerable number of other persons, who had walked or driven from St Helens in vehicles. were met with. A platform had been temporarily erected on the lawn, and around this the meeting was held. Among th,ose on the platform were Major W W Pilkington, J.P., Mr R Pilking- ton, J.P., Mr A Sinclair, J.P., Mr H S Hall, J.P., Mr J C Gamble, J.P., Dr McNicoll, Messrs T Brown, H Martin, W Calton (Liverpool). T Snape (Widnes), J B Leach, H R Lacey, W Smith. J Yates, J Fisher, W H Foster, B A. prom- goole, J Booth, W S Hadley, J Boydell, J J Dutton. W C Eccles, G Pownall, and H B Shores (secretary). Mr R D Holt, president of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Asso- ciation was expected to attend, but he was unable to do so.
