div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

'.Ol Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

BIRKENHEAD V. WREXHAM OLYMPIC.—These association clubs met on the Chester-street ground. Birkenhead, on Saturday. The Olympic won by two goals to one. SOUTHPORT V. hiALLIWELL.—Thie match was played at Halliwell on Saturday, and, in the first half Halliwell scored eight goals. In the second part of the game the home team increased their points to twenty, and won by no less than twenty goals to nil. EVERTON V. PORT VALE —The holders of the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup journeyed to Staffordshire, on Saturday, and met the Port Vale team at Burslem, before 2,000 spectators, the occasion being the opening of a new ground by the Staffordshire club. • The home team, who had the best of the game throughout, scored one goal in the first half, but in the second portion of the contest had mat- ters pretty much their own way, and added six more goals to their total. Want of condition bid severely on the visi- tors, who had not all their expected team.

, RUNCORN RECREATION V. NEW BRIGIITON —This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and, after a well centested game resulted in a draw in favour of the Runcorn team, by one try, one minor point, to one try, the try for ttuncorn being obtained by Lunt. Teems :—New Brighton full-back, W Mason; three- quarters, H Tomkinson (captain), G Mason, D Potts; half- backs, W Edwards, A H Gardiner ; forwards, E Gardiner, H Chesterman, S Pemberton, G Morton, W Vernon, J Mar- tin, W Venerable!, E Edwards, T Clough. Runcorn full- back, S Booth; three-quarter, E Lunt, Whinyates, and W Riley ; half-backs, Wilson, A Clare ; forwards, Collinge (captain), Forster, Littlemore, Pendlebury, ..i Clare, Faulk- ner, P Riley, Couth, and Bowyer. EamEsTower V NORTIEWICII VICTORIA.—The formal opening of the new ground of the Earlestown Football Club, at Wargrave Moss, took place on Saturday afternoon, when a match between teams representipg the Earlestown and Northwich Victoria Clubs was played. It had been exten- sively announced that the first team of the Northwich club (winners of the Cheshire Challenge Cup four years in suc- cession), would meet the runners-uo for the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup, but unfortunately at the last mo- ment, the Victoria Football Club arranged a fixture with the Preston North Ead Club, and having two matches on, neither team was fairly representative of the Northwich or- ganisation. The team which visited Earlestown, however, was a thoroughly good one and the Earlestonians met with a decisive defeat at their hands. Fortunately the weather was beautifully fine and there was a good number of interes- ted spectators in attendance. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors play did not commence until about four o'clock. Having won the toss the home team captain selected to play against the wind and uphill in the first half. The visitors accordingly kicked off, with the sun in their favour. For a few minutes the game was evenly contested, but the Northwich men quickly warmed to their work, and soon made a determined attack on the home goal. Five minutes from the start the goalkeeper attempted to stop a long shot, but he allowed the ball to slip through his bands and through the goal, and the visitors thus scored their first goal. Three minutes later they secured a second ' • and in quick successioa a third. About this time the Earlestown forwards exhibited some dash, and after some good passing by Cameron, Dag- nall, and Appleton, Dagnall made a capital attempt to score, but shot the leather outside the poste. From the goal kick the visitors' forwards ran down the field, and a fourth goal fell to their score. The Earlstonians subse- quently made another attack on the Northwich goal, but Dagnall again shot the leather outside the uprights, though a few minutes later the same player finished a good run up :he field by scoring the first goal for Earlestown amid considerable applause. When ends were changed at half time the scores stood : Northwich five goals, Earlestown one, and in less than five minutes after tho resumption of play a sixth goal was notched by the Victorians. The sub- sequent play, however, was in favour of the home team. Time after time the Earlestonians bore down on the Noith- wich goal, but as often were they defeated, until twenty minutes from the close they secured a second goal from a scrimmage. Several corner kicks fell to the Earlestown team, and excitieg scrimmages followed in the mouth of of the Northwich goal, but the leather was each time sent outside the posts or the goalkeeper returned it up the field. The home team met with hard lines, and had to retire de- feated to the extent of six goals to two. The following were the players :—Earlestown : J Green, goal; F Emmett and R Green, backs; H Bowker, J Duxbury, and J Whalley, half-backs; J Sims and 8 Williams, right wing; A Dagnall, centre; J Cameron and J Appleton, left wing. Northwich Victoria: J Palin, goal; G Whitlow and E Molyneaux, backs; C Whitehead and T Holland, half-backs; J Pye and A Pye, ri.ent wing; R Southern and J Atherton, centre T Levers and F Vickers, left wing. !Moires : Messrs. J Gray (Earlestown), and J Hughes (Northwich.) Referee : Mr P liastie.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

As season after season rolls by the time alloted to the prince of winter games appears to follow more closely upon the footsteps of the departing summer pastime. Even now, in some parts of the kingdom it is bard to tell where one ends and when the other begins, for we find the adherents of the willow and the supporters of the leathern sphere having full bent in their favourite avocation in fickle April as well as in the genial days of August and September. Locally, the football season is just beginning, and clubs are all bustle and animation in view of the approaching contests. So far as Warrington is concerned a new feature is the recent establishment of an Association club—which will, no doubt, secure a goodly amount of support. The Earles- town club and its many exciting contests of last season have done much to popularise the gariae in the district; and a good Association club in Warrington became only a ques- tion of time.

At Earlestown the footballers have already opened their season's engagements, and solar as present appearances in- dicate they have a brilliant season before them. Their new ground appears a capital one in every respect, and it has been excellently prepared in view of the forthcoming con- tests. Fixtures have been arranged with the Northwich Victoria, Crewe Alexandria, Everton (holders of the Liver- pool and District Challenge Cap), Liverpool Stanley, Bootle, Bootle Wanderers, Adlington, Newton Heath, Pres- ton Parish Church, Preston Olympic, Birkenhead, Barnes Rovers, Liverpool Anfield, Sze.; and besides these the club has again joined the Lancashire Association and the Liverpool and District Association. In the challenge cup competition of the former they have been drawn against Ribchester, a club near Blackburn, and the tie will be played at Earlestown on October 4th; while in the Liver- pool and District Competition they will meet the Birken- head Argyle. Among other local clubs the Earlestown Ramblers, Earles- town Rovers, clic., are preparing for entering the football arena, but as yet their matches have not been commenced. Football at Haydock seems as if it will be of a lively character during the forthcoming winter. Foremost comes the Temperance Club, which is connected with both the Lancashire and Liverpool Associations. The Temperance team has some clever men in its ranks; and with practice and a hearty determination to try, try, try again," there is no reason why they should not before lung attain a position second to none in the district. In the Lancashire' competi- tion they meet the Newton Heath Club (Manchester), and the match will be played at Manchester to-day (Saturday). In the Liverpool cor test they have been drawn against a newly-formed though none the less a very powerful club, known as the Liverpool Cambrian. The Haydock St. James's Club has also joined the Liverpool and District As- sociation, and they will meet the Bootle F.C. . .

Several intereating matches were played on Saturday. The Earlestown first team tackled a very strong eleven sent to represent the Northwich Victoria, but the latter proved' far and away too strong for them. The local team seemed thoroughly out of condition, and did not at all appear to have got into proper working order.

At -a comreitte.e meeting of the Liverpool and District Football Association held on Monday night, the first draw of the cup ties took place, resulting as follows :—Birken- head Argyle v Earlestown, St. Peter's v Stanley, Everton v Toateth Wanderers, St George's v St. Benedices,Birkenhead v Liverpool Rambler's, Liverp6ol Liver v St. Mary's, Anfield v Skelmersdale;Earlestown Wanderers v Liverpool Linden, Liverpool Rovers v Bootle Wanderers, Liverpool Cambrian v Haydock Temperance, Iranmere v !Barscough, Southport (Hyde Park) v Southport. and Bootle t, Haydock (St. James's). To be played off on or before November Stb, the club first named in each instance having choice of ground._ __

The following are the results of the chief of Saturday's matches, viz :—At Bolton, on Saturday, Great Lever beat the Derbyshire County Club by six goals to none; Haiti- well beat Southport Dv twenty goals to none; Wanderers defeated Staveley by seven to one; and Astley Bridge beat Padiham by one to none. At Birmingham, Aston Villa beat Stafford-road (Wolverhampton) by four to none; at Dum- barton, Dumbarton beat Walsall Swifts by two to none. The four leadingeßlackburn clubs secured three victories and one draw on Saturday, the last being between the Rovers and Church, on the ground of the latter. The Olympic defeated Eagley, holdersof the Bolton charity can, by nineteen goals to none, a splendid performance. Park- road and Witton were victorious after a well-contested game over Low Moor and Clitheroe. Preston Zingari beat Lower Darwen in the presence of about 1,000 spectators by five goals to nil. The first tie decided in the competition for the Lancashire Football Association Challenge Cup was played at Bomber Bridge on Saturday, when School-lane elefeated Chorley by six goals to none. The draw for the fourteenth Association Challenge Cup was made on Monday, when no objection was advanced on the score of professionalism, as was at ens time expected, more especially in the northern districts. The draw should furnish some exciting contests. Last year's holders have an easy task in the first round, and Stoke-on-Trent will have to travel north to play the powerful Queen's Park. The question of professionalism and importation of foot- ballers is at present deeply affecting the minds of supporters of the game, and the Sporting Life of Monday. remarking on the subject. says that there can be no possible objection to the recognised payment of men who cannot afford to play for amusement,and no reason why the principle which exists in almost every sport should be considered detrimental to football.
Monday was the centenary of ballooning in England. The reception of the new Governor of Victoria, Sir Henry Loch, at Melbourne, has been marked by exceptional enthusiasm.

that as they were called together by the St Helens Liberal 1 Association, they would no doubt have been glad to see their president, Lieutenant Gamble, in the chair—(hear, hear)—but he was away trying to recruit his health by yachting in the North. Next in turn was the president of the Council. (Cheers.) The meeting would feel that the chair would be worthily filled when he asked them to ac- cept as chairman, in his place, his brother, Major W W Pilkington. (Loud cheers.) The Chairman said he scarcely expected to be there to take the chair that afternoon, but inasmuch as he had got a ' chair, and other gentlemen on the platform had got chairs, and the audience had not, he thought the sooner some of them got to speechifying the better. The fact was, they had made a great mistake in coming there at all that day. (Laughter.) It was quite true. Their standing there and all that kind of thing was waste of time. (A voice : " Nothing of the sort," and " What do you mean?") But that was so. At least Sir R Cross said the other day that anybody who said , the House of Lords had rejected the Franchise Bill told a ' deliberate lie. (Cries of " Oh, oh.") If the Lords had not done it there was an end of the business. Some folks thought they had, and he (the chairman) fancied the meet- ing thought so too. (Hear, hear.) Well, in one sense, the House of Lords had not done it; but the majority of the House of Lords had done it. (Hear, hear, and a Voice : "Down with them.") Would they sly they had not rejected it? Well, then, at all events, put it in another way—they had obstructed it. (Laughter and applause.) The fact was, the House of Lords or the Tore majority—he must come back to that, for it was the truth, the real truth—had for years and years done nothing but obstruct legislation—(a voice: "That's true," and cheers); and they, the people, could not stand that sort of thing any longer. (A voice : "We won't have the Howe of Peers any longer," and ap- plause.) It seemed to him that serious as that crisis was— the question whether Lord Salisbury should rule England or whether Mr Gladstone should—whether the House of Commons and Her Majesty's Government were to rule, or whether Lord Salisbury and the Tory majority were to rule —a more serious thing was for the obstruction to go on year by year. (Hear, hear.) Sir Richard Cross had said England was scorned and looked upon with contempt by all the foreign nations in Europe. During the seige of Paris a special correspondent of the Telegraph gave a wonderful description of how the siege was going on as viewed by moonlight on a certain day. When they came to refer to the date, and examine into the state of the solar system on that particular day, they found that the moon was on the other side of the globe. (Laughter) Well, he (Mr Pilkington) thought perhaps that was a "special " of the description that Sir Richard Cross had been consulting. But whatever the foreigners said the English people would not change their way of doing things, and the more they said against England the more those assembled at that meeting might rest assured they were on the right path. (Cheers.)— Mr H S Hall, J.P., was well received and greeted with the song, "For he's a jolly good fellow." He said he bad the honour to propose the first resolution, which man as fol- lows :—" That this meeting approves of the course taken by Her Majesty's Government in calling an autumn session of Parliament for the purpose of passing the Franchise Bill,and , strongly urges them to take all possible means to nuke it law. (Cheers.) He (Mr Hell) hoped the Government , would take all possible metns to swamp at once the present majority in the House of Peers, and, if it was necessary, to do so by creating a number of new peers, as was done when the Reform Bill was passed. (Hear, hear.) Personally he (the speaker) did not wish to interfere with the gilded chamber, and ddi not want to see them abolished. (A Voice: 'We do," and laughter.) Many British men liked a bit of finery and liked to see a fine ship head, but they didn't want to be ruled by ship heads—(hear, hear)—and it rested with that meeting whether they would be ruled by a party of ship heads, or whether they would be ruled by the British House of Commons. with Mr Gladstone at the head. (Cries of "Gladstone.") Mr Thomas Brown, in seconding the resolution, said he did so because in the last seseion of Parliament there had been sufficient time wasted. (Hear, hear.) They were quite aware that the whole business of the country had been brought to a standstill ; that everything that Pirltunent would have done had been obstructed because the Peers had thought right, or rather the Conservative partion of the Howe of Lords had thonght debt at the last moment to kick the Franchise Bill out. His second reason for suppor- ting, the resolution was that on the question there ought to be as little delay as possible. That was a question that de- mended attention at once, because delay would bring distemper and illwill in the minds of men. And then another reason was that he quite believed a Franchise Bill should come first. After referring to the large number of nights taken up in the House of Commons by opposing the Franchise Bill, Mr Brown said it did not matter whether a man voted for a member for St Helens or for South-West Lancashire. Let them now have a vote and afterwards they could My whether they would pluck out Woodstock and Eye, and put in places like St Helens. (Applause.) Mr Richard Pilkington, J.P., supported the resolution, and was warmly received. They knew as well as he did that for some time past an agitation had been going on in favour of the Franchise Bill, and meetings had been held in the majority of instances by the Liberals. In fact, he might say, where were the Tory meetings? It rather reminded them of the days of the flood, when the water, as it were, covered the earth, and the only sign of anything earthy were a few high hills. It seemed to him that the case at the present day with regard to the Liberal party and the Tory party was that the flood of Liberalism was covering the land, and it was difficult, without magnifying glasses, to find one Tory hill or one Tory earthy mound. (Laughter.) But they were lobe found if they carefully looked for them. If they would look at Ormskirk they would find a die- tinguished statesman whose voice was net often heard now in the House of Commons, and if they read the papers they would read the speech he made to two hundred persons who were regaling themselves on cold meat at six shillings a head. (Laughter.) One of the remarks that he merle was characteristic of him. He said, "I have a paper sent me by one of my constituent. It is to hold meetings for the purpose of protesting against the action of the House of Lords ia rejecting the Franchise Bill. Now I have no hesitation in stying that whoever put upon that paper that the House of Lords have rejected the Fr inchise Bill told an absolute and deliberate lie." Now, if it were an absolute and deliberate lie that the Peers rejected the Franchise Bill, what was the truth ? (Laughter, and cheers:) Lord Salisbury said at Manchester that if the House of Commons did not like the action of the House of Lords they could go to the countre, and if this was not enforcing a dissolution of the House' of Commons by the Horses of Lords be would like to know what was ? (Hear, hear.) But although the Liberals had had splendid meetings all over ' the country, it remained for Mr Gladstone to have the most splendid at Midlothian. In the greatest speech of his and , in its greatest passage, lie nailed the Lords to the counter and , assailed the very centre of Aheir position, and he ' showed the danger of conceding their demands. (Applause.) Let them hope that the Lords would retire with dignity, and that they would sea the errors of their ways, that they i would learn sense, and never more thwart the House of Commons and the people of England. (Cheers.) The resolution was unanimously carried. Mr. Martin then proposed "That the electors and non. electors of St. Helens now assembled hereby protest against the obstruction of the Franchise Bill by the House of Lords, and declare the present constitution and power of the house to be highly dengerous to the good government and welfare of this kingdom." (Applause.) Mr. Martin said the House of Lords never had taken direct issue upon any impertint ' measure like the Franchise Bill—they never met it with a direct negative—they always took some side issue or adopted some subterfuge of that sort. He was one of those who did not see the necessity of a second chamber at all. (Cheers.) But if they were to have a second chamber let them have one of a representative character (a Voice: "It will do, that [ will.") He did not believe in the hereditary principle. Many of the things that had been done in the sister isle had been through the obstruction and pigheadedness of the , House of Lords, notably in their dealings with the moderate measure of Lord Stanley on the land question, the Catholic , Emancipation Act, Mr Gladstone's Irish Church Act of 1868, the Abolition of Church Rates, and the Abolition of Purchase in the Army. In the time of Charles the first the Commons passed a resolution that the House of Lards were useless and dangerous and ought to be abolished, and he (Mr Martin) said " ditto" to that. (Loud cheers). Mr Sinclair, JP, in seconding the motion, said he was anxious that the meeting should have time to hear the gentlemen from Liverpool and other speakers, and he would perform his duty in one sentence. He agreed most heartily with what Mr Martin had said, and they must take as their motto the words of Mr John Morley, that the House of Lords must either be mended or ended. (Applause). Mr W (Mtn, president of the Liverpool Reform Club, supported the resolution. _ _

JOMr Ga:nble, J.P., Who WAS received with cheers, pro- posed the third resolution :—" That this meeting of in- habitant householders of the most populous municipal borough in the kingdom which is not directly represented in Parliament declares its adhesion to the policy of the Government in insisting on the passing of the Household Franchise Bill before taking up the question of Redistribu- tion, and is satisfied that it is by adherence to that course that the borough will most quickly obtain the direct repre- sentation to which it is entitled." (Cheers.) He thought the wisdom of the GovernineM in taking up the Franchise ruin and leaving over the question of Redistribution could scarcely be doubted. If anyone knew what he was talking about when he spoke on the subject it was Mr Gladstone— (cheers)—and, looking at the way in which he had faced the difficulties put in their way by the Lords, it was, he (Mr Gamble) felt sure, safe to leave the matter in his hands. (Cheers.) It seemed to him that householders both ire St Helens and throughout the country ought to have a voice in Parliamentary elections. It was not for him (Mr Gamble) to say how they should give their votes—they had a right to say that for themselves, but they had a right to have it. (Applause.) Mr J B Leach, who seconded the resolution, said they in St. Helens had been a very patient people for a great number of years, and that would become very apparent when it was remembered that St. Helens was the largest borough in the kingdom without a member. There had been talk enough about the matter, and it was felt—earnestly felt— that they had a perfect right to one. (Cheers.) Let them stand firm, and insist on the franchise and then on redistri- balms trust their leader—(cheers)—and not be hoodwinked by those who in the past had deceived them so much. (Cheers.) Mr T Snaps (Widnes), in supporting the resolution, said he was not disposed to be very angry with Sir Richard Cross, for when a man had been partaking at dinner he was not always capable of guiding his actions. (Laughter.) If

the bill had not been rejected, as they had been reminded by Sir Richard Cross, he would not only have had to speak of them that day as men of St. Helens, but as electors of St. Helens. (Cheers.) The Chairman having put the resolution, it was carried enthusiastically. Mr W S Hadley proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Richard Pilkington for allowing them the use of the grounds, which was seconded by Councillor Foster and carried with accla- mation.
Dr M‘Nicoll then proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers._

- MO r ulton responded on behalf of the speakers, and pro- posed a vote of thanks to the chairman, which, being carried, concluded the proceedings, which had throughout been of an enthusiastic character.

PR ESCOT. THE SUPPORT OF A MOTHER.—At the Prescot Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday, before F W Earle and W L Evans, Esqs., Martin Lyon, of Widnes, was su.nmoned to show cause why he did met c mtribate to the support of his mother, at pre- sent an inmate of the Prescot Union Workhouss.—Tbe Bench made an order for the payment of 23 per week. THE 11TH HUSSARS AT PRESCOT.—On Friday after- noon the headquarter staff and two troops of 11th Hussars arrived in Prescot under the command of Colonel Kincherley and seven officers, en route from Leeds, via Warrington to Liverprol, and thence to Cork. There were in all 90 men, and they were billeted for the night at the various hotels in the town. They resumed their journey on the following morning.

UNJUST SCALES.—Thomas Corns, a grocer, in High-street, Prescot, was summoned at the Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, for having in his possession an unjust pair of scales.—Supt. Barker said he found the defendant's scales half an ounce out of the balance against the purchaser —The Bench remarked that the defendant could not be allowed to rob poor people who came as customers to his shop, and he would be tined 103 and costs.

PRESCOT SCH-073L—i0TL..—The monthly meeting was held on Monday, when there were present Me,ssrs W L Evans (chairman), Hewitt, Sanders, Fogg, and Cross (clerk). The only business of public interest was the con- sideration of applications for increase of salary by William Hall, assistant master of the boys' school. and Miss Sayer, assistant mistress of the girls' school. The Board decided to let the applications lie over for the present.—Accounts amounting to £74 is 104 were passed for payment. The usual return of attendances for the past month was sub- mitted.

LORD DERBY AND HIS FlSH.—Before Mr F W Earle and Mr W L Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Shaw, a powerfully-built man, was summoned for unlawfully taking trout from a brook, the private pro- perty of the Earl of Derby. About seven o'clock on the Sunday night a constable saw the defendant fishing in a brook in Liverpool-road, belonging to the Earl of Derby. The officer asked him what he was doing there, and the defen- dant replied that he was fishing for " snigs." He was taken to the police office, where he gave his name and address. Mr Barnes, agent for Lord Derby, said that the prisoner had no right to fish in the stream.---The defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 203 and costs. THE CONSECKTENCE OF SMASHING WINDOWS.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday before Messrs F W Earle and W L Evans, Frank Minnion, a young min, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly on the 13th inst, and also for breaking eight panes of glass and the frame of a window of a cottage, thereby doing damage to the amount of 53.—Mr tialsall, rent collector, deposed that he saw the defendant under the influence of drink, and after speaking to him (witness) he smashed the windows of a house where he had been collecting the rent, in Hill-street. —The Bench stated that they could not allow people to go about smashing windows, whether they were under the in- fluence of drink or not. The defendant would be fined 5s and costs for the drunkenness; 5s and costs for the damage total, £1 23 61 ; or one month's imprisonment. THEFT OF A BASEE I' OF FISII.—Jane Mulliern, a Sue- picious-lookinz young woman, was charged at the Petty SesSions, on Tuesday. with stealing a basket containing mackerel and flukes, together of the value of 103, the pro- perty of Thomas Cliesworth, a fish dealer, residing in Chapel-street. On the previous evening the prosecutor saw the basket of fish safe in the backyard of his house, but on the morning of that day (Tuesday) he missed them. He thereupon gave information to the police, and after inquiries were made, P.C. Varley visited the prisoner's house in Allen's-court, and there found the stolen basket and fish. On being charged with stealing them she replied, " Yes, I was drunk; I don't know how I got them home."—As the prisoner had been previously convicted she was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

_ PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.-At the monthly meet- ing of the Prescot Board of Guardians, at Whiston Work- house, on Thursday, Dr Cooper was re-appointed medical officer of health for the Widnes (Lower) division at a salary of £7O per year.—ln reply to a letter from the clerk, the Rev Father Whelan, of Canadi, who had received the children recently sent out from the Prescot Union. wrote stating that the children were properly attended to, and only placed in homes recommended by the parish priests. —Mr Johnson stated that with reference to a discussion at the last meeting relative to the expensive charges made at a funeral, he had called upon the undertaker (Mr Helsby), who had handed back a sovereign, stating that the charge of £3 15s was an entire mistake. It should have been £2 15s.—The XL was ordered to be handed over to the widow of the deceased man.—A cheque was signed for £o,] 79 3s 70 in payment of county rates.
THE CHARGES AGAINST PRESCOT UNION OFFICIALS. LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.

An important inquiry affecting the Authorities of the Preecot Union was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon, when Mr James Stuart Davy, one of the inspectors of the Local Government Board, attended to hold a public inquiry into certain charges which had been made against Dr E F Hall, medical officer of health for the district; Mr S Fl Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardians, and several Guardians, by a person who wrote to the Local Government Board under the signature of "W. Law." The inquiry appeared to have excited censiderable interest throughout the district. There were present a many Guardians, and a few ratepayers. Mr Thomas Swift (bar- rister at law, Liverpool) represented Dr Hall, Mr Hanley, and the Guardians.

At the commencement of the proceedings the Inspector asked if Mr W Law was in attendance, but received no answer. He subsequently stated that he had been directed by the Local Government Board to hold an official inquiry with respect to the charges made by a Mr W Law against Mr Hall, medical officer of health; Mr Hartley, clerk, and generally against the Board of Guardians. He pointed out that Mr Law had written a number of letters to the Local Government Board, and that the Board of Guardians had courted a public inquiry into the charges they contained. The letters were addressed from the same address in Prescot as that at which a certain Dr O'Hara resided, and Mr Law in his letters stated that the said Dr O'Hara could prove the truth of the assrertions. He (the inspector) had caused summonses to be issued against both Dr O'Hara and Mr Law to compel them to attend, and he wished to know if they had been served.—Mr Garner, clerk to Mr Swift, solicitor, St Helens, here stated that they were duly left at the residence named, 29. Church-s'reet, Prescot.—The In- spector (continuing) said that Mr Law in remaining away was guilty of a misdemeanour, and he (the inspector) would have to consider what course to subsequently adopt. —Mr H L Riley, solicitor, of St Helens, stated that he at- tended on behalf of Dr O'Hara, and he was also asked to ap- pear on behalf of Mr W LAW. As, however, he was unable to see Mr Law personally, he declined to accept the fee.—The Inssector remarked that the situation was a very awkward one, as no accuser put in an appearance; consequently he must take the case in his own hands.—Ultimately, at the suggestion of Mr Swift, all the witnesses, including Dr O'Hara, left the room.—The Inspector then proceeded to read voluminous letters which had passed between Mr W Law, the Local Gevernment Board, and the Board of Guar- dians. The gubstance of the charges were that by the assistance and connivance of Mr Hartley the medical officer had secured an increase of salary, and the latter was charged with not reporting a case of smallpox which occurred at a millchouse, and with employing an unquapfied assistant, who performed vaccination, and who also attended the work- house and took away drugs which were pro- vided by the guardians for the use of the inmates. The writer also spoke of the " diabolical conduct of those in power," concluding one letter with the intimation that "God knows what we suffer here by neglect and wilful misrepresentation."—After some conversation Dr O'Hara, of Prescot, was called. On entering the room he informed the Inspector that he would not be sworn until he was paid his fee.—The inspector: I have a perfect right ,to summon you, and you are not entitled to any fee at all ; but to avoid any momentarily delay which might take place I pay you the fee.—Dr O'Hara was then sworn, and was examined by the Inspector. He said his name was Daniel Murray O'Hara. —Are you a doctor of medicine? Yes, I am ; and the Master of Arts of an Irish University.—A letter signed " W Law " was then handed to him, the Inspector asking: Do you know the handwriting of that letter ? Dr O'Hara : I decline to answer.—Do you know W LAW ? I know a person who gives his name as W Law.—Where does he live ? I don't know. He comes and goes in my office when he pleases within reasonable hours.—Have you had any com- munication with Mr W Law as to the charges he brings against Dr Hall? I decline to answer that.—The witness was then questioned with reference to a case of smallpox in the family of a person named Smith at Whiston, and was subsequently asked if he knew what the man Law had written about the affair. Dr O'Hara : No.—The Inspector: Will you swear it? Witness : I will swear it; but I may have known it. I don't know it now.—Mr Swift cross- examined the witness, who said he had already sworn that hie name was Daniel Murray O'Hara. He did not know how long he had been known by that name. He did not know that he had ever been known by any other name. —Mr Swift: Have you ever been known by the name of Owen Patrick O'Hare ? Witness: I decline to answer that question.—ln that name did you enter the service of Mr Winn ? I will not say.— Mr Swift: Do you decline to answer on the ground that the answer might tend to criminate you ?—Mr Riley: I ad- vise you to say yes to that question.—Witness: Yes.—Mr Swift aaked if the witness knew Mr Winn but failed to get an answer, and he subsequently handed a letter towards Dr O'Hara, at the same time asking if it was in his writing. The witness did not take the letter or answer the question, which was Several times repeated. —Witness: I decline to answer any questions connected with such a man as Winn.—The Inspector: On what

ground P—l don't wish to be identified with such a man. Other letters were handed to witness and asked if they were written by him, but he stubbornly declined to answer the z questions.—The Inspector asked if Mr W Law had ever acted as his (Dr O'Hara's) secretary.—Witness: No.—Did be ever write letters for you P—Net that I am aware of. Witness declined to say how long he had been in Prescot ; and ultimately exclaimed "I will answer a respectable per- son —he (pointing• to Mr Swift) has a nw'st atrocious character. (Laughter.) The Inspector : , We will stop a minute and allow us to cool down.—Dr O'Hara: I will answer any proper questions. but I will not be brow-beaten.—Mr Swift proceeded to ask the witness if he had ever been in a hospital at London under the name of James Bromley, but no definite answer could be Obtained. As Mr Swift pressed the Point, DI O'Hara said: I say distinctly that to no scoundrel will , answer that question—Mr Riley said he was pained to hear Dr O'Hara use that expression.—Dr O'Hara (to the inspeci tor) : I will answer you any question ; ,138. • not that man.—The Inspector : But you "av- refused to answer several questions before about the letters. I will now ask you one after what you have just said. Are you the writer of the letters Signed W Law, or not ?---Dr O'Hara: I will not answer that quesi tion. (Laughter.)—Mr Swift : Have you a wife jiving. Dr O'Hara: He is an impertinent scoundrel and I will not answer that question.—Mr Swift: Did you ever live in Dnbr lin ? (No answer.) In her Majesty's prison there? No answer.) Were you ever in prison in Belfast? I will elo'' answer that question, sir. There is not ; more scampish scoundrel anywhere than this Inan...„. have been charged in Prescot with every that man can be guilty of, from murder to theft ; and decline to answer the questions. EARLESTO WINT. MACITINISTS DINNEE.—The machinists employed at the Vulcan Ironfoundry sat down with their wives to an el.' cellent dinner at the Sunbeam Inn, Wargrave, on Satardalr evening. A goodly number of persons partook of the re"' past, Which reflected credit upon the host and hostess (1 and Mrs R Morris.) The subsequent proceedings, enliverle with a number of songs, were of a very enjoyable character* THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH DI,PUTE. T tie seat" tered parishioners of St John's Church are bestirring their selves. The committee appointed to consider theadvisv bility of erecting a new place of worship have met oil several occasions, with the result that certain plans bay° been procured ; and a public meeting of the parishioners has been called to receive and adopt the plans on Mondai evening next. The gathering will be held in the tive Hall; and at the meeting the Rev II E Smith (,'"'" curate) and Mr II J Darman (late organist) will be Pre' seated with tokens of the respect and esteem in which the:, are held. A handsome testimonial has beers drawn UP fcht presentation to the Rev H E Smith, and during the Os few days, while it has been on view in the window of tbe shop occupied by Mr Corlett, it has attracted considerable notice.

, DISCEZi3ION AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.—Ou Wedneddill evening the debate on the House of Lords was resumed et the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, the chair being ' occupied by Mr Thomas Howard. There was a fair attend- ! ance. Mr al Birkhead read a paper on the reform of the House of Lords, maintaining that the interests of the cone' try wculd be best served by election of a second chain; ber by the members of the House of Commons. He wa&e! restrict their power of veto; and whenever a Liberal majority of members of Parliament was returned the,' should have power to elect a majority for the second chain' ber. Unless that was done the two Houses were bound t° jar and oppose each other. Messrs McEvoy, Isaac Picker lug, W Gilmour, and Henry Waywell afterwards spoke, the al debate ultimately being again adjourned. About 60 members sat down to a Mos" substantial repast provided by Mr Joseph Lythgoe. At the after proceedings the chair was occupied by Mr E Edward: son and the vice-chair by Mr John Taylor. The usual - loyal and patriotic toasts were- duly honoured, after wlaie4 the Chairman gave the toast of the evening, " Success to ' the Royal Oale Lodge." In responding, lirother Jobil Woodward, D.C.S, remarked that the lodge was in a flourish. log condition considering the heavy expenses they had.bad, to meet during the plot twelve months. "The Visitors was propos d by the Chairman and responded to by gr, eJohn Taylor, and the toast of "Art, Literature, and Music .was also given by the Chairman, and appropriately reg. : ponded to by Mr II J Darman. The procedings were in' terspersed with a selection of songa by Messrs J Willianls, . Mitchell, P Hastie, W Owen, Grundy, and R Ly thgoe. CAPTURE OF A POACHER.—At the Newton Petty Ses" ' sins on Saturday, before Messrs. T J Gillespie, C to, and A C McCorquodale, John Boardman, of Warring' ton, are old offender, was charged with being on land in the occupation of John Howard at Houghton, for the purpose of taking game on the 9th josh—The defendant said he WaS guilty to a certain extent.—Mr. Husband, solicitor, Wigan, appeared on behalf of Mr Thomas Stone, and stated that the right of shooting over the land in question belonged t° the gentleman name 4. He asked the Bench to impose the full penalty of three months' hard labour upon the prisoner* —Henry Smith said he was a keeper in the employ of Mt Stone. On the night of the 9th inst., about half•pas! eleven he was with another keeper on Howard's land, sh° they saw the prisoner in a field near the road. There WO another man with the prisoner, and they were carryini some sticks and nets. The men started running away, sn; witness's son caught one of them while witness fi.,tiowe° the other. Witness, however, was knocked to the ground, and the man made off. The prisoner was detained and al' timately given into custody. They secured several nete which had been recently used.—The Bench imposed a flee of £5 and costs, or in default of payment, two months' prisonment with hard labour; aud the nets and sticks would be forfeited. SCHOLARS' TREAT: A DEFENCE OF THE VICAR.—The annual treat of the Day and Sunday School scholars of th° St. John the Baptist Church took place on Saturday, an° proved a decided success. It was arranged to meet in the church at two o'clock, by which time over 300 scholars ha° assembled. The proceedings commenced with a short address by the Vicar. After they were marshalled into pro. cessional order, banners and flags were distributed. Ou passing the Vicarage, three cheers were given for the Vicar, Mr Matthews ; the curate, Mr Heffield ; and the organist, Mr Pemberton. On reac!aing their destination, the Oratld Stand, Newton Common, various games were indulged in' The tables in the various rooms of the stand were tastefulli decorated with flowers, and tea was ready for them at about four o'clock, to which they did ample justice. Afier the young folks had finished, the teachers and invited guest° partook of an excellent tea provided in one of the anteroonae The Vicar expressed himself pleased to see so many present, especially after the reports which had gone the round of ' the papers, to 'the effect that he ba° hardly a single friend in the parish. He referred to the taunts to which he was subject, Borne comparing him to a cork that would not sink, and closed hie address by calling upon Mr Heffield, tbe curate, who tooh the opportunity to contradict the report published in one of the local papers, to the effect, that he (Mr Ileffield) Wse leaving the parish because he did not think there w'se enough work for two clergymen. This report he was glad to be able to contradict—the real reason being that a 011' tleman had presented him with a valuable living, and he had accepted the offer. This would enable him to settle down in life, and not be a rolling stone, as he was at Pre' sent. He bad cherished the hope of staying with theroi three years, but circumstances altered cases; and it woul° have been very foolish on his part if he had not gladly ac- cepted of the offer so kindly made him. He concluded 3 short but sympathetic address by a kind reference to 10 Matthews, who, he considered to be " more sinned evil than sinning." He hoped that God would spare him an give him sufficient strength to bear the persecution (for he could not call it anything else) to which be had been snh" ject for so many months past, and although that was tilt, first time he had been with them at a treat, he hoped.' would not be the last. After nuts and sweets bad been ells; tributed among the children, a truly happy day washrohgb to a close at about seven o'clock.

THE GARDEN OF AMERICA. On the Narragansett, and dividing the distance betwixt New York and Boston, lies the State of Rhode Island, of which Newport is the capital city. It is the oldest of the New England cities ; and, it may be said, the prettiest. Sometimes it is called the "Garden of America,' or the "Brighton of the West." Not having been in Brighton pro- per I could not compare the two. I doubt if any part of old England is so richly endowed with sylvan beauty on the one hand, and such a splendid beach on the other. The two features combined give it an attractiveness that draws to- gether a tone of society such as we meet in Buxton, or Mat- lock Bath, without the invalid element, and the drinkers of spa waters. The drives are magnificent, and almost closed in by trees, that give to them at noonday the coolness of evening. Entering one of these drives, Bells Vue Avenue, we have the breeze from the sea to give it additional fresh- ness ; and at a certain hour, the fashionable time, or "high ton," the line of carriages that crowd the avenue reminds one of Hyde Park, save that there are no coronets on the panels, nor other insignia of the "pomp and circumstance" . .

of Princely presence. "But who is that gentleman who raised his hat to us?" "Colonel Jerome Napoleon Bonaparte. We have no princes here. Would you mind an introduction to him 9" I had forgotten there was one of the Bonapartes in America. This was on a visit I paid to Newport, and happened during a drive along the three mile run of Belle Vue Avenue. "Well, I saw nothing very princely about Jerome, not of a type that I have been schooled to believe belonged to noble blood. He was more like a private gentleman. Ha was plainly dr'essed,—a "plug" hat, a coat something like mine, "pants" not over long, with continuations of red hose and low shoes. I did not observe any bearings on his car- riage. Such is his familiarity that he is only spoken of as "Jerome." Bela Vue Avenue would be an ugly looking drive if de- nuded of its trees. The modern mansions are unsiehtly, such as no Englishman would put up in his own country. I can only account for this want of taste by attributing it to a desire to be different to other people, like the wealthy gentle- man who wore a bad hat, so as te distinguish himself from his neighbours. Some of the older buildings are really fine. They belong to a time when riches alone were not accepted as evidences of good taste and good breeding. America is not the only country in which monstrosities of various kinds are intended to be looked up to. A spin along the "Ocean Drive" on a hot day is a luxury; and when relieved occasionally by getting down and inspec- ting some natural curiosity, such as the "Spouting Rocks," and the "Hanging Rocks," is made doubly enjoyable. Get- ting too near the latter place is the reverse, as I very soon discovered, the canopy of the carriage being covered in a twinkling with young mosquitoes, just emigrating from their birthplace in a swamp close by. We had a lively fight with these pests ; and more than one of my friends bore scars. They had heard me say that I had never been bitten, and had driven there on purpose that I might have somethine to boast of when I got back to England. Much to their dis- appointment I came out of the melee scathlese, whilst they were engaged in other things than admiring the beauties of nature. The phenomenon here to be seen is caused by the sea rushing into a narrow cavern having an opening about midway something like the blowhole of a spouting whale, only of dimensions that would admit a man's body without fear of his choking it up. The fugitive sea, not being able to find any other outlet, dashes up this natural blowhole, sending up a column of water sometimes to the height of fifty feet. If anyone is so incautious as to stand near when the tide is a little sportive, and plays "around " kitten like, then makes a spring and, dashes up the hole in its wildest strength, a bathing dress would be the most suitable garment to be worn at the time. This can only be witnsssed when the tide is well up, and a fresh breeze is blowing inshore. " Purgatory" is a chasm that takes a little after the "Lover's Leap," in Dovedale, Derbyshire. It has the tradi- tions that attach to all such places, with this variation,—a youth, to show what he would dare, to propitiate the affec- tions of the lady of his choice, leaped across this chasm, and had the satisfaction of learning from her own lips that any fellow who was fool enough to risk his life for no good pur- pose was not to fool with her, so she "went back on him," as the Yankees phrase it. Anyone must admire the young lady's good sense. Had 'ate lover emulated the deeds of one of America's noblest daughters it would perhaps have had a different effect. On a small island lying under the Fort is the solitary home of Ida Lewis, the Grace Darling of America. I had the privilege, not accorded to everyone, of visiting that lonely nest. My host for the time, Mr. Charles Bickerton, took out a boat one afternoon and after a visit to the fort we pulled to the rock on which the lighthouse stands. Miss Lewis was just returning in her boat from the city, and the guardians of her " sea-girt isle," a pair of New- foundland dogs, were baying " deep-mouthed " welcome to their mistress. At first we were forbidden to land, as she had been bored with visitors, but on learning through her brother that I woe a stranger from England, the heroine of many a gallant rescue waved me a cordial welcome. One of the dogs was ready to assist me up the slippery rocks, had his services been required. D a was chatty about many things, but never for once did she allude to any of her inci- dents that had made her name famous throughout the world. She led us into a room where she keeps her medals; and I felt as if I was in the presence of a being more than human as I gazed upon that precious store, blessed by the grateful offerings of souls whose existence on earth she had been the means of prolonging. I must confess that I was disappointed with the personal appearance of this brave woman. I had pictured her in my mind as a kind of amazon, with sinews of rare power, and. a presence that would overcome a storm. Instead of that I found her to be a slim, wiry figure, of about middle height, and without any indication of being endowed with fins. I know not what the sensation of drowning may be, but a strange feeling came over me as she "tipped me her flipper," and gave my , hand something more than a one-fingered grip. I felt, somehow, as if I was b, ing pulled into a boat, previous to being discharged of a freight of sea water, and a cargo of brandy shipped instead. On our return from the rock my friend recounted to me some of the deeds of daring that had marked the career of this human petrel. One was of her rescuing two soldiers who had been skating on treacherous ice, and had got im- mersed. When other means of reaching them had failed, Ida dashed upon the ice, equipped with nothing but a clothes- prop, and laying herself down held out successfully the hand of deliverance, amidst the ringing shouts of the spec- tators. For this gallant act she was fittingly rewarded. The ordinary duties of Ida Lewis are to attend to the lamp fixed in the seaward corner of the building, for which she receives 750 dollars a year. A successor would only re- ceive 500. The extra 250 dollars are given as a reward of merit. Poor Ida! She was in deep mourning; and our boatmen knew her by that when most of a mile away. "She is coming yonder," he said, as we were nearing the light- house. "She is mourning the death of her sister, who lived with her on the rock;" and I could well understand how one of two such companions would grieve at losing the other. The greatest curiosity to be seen in Newport is not of natural formation. It is .the work of human bands; but when it was built, or for what purpose, history has not a word to say. This structure is called the "Old Mill," from a supposition, nothing more that it was originally used for grinding purposes by an earlier civilization than Columbus introduced. Here. I had best quote the authority of the " Guide to the City of the Sea: "Probably the first striking object for enquiry that will arrest attention is the old stone mill in the centre of Touro Park, near the head of Belle Vue Avenue. It is, most cer- tainly, very old, and as certainly of extremely obscure origin. We dare not tell you much about it, yet there it stands Sphinx-like, awaiting your cleverest guess. . . We will not undertake to prove it to be either a Viking's watch-tower, raised 900 years ago, or simply Governor Arnold's old mill, built by the colonists in 1663; and we would not, if we could, clear the pleasing mystery that hangs about its origin. The wall of this ruin is about twenty-four feet high, built very substantially of rough stone, with lime mortar, and has heart harled, or rough cast, with lime. It is raised on eight pillars, about seven feet high, and from five to six feet apart, a most picturesque object in the landscape, a monument to the taste and skill that fashioned it, whether the head and hand belonged to Norseman' or Anglo-Saxon." Evidently the lime of the mortar used in building this tower was the produce of burnt oyster shells, as bits not properly calcined are to be found mixed with the other material. Said "Old Jemmy," the coloured confectioner, whose stall is near, "a man, Missr Brierley, who could give the his'ry of that yar buildin' need do marlin more. It would be a fortin' for him." The origin of the round towers of Ireland is not hidden in deeper mystery. Through the kindness of my hostess, Mrs. Bickerton, I obtained permission to go through the Episcopal Church, the "Old Trinity," the oldest, with one exception, in the United States, being built in 1726. In this church the cele- brated Bishop Berkeley was wont to preach. On the pastor's returning to England he sent an organ as a present to the church. The piety of the time would only accept the case. The musical portion was transferred to a less puri- tanical place of worship. Since then the stays of bigotry have been unlaced, and the organ has been restored, but with a new filling. The church was built and endowed by English money, and is the only one in the States the spire of which bears on its apex the British crown. It is a con- dition of the endowment that this crown shall not be re- moved. But it is an eyesore to some people who have been raised under the Republic. The bell was presented by Queen Anne, but it has been broken up and re-cast so often that it can hardly be called the same. The pews are the square high-backed boxes of a former period, and are taxed by the State, the seatholder having to pay the tax, in addition to a high"rental. There seems to be nothing but speech that is not taxed.—From " Great Britain over the Sea," by Ben

'Smith: "Milk contains all the elements of the human blood. Why do you call that experimenter an idiot ?" Jones: "Because he intends to try It with New York milk A labouri,,g man, out of work and hungry, went one Morning into the surgery of a parish doctor, eat down and asked to have one of his teeth taken out. The doctor opened the man's mouth and looked at his teeth, but, seeing nothing amiss, said " Which is the tooth, friend ?" " Oh, e'e? a one You like, sir," said the man. " I've got nothing for 'em to do; so 1 thought I might as well get rid on 'em." The good doctor did not charge his patient anything for looking into bLS mouth, but gave him a shilling, and told him to go and eSt his teeth a job for one day, at all events. How co GET OIIIT OF A. DIFFICULTY.—It MUSt have been With infinite amusement that Mr. Henry Ward Beecher during a late vacation, heard one of his own published ser- Mons delivered in an obscure village. At the close of the service he accosted the divine, and said, "That was a fair discourse. How long did it take you to write it ? " "Oh, I tossed it off one evening when I had leisure!" was the reply. " Indeed !" said Mr. Beecher. "It took me much longer than that to think out the very framework of the sermon." "Are you Mr. Henry Ward Beecher'?" "I am," was the reply. "Well, then," said the unabashed preacher, "all that I have to say is that I ain't ashamed to preach one Or your sermons anywhere!" A good story concerning a lady of fashion who has gone on " the boards" was told the other day. Whilst she was in New York she sent for a young American dramatist who had been recommesded as a good person to write a play for her. Re called, and was given a seat. Mrs. X. entered the room. Without a word of formality she surveyed him with a cold Xnglish stare, and then walked clear around him, looking at him the whole time. It was, of course, eminently agreeable to be surveyed like a horse on sale. Bat the playwright Stood it. Having completed her surrey, she asked almost contemptuously, "And do you think you could write a Play ? " The author, who had made several successes, answered in a civil tone, "Well, Ido not know. I dare Bay I may be about as competent to write a play as you are to act one." They did not come to terms. A contemporary says that a well-dressed man standing at an hotel door in Manchester not long since was hailed by a shoeblack with the usual question, " Clean your boots, sir? " "What do you charoe ?" asked the man, who was noted for his stinginess. "A penny, sir," was the reply. "Too much; rn give you a halfpenny," said the man. "All right," said the youngster; and at it he went with might and main. 'Very soon he had one boot shining like a mirror; but, in- stead of commencing on the other, he began to pack up his brushes. "You haven't finished!" exclaimed the man. "Never mind," replied the shoeblack, with a twinkle in his eve. "I won't charge you anything for what I've done Here comes a custonvr who always pays." The man glanced at the shining boot, then at the other, which was rusty and bespattered with mud, thought of the ridiculous figure he I Would make with only one polished boot, and at last, amid the laughter of the bystanders, agreed to give the witty lad threepence to finish the job, which he did in double-quick time. A " QIIIET CHAP."—In his Romance of the Coast Mr. itunciman tells the following stories of a pilot who Was quite a character in his way. Be was very intolerant of railways but his first experience of the locomotive engine was not pleasant. Somehow he got on to the railway-line on a hazy night; and just as the train had slowed down to enter the station the engine struck him and knocked him over. The engine-driver became aware of a brief burst of strong lan- guage, and, in great alarm, called upon two porters to walk along the line to see what had happened. 'They did so; and when they got to the place of the accident, the light of their lanterns reveated the pilot Perfectly sound and engaged in brushing dirt of his clothes. When he saw the bright but- tons of the railway officials, the thought of the police came instantly into his mind, and he said, "Here, now, you needn't be taking me up; if I've dona any damage to your engine, I'll pay for it." At another time he was bringing a ship northwards, when he was invited by the captain to run down below and help himself to a nip of brandy. After taking his brandy he proceeded to light his pipe at the stove. Now the captain possessed a Inge monkey, and the creature was shivering near the fire. The pilot said," A gusty day, sir," and the monkey gave a responsive shiver. The pilot went on with affable gruffness, "The Soutar's light's away on the port bow now, sir ;" and still the monkey made no answer. Not to be stalled off, the pilot n• •ceed‘d, " Well be over the bar in an hour, sir." But failing to elicit a response even to this pleasant informariort, he stepped up on deck, and ranging himself alongside of the captain on the o. said, "-What a quiet chap your father is !'
Mr Sam. Mendel, for many years a leading merchant in Manchester, died early on Wednesday mormog at his resi- dence, Balharn, Surrey.

Two more deaths have resulted from the explosion at Hall End Colliery, West Bromwich, making six in all. Five of the injured men remain in the hospital. The body of a naval officer, named Alfred Shaw, be- longing to the Pembroke flagship, was found on Thurs- day morning in the basin at Chathain. An inquest will be held. Intelligence reached Galway on Wednesday night that a man holding a boycotted farm near Cong had been fired at and wounded in the legs. An attempt was also made to burn down his house. RIDING A HORSE ON THE FOOTPATH.—At the Newton Town hail on Saturdas; James Glynn pleaded guilty to ob- structing the footpath by riding a hose thereon, at Win- wick, on the 9th inst., and was fined 23 Gd and costs. SOCIALSCIENCE CONORESS.—The proceedings of the So- cial Science Congress at Birmingham were begun on Wed- nesday evening. when the Right Hon. G. Shaw Lefevre, M.P., First Commissioner of Works, delivered his presi- dential address. He reviewed the progress of social legisla- tion for about 20 years, and declared that in protecting the young and weak, in saying life, and in changing land tenures, the Government was carrying out a beneficent programme approved by the people and by modern ecmomists. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A "STEEPLE JACE."—On Thursday morning Charles Lees, a steeple Jack, died at the Oldham Infirmary from the effects of a fearful fall on Wednesday afternoon. Lees was repairing a chimney at Green's bolt works when he fell from the top, a distance of twenty-six yards, into the street beneath. At the police station the thud of his fall was distinctly heard. When picked up Lees was insensible, his skull was fractured, and his and leg broken. He was conveyed to the infirmary, where be died next morning. AN AWFUL CONSPIRACY.—At Fall River it is said that there has been collusion there between the medical exami- ners, agents, and others for two years in graveyard insur- ance scheme. Broken-doyen drunkards, consumptives. and unhealthy persons have been insured for sums ranging from I 51000 to $5,000, and physicians, agents and others would hold policies till death of the insured and pocket the insur- ance, or sell the policies to rumsellers, who would give the victims enough rum to hasten death and then collect the insurance. A flatman named uwens is in custody at Liverpool char- ged with causing the death of a little Ord named Pollard, whose dead body was found in the canal on Thursday after she bad been seen on Owens's boat. Two goods trains were in collision early on Thursday morning, during a fog, on the Midland Railway, near Bar- row-on-Soar. Some damage was done to the line and rolling stock, and a guard was slightly injured. The Damen magistrates on Thursday refused to renew a public-house license on the ground that the place was not required for public convenience, and that it was merely a " tippling-house." whose existence was likely to create drunkenness and disorder. Mr Bradlaugh has published a paper in which he calls upon Radical members of Para irnent to introduce a bill for the abolition of a hereditary House of Lords. He depre- cates a " revolution," but thinks such an upheaval of so- ciety likely if the reform is refused.

div.p: FARNWORTH AGRICULTUP.XL
SOCIETY.

The 20th annual show in connection with this society was 'held in the show field. Farnworth, on Thursday, and the usually quiet little village presented a scene of festivity. The arrangements of the show field were exactly similar to those adopted in former years. and therefore need no de- scription, but it may be stated that they afforded every convenience to exhibitors, visitors, and officials. Although the society is handicapped with a considerable debt, the Committee of Management were able to offer substantial in • ducements to farmers and others to become exhibitors, no less than £5OO being offered in prizes. There were also offered for general competition eight silver cups. These had been presented to the society by Mr Frank Gaskell, Widnes; Spratt's Patent Biscuit Company; Mr if C Joplin, Gras- mere Park, Huyton ; Mr James Boyle, Oldbam-road, Manchester; Mr James Frame; and the Fox Terrier Club. The entries showed an increase of about 200 on last year, when, however, the farmers had a great disinclination to show stock of any description in consequence of the preva- lence of foot and mouth disease in the district, and the fact that the season bad been a bad one. Compared with previ- ous years, the total entries show that the general average has been attained. But the increase ia cattle, horses, and implements is very noticeable, while it is rather strange to observe that the entries of poultry have gradually declined
from 1879. The following comparative table for the past six years will be read with interest :

1879 1880 1881 1882 1893 1834 Cattle 33 48 39 35 36 58 Horses, ste Pigs Butter 9 7 11 • 9 8 6 Roots Potatoei Beet, e •rn , /1e Ppultry, ae 216 229 163 184 107 139 Pige MIS D ogs 274 267 291 282 247 253 Implemsnts Extra stock 0 0 4 5 19 0

Tetals.. 1000 1089 1098 1001 848 1041 A large number of entries does not necessarily imply a great number of exhibits, but on Thursday there were numerous exhibits in the various classes, and the quality was generally acknowledged to be mach in advance of former years, especially as regards cattle and horses. In fact, the show was one of the most successful ever held by the Society, and was in marked contrast to the show of last year. Oa that occasion rain descended in torrents the whole day, and the receipts at the gate did not exceed £lOO. On Thursday, however, the atmospheric elements were very propitious. The sun shone from an altnost cloudless sky, the intensity of its rays being tempered by a slight westerly breeze. Under such circumstances an agricultural show holds out attractive inducements to the dwellers in town as ' well as to those interested in agriculture, and visitors were continually arriving on the ground up to four o'clock. It was computed that between eight and ten thousand persons paid for admission. The first event of the afternoon was j the jumping of the horses, and the grand stand was filled with interested spectators, whilst at least three thousand people encircled the enclosure. Although one or two of the" jockeys" had a spill no mishap occurred. The Star of Temperance Brass Band was present during the day and played choice selections of music. The arrangements of the show were efficiently carried out by the courteous secretary, Mr R Whiteside, and Messrs W Longton, James Warburton, and John Halsall, directors of the show yard. assisted by the following stewards of departments:— Horned cattle and pigs: Mr George Swift, Bold ; Mr W H Johnson, Halegate ; Mr Thomas Hedgcock, Upton ; Mr R Hedgoock, Huyton. Heavy horses: Mr Joim Kenwright, Tarbock; Mr H Mawdsley, Rainhill ; Mr James Johnson, Eccleslon ;Mr Thomas Baker, Bold. Light horses :Mr W B Longton, Crouton Hall; Mr John Goldsworth, Windle ; Mr John Ilednock Warrington; Mr John Whalley, Bold ;

Mr John Pugh, Garston. Butter, roots, seed corn, and im- plements: Mr Isaac Houghton, Cronton ; Mr Thomas Ger- rard, Widnes; Mr John Johnson, Caerdley ; Mr Jas Wright, Cuerdley. Poultry: Mr T H Rowe, Hale; Mr W Golds. worth, junr, Eccleston ; Mr Sampson, Warrington. Pigeons: Mr John Matthews, Widnes;. Mr T Shuttleworth„ junr, Fernworth. Dogs: Mr James McKay, St Helens; Mr G Pilling, Warrington; Mr R H Wright, Newton; Mr W Longton, Wt.:boon ; Mr T W Husband, Garston ; Mr D Wright, Widnes. Inspector Wood and a force of constables were present to preserve order. An efficient corps of judges had been procured, and we did not hear of any instances in which their decisions were questioned. Following h a list of their names : Horned cattle and pigs: James Parr, Esq, Hatton, Warring- ton. James Drinkall, Esq, West Derby. Heavy horses: P Blundell, Esq, Weeton, near Kirkham, Fylde ; Wm Dale, Esq, Somerville, Seacombe. Light horses: W A Meadows, F W Earle, Esq, Roby. Butter. roots, seed corn, and imple- ments R Webster, Esq, Litherland ; John Hulme, Esq, Melling; R Mawdsley, Esq, Rainhill. Poultry: It Teebay, Esq, Fnlwond, Preston; George Fell, Esq, Warrington. Pigeons: E C Stretch, Esq, Ormskirk. Dogs (Mastiffs and St Bernards) H C Joplin, Esq, Huyton, (greyhounds) Jae Taylor, Esq, Rochdale, (Fox Terriers and Dachshunds) E M Southweil, Esq, Bri North, (Sheep dogs) Frank Gas ken, Esq, Widnes, (other non-sporting dogs) P Eden, Esq, Sal- ford, James Taylor, Esq, Rochdale, (other sporting dogs) James Freme, Esq, Flint, T B_Bowers,_Esq, Chester.

div.head: THE' LUNCHEON.
div.p: THE' LUNCHEON.

At one o'clock luncheon was served in a tent upon the ground by Mr J II Mondsell of Sr. Anne-street, Liverpool. Sir R A. Cross, M P, the president of the society, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Cal J Ireland Blackburne, M l', Major Meade King, Major Ireland, South- port, Col Wyatt (agent to the Earl of Sefton), Captain Willis, J P, the Revs G Bond, J Wright Williams, J Cassells Brown (late vicar of Dittos), Messrs Robert Davies ( War- rington), John White, J P (Warrineton), T W Tanen ( With- enshaw), C Southeby (high sheriff for Northamptonshire), W Gibson (Liverpool), and W F Husband (Widnes). The judges and siewarits vid.e also present. '

The Chairman having given' the usual loyal toasts pro- posed "The Bishop and clergy of the diocese, and minis- ters of all denominations," remarking tkat he knew no set Of men who worked harder or who were more worthy of their pay than the clergy. The Rey. George 13.0 d fesponded. He ob9Stveol that the Bishop WAS showing great energy by a number of questions addressed to the clergy of every parish at the present time, and they had to give a good account of themselves if they could. As regirded the clergy, they were only too glad to receive recognition and help from their parishioners. They tried to do the best they could in the Farnworth parish. They could not b a s tid to derive much from land—all their tithes went to Prescot—and they had to depend upma the generosity of the parishioners. But for all that they had a bit of glebe, and therefore there was a little bit of sympathy between the clergy and those who cultivated land elsewhere. He was glad that they, like others, had had a good crop, and he only hoped that when they came to thrash it would turn out better than they expected. (Applause.) Cal. Wyatt gave "Success to Farnworth Agricultural Society." There were three things, he said, necessary for the success of an agricultural meeting. namely, tine weather, a large quantity of exhibits, and a large number of visitors. Last year the Clerk of the Weather was not in a very good humour, but that day they had to be thankful for a most magnificent day, and judging from the thousands of people who bad gone through the turnstiles the show would be a financial success. There was one important matter and that was to have a good chairman of the Management Committee, and in Mr Longton they had a most excellent chairman, and he begged to couple that gentleman's name with the toast. (Applause.) Mr Longton responded on behalf of the committee, and thanked those present for the hearty manner in which they had received the toast. The society was managed and car- ried through solely by small tenant farmers, and they would be strengthened and encouraged by the pre3ence of so many influential gentlemen, and continue to make the society the success it had been hitherto. (Applause.) 134. fore he sat down he would give the toast ef health to Sir Richard Assheton Cross.

The Chairman, in reply, said it gave him great pleasure to be present on that occasion. He must thank them very heartily for the way in which they had received the toast. Colonel Wyatt had told them three things were necessary for the success of an agricultural show—fine weather, plenty of entries, and plenty of visitors. (Hear, hear.) He quite agreed with him, but he should like toadd a fourth,and that was the quality of the stock which was shown. (Hear, bear.) It had been his privelege to go through the show that morn- ing with considerable care, and he must say he was very much struck at the excellent stock of the farmers shown in the yard that day. All he could say was that he hoped they would go on and prosper. (Hear, hear.) As Mr Longton bad said it was an excellent thing for the farmers by ex- hibiting their stock in a small show to gain encouragement to compete at the larger shows. (Hear, hear.) He was not a great advocate for a great number of small shows, but there was room for both large and small, and he could tlsify that that show had for years past done good work in this district. (Applause.) He congratulated the farmers upon having bad a good season for their harvest. It was a long lane that bad no turning, and the farmers lane had been a very long one. (Applause.) They had had at all events the sympathy of those who had studied their case, and he hoped that in future years they weuld be rewarded for their patience and perseverance. But he was quite aware that though the crops were good their labour bill did not de- crease, and prices were very low. He was sorry to say that rates had still a tendency upwards instead of downwards. He hoped it would not be long before those promises which had been held out before them so long, and were still un- fulfilled, might yield fruit some time or other ; the sooner the better ; and that some further relief would be given to rural ratepivers than had been given up to the present time. The tax collector was bad enough, but the rate collector always put his hand still deeper in their pockets than the man who collected the taxes. He thought it was one of those matters that had been so long before the public that the Government of the day—he was not speaking ef one Government or the other—ought seriously to make the matter a primary question, and the promises made should be fulfilled and relief should be given. (Applause.) He was much obliged to them for the way in which they had received the toast, and he had now great pleasure in pro- -posing the judges. Mr Webster responded, and in doing so he said there was no doubt the farmers had had good crops of wheat, and fair crops of barley, but he was sorry to say he did not think they had had fair crops of oats. These would be poor. He had been over 40 farms this season, and that was his opinion as to the crops. Foreign competition was very great, and it was time they came to fair trade. They would never have fair prices till they had fair trade. (Hear, hear.) They

ought to have the sparrows eradicated hero the Birds' Act. (Laughter.) In some parts no less than a third of the crop had been destroyed by sparrows. It was not what they ate. but what they picked out and dropped on the ground. Sparrows ought not to be in the Act at all; he believed they were not named, but still there was a close time for them. (Applause) Mr James Warburton proposed "Our friends and sup- porters ;" and Mr Sotherby respended. Colonel Blackhurne then proposed the toast of "The Press," to which Dr Mackie responded. CA TTLE AND HORSES. The cows on exhibit were a very good lot, the milking stock being of a particularly fine quality. On the whole there was plenty of flesh about them. The bulls were genet.- ally rather a moderate class, but two fine animals, owned by Mr Cook, of Chester. were the subjects of considerable notice. There were some very fair specimens of heifers. In all there were twelve classes for horned cattle, with 58 entries. This year, although there was a considerable in- crease in the number of horses brought to Farnworth, the quality had in no way deteriorated. In the classes for draught horses were seen some splendid animals, possessed ot plenty of bone and muscle, and in the light classes the exhibits were of uniform excellence, so that the judges ex perienced some little difficulty in awarding the prizes. The turnouts in the harness classes were also pretty numerous, and some stylish concerns were entered. The jumping con- tests were, of course, the centre of attraction for a large num- ber of spectators. div.head: PIGS.
div.p: PIGS.

There were twenty-five entries in six classes for pigs, most of the exilibitors being locsl keepers, and some good animsls were entered, the boars being a fine lot. Prizes:— For the best bnar, large or middle breed, any age, James B'eph9n3 1 John Cartwright 2. For the best boar, small breed, any age, Jlt Whalley 1, Joseph Ball 2. BUITER, ROOTS, POTATOES, AND SEED CORN. There was only one class for butter, which brought for- ward half-a-dozen good entries. The class with the best basket of butter, not less than six pounds, prizes of £2, £l, 103, and ss, being offered. The first was awarded to Mrs T Johnstone, the second to Thomas Foster, the third to T Hedgcock, and the fourth to Mrs R H Wright. For roots there were four classes and thirty-four entries, which in- cluded some first class exhibits of roots, the mangold ' wurzels being of enormous 3i29. The combined weight of half-i-dozen of the exhibits of mangold wurz3ls was ona cwt. Margaret Garnett and Isaac Houghton were first and second in the class for the best Swedish turnips (six bulbs), and out of only three entries in the class for the best Scotch cabbage (not less than three) Jamas E Pardey and James Warburton were awarded first and second places. POULTRY AND PIGEONS.

There were over a hundred entries in the poultry classes. which numbered twenty-four. The exhibits were generally considered very commendable, and came in for their due share of notice. There was also a large show of pigeons. The first and second prizes for carriers were awarded to a dun and black respectively, and both were good lengthy birds. [here were also some very good Equeakers. To the class for pouters only two birds were exhibited, which re- quire nothing more than a passing mention. A couple of very good nuns were shown. The six barbs awarded prizes were really excellent birds, one, though rather poor in feather, being admirable about the bead points. There was a good collection of English doves, and sortie good specimens of long-faced tumblers. The Jacobins were also a giod class, and there were a couple of splendid birds shown in the trumpeter class. In the class for the best exhibit of any variety, Mr. J. P.
