THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND THE WELSHMEN. Sir,— Your correspondents " Pendennis " and " Captain Cuttle " are, I think, right in the conclusion they have come to with regard to the decision of our Town Council in this matter. I speak out of fulness of sympathy with our Nelsti friends. But it seems to me that in establishing an important precedent with regard to the letting of rooms to religious bodies. our Corporation have done more for the cause of religious equality and progress than in following their evident inclination and letting a room for religious worship. I speak as a Dissenter, objecting to State, county, or mnnicipal patronage, and I would include within the meaning of the term" patronage" connections such as alit which it was sought to establish in the present case. Dis- tinctions between different sorts of patronage or connection in religious matters soon become lost, and in their present disappointment our Welsh friends are saved from a pos- sible future reproach and scandal. Knowing what their re- ligion is to Welshmen, I have no doubt they will soon find a room well suited to their needs; indeed, I should not be surprised if in a little while they were in possession of a handsome church erected by their own efforts. With regard to the important and wise precedent es- , tablished by the Corporation, one thing only remains to be said : Let them see to it that it be resolutely and unhesi- tatingly followed. Let us hear no more of the lending of the Mayor's parlour to Churchmen; no left-handed patron- age of Church institutions. Dissenters don't want it ; the works of their hands, their churches and schools, are evi- dence of this, and what they havedone they will continuo to do. Let Churchmen provide for their own spiritual re- quirements, and let the Corporation keep itself free from all sectarian connections whatsoever. Y ur eorrespoadent " Pendennis " could not refrain from a few re,earks of doubtful taste upon recent conduct of the Rev. J. Yunge. " Pendennis" seems to think that pastoral effort and energy are to be limited to the pulpit. On what grounds he justifies this narrow view I do not understand. I suppose there were pastors before pulpits, and I dare say the latter will be the first to disappear. " Pendennis " ought to know that it is a minister's duty to combat sin in every shape and form wherever found. S) far from Mr Yongeel interfering in that which does not concern him in suggest- ing remedies for the evils consequent on the use of intoxi- cants, it seems to me he is emphatically minding his own , business. It is surely as much his duty and privilege to endeavour to save the lives of men as it is that of the pub- lican to help to destroy them. I need not point out that the contusion that exists in " Pendennis's " mind between the " legal " and the "legitimate." "Pendennis " would surely not argue that what has legal recognition is neces- sarily legitimate. If so. what need for political agitation or reform ? Does " Pendennis" assent to the proposition that " whatever is. is right ?" I could classify with the drink traffic eneny trades having legal sanction which " Pendell- nis " might not think so unobjectionable. "Pendennis" sarcastically alludes to the philanthropic (correctly speaking) efforts of "tradesmen." Not content with confining the parson to his pulpit, he would likewise confine the tradesman to his counter. And thus he would forbid them to cherish all political and social ambition ; he would have them become contemptibly selfish and narrow minded, limiting them to a mere daily struggle for bread, without any exercise of those mental and moral and spiritual gifts and qualities that lift man above the level of the brute. Looking at this estimate of the capabilities of man, one experiences unbounded satisfaction in the reflec- tion that "God bath made us, and not we ourselves." Rather than rebuke the tradesmen, whose soul rises above the level of the counter, our deep regret should be that so few of his class do demonstrate the possession of a soul at all—a fact that must be infinitely pleasing to "Pen- dennis." Before I close. I should like to refer to some remarks of "Cap'ain Cuttle." I should be thankful if "Captain Cuttle " would disclose his real name; or, if he cannot do that, if he would drop a nom de plume which brings to the minds of readers of Dickens a character 80 rich and humor- oas that the association of; the beloved name with the fiat and gelatinous ideas of your correspondent is a source of piquant irritation. So long as your correspondent chooses to adhere to this none we must, I suppose, do violence to our feelings in mentally connecting it with one who does not display one-twentieth part of the charity and kindness of heart so conspicuous in Dickens's immortal character. It was only to be expected from the Previous letters of "Cap- tain Cuttle " that if he entered this controversy at all it would be as the uncompromising foe of Christian effort. That is his standpoint, and in proceeding with his attack he leaves nothing unsaid that is calculated to wound the feel- ings of religious people. Whenever I perform the painful task of reading the jibes and sneers of 'Captain Cuttle," I am led to wonder if difference of opinion with regard to the merits of religion is to wipe out all sympathy between minds and hearts that with equal striving are searching for truth. Is it impossible for "Captain Cattle to believe that the professing Christian is capable of putting into prac- tice the precepts of his faith ? Would "Captain Cattle," in the face of history, in spite of the many lives he must have known that were lived in pure and unselfish devotion to the welfare of others, still affirm that consistency is not a Christian virtue? I wish to establish this point, because it is the main argument of "Captain Cuttle." He never attacks the grand principles of conduct that Christianity lays down. He, like all men unskilled in argu- ment, sacrifices everything for an araumentam ad hominem. And as everybody knows in cases where principles are con- sidered such an argument is as ungenerous as logically un- sound. I say that "Captain Cuttle " makes the character of religious men the cover of tie attack upon their faith. I suppose he would never forbid the exercise of charity, of goodwill, of pity, compassion, brotherly kindness? I sup- pose be does not object to follow the golden rule of action —to do to others as be would be done by? And yet Chris- tianity teaches all that. He would declaim against selfish- ness, prlde, tyranny, avarice ?—the Christian is bidden to reject and denounce slide things. Let us suppose th Lt., fol- lowing historical precedent, " Captain Cuttle" and his fol- lowers set up in our local Notre Dame the worship of the Goddess of Reason. Doubtless there would arise Well Sha- drachs, Meshechs, and Aheinegoe to declate that they would not bow the knee to false gods, And if, keeping to the precedent, the cattle-fishes were to visit on the stiff necks of these men the rewards of their obstinacy, and Church- street ran with blood, could reasonable men find fault with Reason because her votaries had behaved irrationally? And not until "Captain Cattle " ceases to gaze at the dancing and distorted reflections of the sun of the Christian ideal life upon the waters of human conduct, and directs his at- tention to the life-giving orb itself will his arguments be worth the consideration of thoughtful men. As we have seen, it is only when we come to the grand motive of our conduct that his path and mine diverge; he to follow the promptings of a fallible conscience; Ito strengthen and fix it by the pole of a righteous and omniscient God. Tnen why does he attack the ground on which he himself stands 70 "Captain Cattle" would bid the avalanche of Christianity stop in its progress, he would have the express train wait for the humble trolly that bears the followers of Mr Bradlaugh. These illustrations disclose the absurdity of "Captain Cuttle's "demand. I must ask your pardon, Mr Editor, for entering upon an argument of a theoligicil nature in your paper. This reply has been stung from me by the unfeeling and frivolous re- marks of " Captain Cuttle" upon the practice of weak and faulty professors of our religion. And in conclusion let me implore "Captain Cattle "to desist from his efforts to draw the working man downward to the atheistic level of life and conduct—efforts the success of which he knows is founded in dissatisfaction that has its root in other than the affairs of religion—in the present social inequalities and in the evil relations of capital and labour, a dissatisfac- tion which predisposes him to scepticism and unbelief. If the working-man has nothing else of value; if unceas- ing alternation of work and sleep has made life for him void and bitter, and the univerall brotherhood of men a farce and a sham, he has an equal share with us all in the "larger hope " whose fulfilment will remove to illimitable distance of relative happiness the life that is computed by years.—Yours faithfully, FRED R. ROBERTS. 92, Bewsey-road, Warrington. A SHARE IN THE PROFITS. Sir.—l think you will need no pressing to throw open your columns to the discussion of a subject second to none in im- portance to the working-man. Mr Frederic Harrison, writ- ing to the Pall Mall Gazette on a "New Industrial loquiry," draws attention to the importance of this inquiry being free from all "doctrine and open to all interests." Sometime early in the year a Scotch gentleman, strongly impressed with the necessity of putting an end to the ever- lasting feuds that exist between capital and labour, placed In the hands of trustees the sum of £I,OOO for the purpose of keeping before the public the following question—" What are the best means, consistent with equity and justice, for bringing about a more equal division of the accumulated wealth of the country, and a more equal division of the daily products of industry between capital and labour, so that it may become possible for all to enjoy a fair share of material comfort and intellectual culture, possible for all to lead a dignified life, and less difficult for all to lead a good life." The bases of operations as thus sketched out are cer- tainly comptehensive, and ought to lead to something definite. A straeg wish on the part of the committee exists to start with the ground as clear as possible. With this view they have held a series of meetings at which they "have sought to reduce to a minimum that inevitable part of every inquiry into these wide questions which is desultory, unscientific, anarchical, and doctrinaire." The ground being thus cleared, it is proposed to hold a confer- ence in London in January next, to which are to be invited such representative men as are best acquainted with the labour question. To a working man, daily set with his face to the grind- stone, few opportunities are afforded for quiet reflection and study. He only knows this, that with all our advances in machinery and in organisation, no leisure comes to the human workers. Hence, when brought face to face with capital his resistance is spasmodic without a delloite course of action. He fritters, and wastes away his strength. and, instead of his society's funds being to huh a source of strength, they become the means of beguiling him into a very serious and ruinous dispute. But the work this proposed conference has before it embraces something more than the mere benefiting of what is called the skilled artizan. As the toiling millions are growing in political power and in the knowledge required to epeculate upon their lot, and the wav to improve it, they will naturally seek for their sons to be better placed in life than they themselves have been. Strikes, the present weapon for resisting capital, will be laid hold of as opportunities for introducing the unskilled, into the ranks of the skilled, still leaving outside a large army of men, and I think we must now say women, who unfor- tunately hang like a mill atone round the neck of everything

at. deal: Years ago methods have been suggested, and in some few in- stances attempts have been made to carry out, what have been called Utopian ideas, with respect to capitalists dividing the profit made in business, with those who created it. A strong argument with employers who objected to this has always ' been, will the workman divide the losses? This of course is an unreasonable question. Labour must be taken as the forerunner of all capital, and unless this position be accep- ted, argument will not settle the dispute ; but anarchy will, and out of this will come peace. When we look abroad with a wish to see how other nations are dealing with the labour question, what is it that meets our eye? From America we have just had a column printed in the notes giving such a picture that one may well tremble for the sta- bility of Greater Britain. "There is a rush, a burry, a pre- occupation which apparently knows no leisure, an increase of aggregate incomes beyond precedent probably in any country, and an absorption in business which leaves little energy or care for political duties." Look to Germany, and we find such an absorption of all social duties into the Bismarkian ratri- archial system. that is threatening to reduce the German workman to a mere machine, and I am sorry to say, on this point, that we have in this country politicians of the stamp of Lord Lytton, who, had they their own way would speedily reduce Englishmen to a state of German serfdom. Turn your attention towards Russia, and what do you see? A mighty empira struggling, as it were, blindfolded, towards civil and religious freedom, yet gradually building up a home trade. But at what expense? Where is the freedom of the workman? A mere will-o'- the-wisp leading in too rainy cases from the banks of the Neva to Siberia—l should like to give my fellow townsmen a short sketch of this fiendish system, reigned over by one of England's daughters, when convenient to you. Return- ing to the continent, what do we see in France and 8,1- glum? In the latter there seems to be no difference between the steam engine and the human being. You start the two together, and the wear and tear in the unequal contest is simply made up by the fecundity of the human machine, leaving the capitalist master of the situation. In France, just now, the potentiality of all that is desirable and attain- able, seems to be directed towards a mistaken scheme for a "spirited foreign policy" the outcome of which will be, the continued false position, so unnatural to a light-hearted Frenchman. Before leaving the continent, allow me to give an extract , from the report of the Factory Inspectors for 1882 : 'Everywhere the lame story, women and children replacine. , the men of the family in f tctories ; long hours and such starvation wages that, as a last chance, parents are forced into exploiting their own children ; everywhere immerality, disease, and death for the workers." The law which pro- hibits women from working in factories within three weeks of confinement, is daily infringed, " These wo- men," the Inspector s " try to get back to work as soon after their confinement as pos- sible in order to lessen the loss of wages, and also from fear that if they are absent from the factory too long their places will be lost." If this state of things is to continue, despair may well fix herself in every man's brain. But will it continue? No ; there is a truthful spirit abroad just , now which points to a kindred spirit of inquiry. On all hands may be seen admissions as to the inequalities of our un-social laws. Leek over our own land, and what is to be seen? Why incident after incident tending to prove that the system of usury, or in other words, the insatiable grasp- ing after profit is at the bottom of all our misery. You may see neutral editors taking advantage of disunited composi- tors, and docking their wages half a crown per week; em- ployers of disunited and unskilled wiredra eers taking ad- vantage of their workmen's defenceless position to ;educe their already miserable pittance to a mere sum barely suffi- cient to supply prison skilly to their families. It is not enough to make admissions as to our social degradation. To keep pointing to the immense fortunes made by individuals achieves no good. We must, in the , words of Emerson, understand that "Every great and corn- mending movement in the annals of the world, is the triumph of enthusiasm." What interest does the workman of to-day take in his labour? None whatever; pride in it is all gone. He feels that the more work he does and the greater the excuee for his employer to reduce his wages; that "piece work " is simply a test as to his physical endurance; that once accurately gaueed. his maximum wage is soon determined. The weakly and in- capable workman is unequal to the contest, and the Dar- winian theory seizes him in its clutches. Now the question is, what is the remedy for all these evils? Will the inquiry to which I have pointed give us the answer? Not unless , there is united action on the part of workmen. We have just seen the Trades Congress meet and separate. Warring- ton never takes any part in this workman's Parliament. , Will she act the same in the forthcoming "Industrial Inquiry?" I hops not. It is a question of great import- ance. How to make the world's industry steady is a big , subject. We seem to have periodical depressions in trade which rob the workman of all possibility of laying by for a , rainy day. When particular trades are brisk freak capital and more lends are attracted, and each renewed depression becomes more acute. What is required is that labour shall have an active interest and profit above and beyond the mere acquirement of a pittance upon which to live. In your hands lie the means! Work but with unity! Hold ye but firm together, Then ye will soon be free. In concluding I would suggest to Trade Unionists the subject of federation initiated by the Trades Councils of the king- dom as a means towards solving the greatest question of the day—the distribution of profits. September 15, 1584.
HENRY WHITHAM.
GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.

% The first meeting of the newly-formed School Board for Great Sankey was held in the School-room, near Sankey station, on Thursday afternoon. There were present at the meeting Messrs James Turner, W D Houghton, J C Ridg- way, John Cook, W B Kerfoot, and 8 Sutton (clerk pro tens). THE ELECTION OF CHAIRM&N.—MT SUTTON said the first business of the Board would be the appointment of a chair- man for the ensuing year.—Mr Houghton said that inas- much as they were now a legally constituted School Board for Great Sankey, he had very much pleasure in proposing that Mr Ridgway be chairman of the Board. Mr Ridgway had been more or less occupied with the late school management and would therefore necessarily more Cr less acquainted with the policy that had actuated that body up to the present, and as to how far that policy had, been conducive to the success or otherwise of the schools) Mr Ridgway was also, as they knew, a business man well known in that township; a large ratepayer and employer of labour, and besides that, a resi- dent there. He thought Mr Rdgway was in every way fitted to occupy the position of chairman, and that he would act with credit to himself and to the satisfaction not only of the members of the Board, but to the ratepayers as a whole. —Mr KERFO9T said it was unfortunate that they should have a difference of opinion, but he thought they had the most suit able per- son for the post of chairman in Mr Turner, whom he would propose. He found that Mr Turner had a very great know- ledge of the Education Act, which would be of advantage to the Bna'd. Besides, he thought they ought to have a man of very genial temper as chairman, and this quality he thought would be found in Mr Turner. As to the residence in the neighbourhood, he thought Mr Turner possessed that advantage also.—Mr COOK seconded the proposal that Mr Turner be chairman.—Mr HOUGHTON said with regard to the reasons put forward by Mr Kerfoot, he did not think there could be anything slid against Mr Ridgway on the score of geniality; and with regard to knowledge of the Education Act, he presumed they would be more or less de- pendent on their legally appointedclerk. He presumed that the position of Mr Turner was such that he might be re- moved from the district in six or twelve months, so that they could not look upon him as a permanent resident. Mr Ridgway was a permanent resident, a property holder, an employer of labour, and a large payer of taxes.—There being no seconder to Mr Houghton's proposal, Mr SUTTON said it fell through as a, matter of course.—Mr RIDGWAY thanked Mr Houghton for kindly proposing him as chairman. If he had met with the support of the other members he should have been glad to accept the post, but he could not accept any post that was not unanimously, or pretty nearly unanimously, given. He must say that he took exception to one remark by Mr Kerfoot, which was that he was not of a genial disposition. He could only say this, that while he was in Sankey he would try to behave like a gentleman-Mr Turner was then declared elected, and took the chair.—Mr COOK then proposed that Mr Kerfoot be elected vice-chairman, and this proposition having been seconded by the Chairman, it was carried. MISCELLANEOUS BUSINESS.—It was agreed, on the motion of Mr HOUGHTON, seconded by Mr RIDGWAY, that the quorum of members should be three. It was further agreed, on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr Com, that the ordinary meetings of the Board be held in the School on the first Tuesday of every month at half-past two o'clock in the afternoon.

THE POSITION OF THE BOARD.—Mr SUTTON mentioned that as instructed at an informal meeting of the Board he had written to the managers of the schools asking them to con- tinue the management of the schools until the Board c uld legally assume the jurisdiction of the district. He wrote to the Rev E 8 Jackson, who replied that the managers had been informed by the Education Department that they would receive no grant after the beginning of May. The managers therefore declined to be responsible for the schools any longer. He (Mr Sutton) had written to the Education Department asking their opinion as to what action should be taken with regard to the management of the schools until the Board could make their own arrangements. To this letter he had received no reply. He had also received a letter from Mr Jeans stating that there was no law to com- pel the managers to conduct the schools at a loss any longer. A further communication was read from the Rev E S Jack- son offering the use of the schools and furniture to the Board for £2O a year.—After some conversation it was agreed to ask the managers to meet the members of the Board next Thursday to endeavour to make satisfactory arrangements.

--- APPOINTMENT OF CLERK AND TREASURER.—There were five applications for the clerkship of the Board, and these leaving been considered, it was ultimately agreed, on the motion of Mr Houghton, seconded by Mr Ridgway, that Mr S Sutton be appointed clerk. The salary was fixed at £2O per annum.—Mr Dun, of Parr's Bank, Warrington, was ap- pointed treasurer to the Board.—Applications for posts of schoolmaster and attendance officer were left over for future consideration, and the clerk having been instructed to pur- chase the necessary books, &c., the meeting adjourned till , next Thursday.

CARDINAL MANNING AT ST. lIELENS. The visit of his Eminence, Cardinal Manning, to St Helens during the present week, has been an event of all- absorbing interest to the Catholic community, and one claiming much attention from the inhabitants of the town in general. The primary object of his visit has been the opening of the Providence Hospital—an institution which is destined to be of considerable advantage and benefit to the working-classes of the town. Hitherto the only public hospital in the neighbourhood has been the Cottage Hospi- tal at Peasley.cross, admission to which has necessitated the payment of a small sum per week on behalf of the patients. A good and excellent work has been accomplished at that institution, but the establishment of a much more com- modious and centrally situated hospital has been a long-felt want. As wiil be seen from the statement which appears below, the Sisters connected with the Catholic Church of the Holy Cross have conducted an hospital on a small scale in a house in George-street for the past eigtleen months; but they have recently secured the large building known as Hardshaw Hall, in Hardshaw-fields ; and in future it will he used as a free hospital for all parties irrespective of religious creeds or religious opinions; and the institution was publicly opened under happy and encouraging circum- stances on Monday afternoon. In view of the opening of the building which received the name of the " Providence Hospital." the Sisters of the Holy Cross Hospital drew up the following ienort "Toe sisters of the Free Hospital, in presenting the first re- port of the hospital, have the great pleasure of being able to state that it is in a satisfactory condition. Begun in 1882, in a sin ill house in George-street, it, has now been re- moved to Hardshave Hall, which his been kindly let to the Sis'ers by Mrs Wahneeley for this puepose, on a lease for , 999 years. During the eighteen months of its existence I passed in George-street, seventy-one pitients have been re- ceived. The need of a free hospital in St. Helens is ex- treme. We hardly think that any town of equal extent and population in England is without one. That admirable in- stitution, the Cottage Hospital at Peasley Cross, is open for those who subscribe to its funds, or who pay a weekly sum. The Free Hospital is open to all corners who have the claim which poverty and sickness give. No distinction is made as regards religion, all are equally welcome. It is supported entirely by charity, and the sisters gratefully acknowledge the hind help they have already received. They are cond- dent that this help will not fail them in the future, and that the people of St. Helens will not be backward in giving their aid to the work. They are a people free from unworthy prejudice, and as they know the hospital is intended for all, I they will all sympathise with its prosperity. Many addi- tions have to be made to Hardshaw Hall, the new wards have to be supplied with beds and other furniture. For all this, and for the necessary support for the hospital, the sisters look to charitable contributions: and trusting in the blessing of that Divine Providence which has not failed them since the beginning, they are confident that this aid will be forthcoming. Besides aid in money, the Sisters will be thankful for articles of furniture, new or old clothing of any kind (patients leaving the hospital are often insuffi- ciently clad), old linen is most valuable, flowers, pictures, books, newspapers, in short anything and everything can be turned to good account." The conditions of admission to the hospital were stated as follows :-1. Admission to the hospital is perfectly free. 2. No distinction is made as regards religion. 3. No case of sickness is admitted or discharged without a medical certificate. 4. Accidents admitted at all times. 5. No case of contagious or infectious disease is admitted. G. Patients must consent to observe the printed regulations of the hos- ' pital. Under the heading of "Regulations of the hospital." the following appeared at the end of the report :-1. No patient is received without a medical certificate, and no pa- tient is discharged without the order of his or her medical man, and when so discharged must leave at once. 2. Strict attention must be paid to the orders of the doctors. 3. No patient can go out of his or her ward without leave of the sister in charge. 4. No smoking is allowed, and no pipes or tobacco of any kind may be kept in the wards. 5. No pa- tients may have any food, drink, or medicine in his or her private keeping. 6. Silence must be kept at night from 9 a.m. to 8 a.m. in order not to disturb the other patients. 7. The friends of patients must undertake their washing. 8. Visitors can only be allowed at stated times, viz, on week days from 2 p.m. to 4 pm. On Sun- days from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. From 4-30 p.m. till 6 p.m. The medical gentlemen of the town have displayed a kindly help and sympathy in support of the public institution, and the following have willingly promised to attend and render any service or assistance that might be required :—Dr Twyford, Dr Jamison, Dr Ricketts, Dr Bellew, Dr Donnel- lan, Dr McNicoll, Dr Casey, Dr Reid, Dr Garton, DriFraser, Dr Hikernan, Dr Marsh, Dr Gaskell, and. Dr Mason. Special sermons were preached in Holy Cross Church on Sunday in aid of the funds of the new institution. At high mass in the forenooon it had been announced that the preacher would be the Rev Father Clare, but that rev gen- tleman being unable to attend the sermon was preached by the Rev Father Dignam. In the afternoon his Eminence Cardinal Manning attended a meeting of the scholars and gave them a touching address; while in the evening he preached in the Church to a crowded, but nevertheless, thoroughly attentive and patient congregation. He took for his text ltomans viii., 22 : " For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now." His Eminence, after referring to the benefi- cence of God in sending His only Son into the world to share in its sorrow and misery, remarked that even as it was more blessed to give than to receive, he asked them to, give their aid on behalf of the free hospital which was to be opened on the following day in St Helens. The revered mother to whose care the institution would be entrusted had gained her experience in the hospitals in the Crimean war—that most terrible time, when every form of death and suffering existed in a degree which perhaps the 'history of no country could parallel. He knew of no town with a population equal to that et St Helens without a pub- lic and free hospital. The time had new come when such an institution should be established in the town. When he considered the large population of St Helens and the per- nicious and dangerous nature of its works he could hardly ' conceive that such a place could be exempt from a great multitude of bodily evils which required constant, vigilant, and sympathetic help. He was thankful to know that the hospital would be absolutely free to all—not a penny would be required for any patient for admission. Moreover, this lhospital had two foundations—it was founded on human suffering and Christian sympathy. He believed that wheresoever there was great need the Father of all would never fail to supply it. He very heartily commended the institution to their charity. The collections for the day amounted to £95.

div.head: T. HELENS AMAIN SPORE'S.
div.p: T. HELENS AMAIN SPORE'S.

The St Helens autumn athletic festival was held on Satur- day, in the cricket field, Denton's Green-lane, St Helens. The weather was excellent, and the sports opened under- very favourable conditions. Over 1,500 people assembled on the ground, a large number coming from Liverpool and other district towns. The St Helens people did not turn out in force owing, no doubt, to the Liberal demonstration held that day in the town, which proved a greater attraction than the sports. The management of the events was very satis- factory, the times on the programme for each event being adhered to with considerable accuracy. The starting was also very good, there being, indeed, little cause for grum- bling throughout the whole day. In the mile fist race handi- cap there were 34 entries, but only 25 of these turned up at the starting point. Among those who it was expected would compete were W G George and W Snook, of the Moseley Harriers, but neither of these well-known athletes made • their appearance in this race. Nevertheless, a good field turned out, the event ultimately being won in splendid style by T Crellin, of Liverpool. H Bate, of the Birchtield Harriers, made a good second, the latter keeping a lead of three or four yards until about one hundred yards of the winning point, when Crellin quickly overhauled him win- ning by about two yards. In the Two Mile Bicycle Handi- cap W N Armstrong, Wirral, proved the victor in a field seven in number. The race was a good one, being rue in very fair time, 7 mine 23 2-5 secs. Armstrong took the lead early in the race, and kept it all through, notwithstand- ing the efforts of A M Dutton, of Tranmere, who finally came in second, to dislodge hint. Considerable dissatisfac- tion was expressed at the running in the final heat of the Quarter-mile Flat Race Handicap, which was won at a very slow pace by J Danville, of Warrington. The second man, T Laws, of Widnes, appeared to make little effort to gain the prize, and a number of the spectators evidently looked upon it as a prearranged affair. The following are the reedits:—
300 Yards Boys' Race (under 15).-1, F Marsh, Hay- dock; 2, W Cooper, Earlestown; 3, T Purcell, Liverpool. Time 32 sees.
220 Yards Maiden Race Handicap.-I,W Preseot,Earles- town ; 2. H Dodd, Higher Tranmere; 3, H Rye, Wavertree. Time 24 2.5 secs.
Half-mile Flat Race Handicap —l, T Laws, Widnes; 2, C E Ridehalgh, Liverpool; 3, J Mitchell, Liverpool. Won by three yards; one yard between second and third. Time 1 min 59 secs.
Mile Bicycle Handicap.-1, AM Dutton, Birkenhead; 2, W Armstrong, Wirral; 3, J Jackson, Altrincham. Won by five yards; same distance between second and third. Time 3 min 28 1-5 am.

Mile Flat Race Handicap.-1, T Crellin, Liverpool; 2, H Bate, Birchfield Harriers ;3, W Kelly, Widnes. Won by two yards. Time 4 min 243 i secs. 100 Yards Flat Race Handicap.-1, J Hartley, St. Helens; 2, J Hobbins, Prescot ; 3, H W Barlow, Liverpool. Time 94-5 secs.
Quarter-mile Flat Rue ilaculicap.-1, J Danville, War- rington; 2, T Laws, Widnes; 3, J Kean, Liverpool. Time 544-5 secs.
Two Miles Bicycle Handicap.-1, W N Armstrong, Wir- ral ; 2, A IV Dutton, Tranmere; 3, P E Ross, Birkenhead. Time 7 min 23 2-5 secs.

IRLAH FLOWER Ssow.—The annual flower show was held in a field, near the church, on Saturday afternoon. The weather was favourable, and in consequence there was a large gathering. The display of flowers and vegetables was large and beautiful. The only drawback was in the show of fruit, which was but secondary. A new feature was the ex- hibition of samples of fresh made butter. The number of exhibits was considerably above that of last year. The competitors were confined to Irlam and Cadishead, and the immediate neighhourhood. The competition in each class was keen. The judges were—Mr J Bailey, of Eccles, Mr Northwood, of Swinton, Mr Eckersley, of Little Hutton; and for butter Mr Alderman Nuttall, of Pendleton. A large number of prizes was awarded for first-class flowers and vegetables. The Cadishead brass band discoursed suit- able selections of music on the green. SOUTHWORTH WITH CROFT SCHOOL BOARD• - The monthly meeting of this Boa-d was held at the Board school on Tuesday evening. Present—the Rev T P Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs Lewis Birchall, Richard Turner, and Alfred Dixon (attendance officer). The Atten- dance Officer submitted his report which stated that he had visited the various schools in the Board:s district during the I past month, when he found that the total number of chil- dren on the books was 208. The average attendance at the Board school for the past month was 118. He had warned 11 parents during the month, and two employers, for em- ploying children without the necessary certificates. The report was adopted, and instructions were given respecting the various cases. It was resolved that two new desks be Purchased, and that the sum of £3 be allowed for providing far the children's treat as in past years.

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.

Mr W Woodall, M.P., is lying ill at his residence at Burs- lem with symptoms of typhoid fever. Fire broke out on Friday morning in the lamproota at Alma Colliery, Claycross. Much damage was done, and the colliers are all laid idle. By a collision between goods trains on the Great Western Railway, at Highbridge, on Friday morning, a guard named Perkins was seriously injured. It has been decided to refer the wages dispute in the North of England iron dispute to the arbitration of Dr. Spence Watson, of Newcastle. Mr. Sexton having decided to seek the suffrages of another constituency at the general election, the Nationalist midi- date for Sligo will be Mr. Clancy, licensed victualler, of Dublin.
On Friday afternoon Joseph Meir Watkin, brick and tile manufacturer, carrying on a large business in Burelem, was arrested at Trentham Railway Station on charges of forgery and fraud.

I Ti ROTHERHAM ACCIDENT.—At Rotherham, on Friday evening, a coroner's jury returned an open verdict in the case of the three men who were killed at Phcenix Bessemer Works on the 10th inst by the capsizing of a ladle containing over 70 tons of molten metal. RETURN OF TRoOPS FROM EGYPT.—Last evening a large party of the Chatham division of Royal Marines who have been serving in the boudan arrived at Chatham. The men have been invalided home, and they have suffered so much from the effects of the climate that the majority will have to be discharged as being unfit for further service. TRAGIC SUICIDE OF A GERMAN SOLDIER —On Friday morning, a young German went up to a policeman in Bic- ; mineham, and asked the way to the German consul. The policeman accompanied him, when he suddenly pulled out a bottle of prussic acid, broke it with his teeth and steal- lowed the contents dying immediately. A portion of the bottle was found in his throat. He had received orders to rejoin his regiment in Germany.

div.head: TEIE FIRING ON THE ZEPHYR.
div.p: TEIE FIRING ON THE ZEPHYR.

TIENTSIN, FRIDAY—The Chinese yesterday made an apology to Sir Harry Parkes, British Minister at Pekin, for the action of the Kinpai forts in tiring on her ; Majesty's gunboat Zephyr. FURTHER MESSAGES FROM GENERAL GORDON. CAIRO, FRIbAY.—Two more telegrams have been received from General Gordon. He complains bitterly of the slackness of the relief expedition, and says the number of rebels round Kh irtoum is increasing. Colonel Wilson has left Cairo to join Colonel Stewart.

Orders were received at Aldershot, on Friday, for 200 men of the Army Hospital Corps to proceed to Egypt. A detach- ment of the Commissariat Corps are ordered to hold them- selves in readiness for embarkation. REPORTED CAPTURE AND DESTRUCTION OF BERBER.

CAIRO. FRIDAY.—The Mudirof Dongola wires that a messenger from Berber has arrived at Dongola, who reports that Colonel Stewart has captured and burnt Berber. This accords with the plan sketched out in Gordon's letter. The Mudir, encouraged, perhaps, by the success which seems to attend the aggressive movements in the south, offers to undertake the task of relieving Gordon on condition that 5,000 troops are sent to assist him the enterprise. Colonels Bedford and Henderson have proceeded for Wady Haifa. Lord Wolseley has been inspecting the troops every day since his arrival. He expresses the greatest satisfaction with their appearance and general condition. CAIRO, FRIDAY EVRNING.—Several regiments leave for the Upper Nile next week. Lord Wolseley remains here for the present. _

div.head: CHOLERA.
div.p: THE CHOLERA.
NAPLES, FRIDAY Monwaro.—During the 24 hours ended at eight o'clock this morning, 383 fresh oasis of cholera and 123 deaths were recorded.
ROME, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The public health here is excellent, but in the provinces a number of deaths from cholera have been reported.

THE EISTEDDFOD.—The annual Welsh musical festival began on Monday at Liverpool. In the afternoon the first of the series of gatherings organised by the Cymmrodion Society was held at the Town Hall. and in the evening there was a concert in the pavilion erected at the Havinar- ket. At the former, an address on the relation of Wales to England was delivered by Mr Henry Richard, M P, who said he believed that the future relations between England and Wales would grow closer and closer day by day. They did. not want Wales as a nation to be absorbed into England, 80 that their habits and characteristics would disappear. He I Commented upon the fact that in the Princip ility the Welsh language was more generally spoken than it was in the time of Henry VIII. He complained of the policy which had been pursued for nearly three centuries by English states- men of seeking the extinction of the Welsh language, just as Russia aimed at extinguishing that of Poland. A better feeling, he rejoiced to say, had sprung up. Englishmen must take Welshmen as they found them. and Welshmen must discard prejudices, jealousies, and suspicions, for which there was no justification. On Tuesday the first meet- ing in thePavillion, presided over by the Mayor of Liverpool, was very largely attended, especialy during the choral com- petition between choirs from Liverpool, Manchester, Owes" try, and Penrhyn. The last-named choir carried off the prize for choral singing. A conference of bards was au- thorised to decids between the claims of Aberdare and Car- narvon as the place of meeting next year. The feature on Wednesday was a choral competition for which five Tonic Sol-fa choirs entered. The Burslern choir won the prize. The president for the day was Major Cornwallis West, who delivered an address on the fine arts in connection with the Eisteddfod. A paper on voice-training in children was read by Mr Curwen, of the Tonic Sol-fa College. Oa Thursday Sir Watkin Wynn, M.P., who had been announced to pre- side, was unable owing to illness, to take any part in the proceedings. In his absence the chair was taken by Mr. Osborne Morgan, M.P., who delivered an address on the importance of keeping up the knowledge of the Welsh lan- guage and the advantages promoted by these national festi- vals. Ire contended that the Welsh language was still a living power, and Opt the Eisteddfodd was a great educa- tor. The meeting was again very largely attended. During the afternoon the Rev. Evan Rees, of Carnarvou Univer- sity College, was installed in the birdie chair according to the "ancient rites of the Bards of the Isle of Britain." It was decided to hold the next National Eisteddfod at Aber- dare. In the evening there was a crowded assemblage to hear the performance of the new sacred cantata, " Nebu- chadnezz tr," composed expressly for the occasion by Dr. Joseph Parry.

Milling Machi- nery generally, the equipment of Flour Mills, and general En- gineering and Millwright work. The acquisition of the War- rington Works, together with the above, will place the Firm on a footing equal to any in the United Kingdom, as Manufac- turers of every branch of Engineering and Millwright Work, Machinery, Boilers, Engines, Hoists, and Warehouse Machi- nery. , Flour Mill Machinery, on the new Automatic Roller Mill or gradual reduction principle, is an invention of comparatively recent date, but it is based on scientific principles, now well understood and appreciated. Since its invention many of the ' largest millers in America and Europe have adopted it, to the entire exclusion of the old Millstones. It has consequently opened out a vast field of highly profitable industry. 1 The chief merits of the new process are (1) superior neanufac- ' tyre, and consequently enhanced value of flour, (2) reduced ,cost of manufacture. and (3) it commands a better market and higher prices than flour made on the old principle. Since its original invention it has undergone many improve- ments, use and experience having brought out imperfections which have since been remedied, so that now the machinery has attained to a maximum state of perfection. The natural result produced in the system of milling on the European and American Continents has been and is now the importation into this country of large quantities of foreign 'flour of superior quality to home made, and this has compelled the millers of the 1:f K. to recognise that if they are to com- pete with foreign flour manufactured on the new system, they must st: once remodel their mills and adopt the new system To meet the exigencies of the times and the altered circum- stances of the trade, and to be able to compete succesifully with foreign importations, many of the largest British Millers have already dete mined to remodel their Mills at once. There are in the United Kingdom and Ireland about 11,000 Mills. and of these about 200 have already been altered or are now in course of reconstruction upon the new Ironer principle Con- tracts for a large number of Mills ( which rank among the largest in the United Kingdom) have been executed by Messrs. John Feichter and Sons, on th&r " Fir" Automatic Roller Mill System and with the best results, and it is obvious that the adoption of the Roller System by the remaining Mills in the United Kingdom is only a question of time with the Millers. The above remarks apply still, to alarge extent, to the Conti- nental Mills,of which thee are a large number. The Directors therefore anticipate that the acknowledged superiority of Fiechter's Automatic Holler Mill System will ensure for the Company a very large share of the work of reconstructing and furnishing the mills in the Un ted Kingdom and the Conti- nent. In support of this view Messrs Pechter and Bons have recently been invited to tender for contracts representing in the aggregate about £19,0' 0. The work of, remodelling the old mills will take some years to accomplah, and when this has been done there will necessavily arise a constant and con- tinuous demand tor renewals and repiirs. The new Boller System possesses the important advantage that millers may adopt it, either altogether or partially, arid in the latter case can be worked in combination with the Old ' Mill Stones, thus attaining results not now possible by the old Mill System. Messrs. John Fiechter and Bone Machinery and al Li Ap. paratus have been exhibited at many Exhibitions of Milling Machinery in the United Kingdom, Amer ea, aid France, and their simplicity anil durability, combined with moderate cost, han secured for them marked approval. (From the Runcorn Guardian.) • PRESENTATION TO s• PROFESSOR " ELETCHER AT RUNCORN. ri Professor " Fletcher, who for several years has carried on business in Ellesmere-street Ruucorn, as an herbalist. was on Wednesday night, August 13th, 1884, made the recipient of a gratifying testimonial from a number of per,ons, who state they have received undoubted be efit at his hands. Tots prac- tical testimony of their gratitude arose entirely amongst a number of working people by whom Mr Fletcher has been con- sulted, and who have been under his treatment for various dis- eases. The subscription list contains the names of a large num- ber of peopie, who are unanimous in their feeling of gratitude. The present was a gold watch and a guard with appendage, and the presentation took place at a public meeting on Wed- nesday night. in Bethesda Schoolroons. The chair was occupied by the Rev W Vause, who was supported by Messrs J Woods, Parker, J Fairless, Jones, J Rushton, Mrs Rushton. while there were p, esent, other members of the committee. The at- tendance was very goad, and the proceedings were of a harmo- nious description. The CHAIRMAN. in opening the meeting, said they had met to express their grateful feelings towards Air Fletcher. (Ap- plause.) It was not his business to, explain tlie full mean- ing of the prestntation, because most of them were ac- quainted with it. and those who were not aware of it would be told as the mestiog progressed He (the chairman) was glad to be present to Join in that expression of grati- tude, because M . Fletcher was a member of the church with which be stood con- ected. When he was asked to occupy that position he remembered that Mr. Fletcher was a member of his churchi—a respected member, and one of whom he had never heard a really adverse word spoken, and one whose moral and religious character stood high—and under circumstances like these, he found it was not in his power to refuse to preside over that meeting. He was glad that a number of Ru corn people had found cause in their I hearts to present a member of his church with a prtictical I proof of their feellnge towards him. He (the chairman) was known in Runcorn as a pretty warm advocate on the temper- ance platform. There were various methods of working in the tempesance cause, and he thought Mr. Fletcher was doing as much for temperance as any other man in Runcorn. (Ap- plause.) There had been plenty of charges flung at temperance advocates, and some of them had had truth behind them. One of the charges that used to be made was to the effect that they could not expect men to give up frequenting the public-houses when they had no drink of any kind to take the plane of intoxicating liquor. Coffee-houses had been established to meet the charge, and he believed much good had been done by their operation. Mr. Pleb:ll3er had. hors ever. adopted another method, for, as they knew, he WAS every Saturday night in the Market-place disp-sing of a drink that was a soling at a reason- aisle charge There was now no necessity for people to go to the public house, because Mr. Fletcher had provided a substi- tute which was greatly to their advantage. After some further words the Chairman called upon Mr. J. WOODS, who testified in high terms of praise to the real good whim Mr. Fletcher had been the means of doing in Runcorn. He mentioned several instances which had come under his own notice of Mr Fletcher's kindness and considera- tion to those about him, and held up his life scone to be emu- lated by all. The testimonial of that evening was but a feeble expression of the regard of many people, and they trusted that the biessinz of God woul I rest upon all his labours, and that he would be spared a long time to live and do good amongst them. (applause). Mrs. RIPETON followed with a short speech, 'couched in kindly and expressive language, which was Warmly ap• plauded. Mr JONES and Mr. J FAIRLESSIoaISO addressed the audience. and alludet to Mr. Fletcher's sincerity and upright course of life since he had lived in Runcorn. They also referred to cases where his medical treatment had wrought much good, and they exprersed a hope that he would long be spared to live in the town. Mr. PARKER then made the presentation. He said the testimonial had been made spontaneously end with a feeling of heartfelt gratitude towards one who had done good in the town. (applause.) The watch was inscribed as follows : it Presented to Professor Fletcher, by many of his patients, sea token of their great esteem. May he long live to do good In Runcorn." On rising to acknowledge the presentation, Mr. FLETCHER was received with much cordiality. He could assure them that he felt great pleasure in meeting so Many whose faces were familiar to him. He had had many presentations. Ho had received a present from the hands of Her lisjesty, while he had several medals from various societies, but he had never had one like that he had just received from the Runcorn people. (Applause.) It was one that be should always look upon with great interest, especially when he remembered from whom it had come. Mr. Fletcher then alluded in kindly terms to those who had subscribed to the tokora, and with much feeling observed that he never sent out a drop of medi- cine without both he and his wife praying that God's blessing might rest upon it. (Applause ) Having again thanked the audience for their kindness, Mr. Fletcher concluded by express- ing a hope that he might be spared, guided by Providence, to do good. (Applause.) During the evening several recitations and songs were given by Mr and Mrs. Rushton and Mr and Mrs. Bates.

THE PRESIDENTIAL CONTEST.—CHARGES AGAINST MR. BLAINE. NEW Yang, MONDAY.—A great sensation has been caused here by the publication this morning of a series of letters written by Mr. Blaine betweenlB69 and 18S to Mr. Fisher, the railway contractor, for whom Mr. BlaMe acted as bond- seller agent while he was also Speaker of Congress. The letters are similar to those published eight years ago, called the Mulligae Letters, and are held to conErm the worst re- velations those contained. They are published for the pur- pose of showing that Mr. Blaine used his official position for purposes of private gain, that he told'falsehoods about his operations upon the rime of Congress, and that be made large amounts of money through his behaviour. It is be- lieved that the letters will destroy completely what little chance Mr. Blaine had of election to the Presidentship.— Daily Ylews. THE CROATIAN ELECTION.—FATAL DISTURBANCES.
